text: The Ganges River, also called Ganga, is a river located in northern India that flows toward the border with Bangladesh. It is the longest river in India and flows for around 1,569 miles (2,525 km) from the Himalayan Mountains to the Bay of Bengal. The river has the second greatest water discharge in the world, and its basin is the most heavily populated in the world with over 400 million people living in it.    The Ganges River is extremely important to the people of India as most of the people living on its banks use it for daily needs such as bathing and fishing. It is also significant to Hindus, as they consider it their most sacred river.      The Course of the Ganges River    The headwaters of the Ganges River begin high in the Himalayan Mountains where the Bhagirathi River flows out of the Gangotri Glacier in India's Uttarakhand state. The glacier sits at an elevation of 12,769 feet (3,892 m). The Ganges River proper begins farther downstream where the Bhagirathi and Alaknanda rivers join. As the Ganges flows out of the Himalayas, it creates a narrow, rugged canyon.     North Indian River Plain    The Ganges River emerges from the Himalayas at the town of Rishikesh where it begins to flow onto the Indo-Gangetic Plain. This area, also called the North Indian River Plain, is a very large, relatively flat, fertile plain that makes up most of the northern and eastern parts of India as well as parts of Pakistan, Nepal, and Bangladesh. In addition to entering the Indo-Gangetic Plain in this area, part of the Ganges River is also diverted toward the Ganges Canal for irrigation in the Uttar Pradesh state.     Changes Direction    As the Ganges River then flows farther downstream, it changes its direction several times and is joined by many other tributary rivers such as the Ramganga, Tamsa, and Gandaki Rivers, to name a few. There are also several cities and towns that the Ganges River passes through on its way downstream. Some of these include Chunar, Kolkata, Mirzapur, and Varanasi. Many Hindus visit the Ganges River in Varanasi as that city is considered the holiest of cities. As such, the city's culture is also closely tied into the river as it is the most sacred river in Hinduism.     Flows Into Bay of Bengal    Once the Ganges River flows out of India and into Bangladesh, its main branch is known as the Padma River. The Padma River is joined downstream by large rivers like the Jamuna and Meghna rivers. After joining the Meghna, it takes on that name before flowing into the Bay of Bengal. Before entering the Bay of Bengal however, the river creates the world's largest delta, Ganges Delta. This region is a highly fertile sediment-laden area that covers 23,000 square miles (59,000 sq km).       Complex Hydrology    It should be noted that the course of the Ganges River described in the above paragraphs is a general description of the river's route from its source where the Bhagirathi and Alaknanda rivers join to its outlet at the Bay of Bengal. The Ganges has very complicated hydrology, and there are several different descriptions of its overall length and the size of its drainage basin based on what tributary rivers are included. The most widely accepted length of the Ganges River is 1,569 miles (2,525 km), and its drainage basin is estimated to be about 416,990 square miles (1,080,000 sq km).      The Population of the Ganges River    The Ganges River basin has been inhabited by humans since ancient times. The first people in the region were of the Harappan civilization. They moved into the Ganges River basin from the Indus River basin around the 2nd millennium BCE. Later, the Gangetic Plain became the center of the Maurya Empire and then the Mughal Empire. The first European to discuss the Ganges River was Megasthenes in his work Indica.     Source of Life    In modern times, the Ganges River has become a source of life for the nearly 400 million people living in its basin. They rely on the river for their daily needs such as drinking water supplies and food and for irrigation and manufacturing. Today, the Ganges River basin is the most populated river basin in the world. It has a population density of about 1,000 people per square mile (390 per sq km).      The Significance of the Ganges River    Aside from providing drinking water and irrigating fields, the Ganges River is extremely important to India's Hindu population for religious reasons as well. The Ganges River is considered their most sacred river, and it is worshiped as the goddess Ganga Ma or "Mother Ganges."     According to the Myth of the Ganges, the goddess Ganga descended from heaven to dwell in the waters of the Ganges River to protect, purify and bring to heaven those who touch it. Devout Hindus visit the river daily to offer flowers and food to Ganga. They also drink the water and bathe in the river to cleanse and purify their sins.     'Pitriloka,' the World of the Ancestors    Hindus believe that upon death the waters of the Ganges River are needed to reach the World of the Ancestors, Pitriloka. As a result, Hindus bring their dead to the river for cremation along its banks and afterward their ashes are spread in the river. In some cases, corpses are also thrown into the river. The city of Varanasi is the holiest of cities along the Ganges River and many Hindus travel there to place ashes of their dead in the river.    Along with daily baths in the Ganges River and offerings to the goddess Ganga, there are large religious festivals that occur in the river throughout the year where millions of people travel to the river to bathe so that they can be purified of their sins.      Pollution of the Ganges River    Despite the religious significance and daily importance of the Ganges River for the people of India, it is one of the most polluted rivers in the world. Pollution of the Ganges is caused by both human and industrial waste due to India's rapid growth as well as religious events. India currently has a population of over 1 billion people, and 400 million of them live in the Ganges River basin. As a result, much of their waste, including raw sewage, is dumped into the river. Also, many people bathe and use the river to clean their laundry. Fecal coliform bacteria levels near Varanasi are at least 3,000 times higher than what is established by the World Health Organization as safe (Hammer, 2007).     Little Regulation    Industrial practices in India also have little regulation and as the population grows these industries do as well. There are many tanneries, chemical plants, textile mills, distilleries and slaughterhouses along the river and many of them dump their untreated and often toxic waste into the river. The water of the Ganges has been tested to contain high levels of things like chromium sulfate, arsenic, cadmium, mercury and sulfuric acid (Hammer, 2007).    In addition to human and industrial waste, some religious activities also increase the pollution of the Ganges. For example, Hindus believe that they must take offerings of food and other items to Ganga and as a result, these items are thrown into the river on a regular basis and more so during religious events. Human remains are also often placed into the river.     Ganga Action Plan    In the late 1980s, India's prime minister, Rajiv Gandhi began the Ganga Action Plan (GAP) to clean up the Ganges River. The plan shut down many highly polluting industrial plants along the river and allotted funding for the construction of wastewater treatment facilities, but its efforts have fallen short as the plants are not large enough to handle the waste coming from such a large population (Hammer, 2007). Many of the polluting industrial plants are also continuing to dump their hazardous waste into the river.    Despite this pollution, however, the Ganges River remains important to the Indian people as well as different species of plants and animals such as the Ganges River dolphin, a very rare species of freshwater dolphin that is native only to that area. To learn more about the Ganges River, read "A Prayer for the Ganges" from Smithsonian.com.

As a result, Hindus bring their dead to the river for cremation along its banks and afterward their ashes are spread in the river. In some cases, corpses are also thrown into the river. The city of Varanasi is the holiest of cities along the Ganges River and many Hindus travel there to place ashes of their dead in the river.    Along with daily baths in the Ganges River and offerings to the goddess Ganga, there are large religious festivals that occur in the river throughout the year where millions of people travel to the river to bathe so that they can be purified of their sins.      Pollution of the Ganges River    Despite the religious significance and daily importance of the Ganges River for the people of India, it is one of the most polluted rivers in the world. Pollution of the Ganges is caused by both human and industrial waste due to India's rapid growth as well as religious events. India currently has a population of over 1 billion people, and 400 million of them live in the Ganges River basin. As a result, much of their waste, including raw sewage, is dumped into the river. Also, many people bathe and use the river to clean their laundry. Fecal coliform bacteria levels near Varanasi are at least 3,000 times higher than what is established by the World Health Organization as safe (Hammer, 2007).     Little Regulation    Industrial practices in India also have little regulation and as the population grows these industries do as well. There are many tanneries, chemical plants, textile mills, distilleries and slaughterhouses along the river and many of them dump their untreated and often toxic waste into the river. The water of the Ganges has been tested to contain high levels of things like chromium sulfate, arsenic, cadmium, mercury and sulfuric acid (Hammer, 2007).    In addition to human and industrial waste, some religious activities also increase the pollution of the Ganges. For example, Hindus believe that they must take offerings of food and other items to Ganga and as a result, these items are thrown into the river on a regular basis and more so during religious events. Human remains are also often placed into the river.     Ganga Action Plan    In the late 1980s, India's prime minister, Rajiv Gandhi began the Ganga Action Plan (GAP) to clean up the Ganges River. The plan shut down many highly polluting industrial plants along the river and allotted funding for the construction of wastewater treatment facilities, but its efforts have fallen short as the plants are not large enough to handle the waste coming from such a large population (Hammer, 2007). Many of the polluting industrial plants are also continuing to dump their hazardous waste into the river.    Despite this pollution, however, the Ganges River remains important to the Indian people as well as different species of plants and animals such as the Ganges River dolphin, a very rare species of freshwater dolphin that is native only to that area. To learn more about the Ganges River, read "A Prayer for the Ganges" from Smithsonian.com.

text: Article Preview :              ABSTRACT    An assessment of the water quality of Cagayan de Oro Rver was conducted in Uguiaban Bridge in Sitio Balaun, Rafting Site in Barangay Mambauaya, and the New Bridge in Poblacion Area. The assessment of the river was based on water quality indicators (flow rate, pH, temperature, and total coliform), social indicators (anthropogenic activities), and level of environmental awareness. The research design used qualitative and quantitative methods to analyze the data obtained. The findings of the study showed values in water quality testing that were within standards except for total coliform that always showed exceedingly high values. In terms of the total coliform, the water quality is not within Class A standards. The highest coliform values were obtained from the Poblacion Area. However, compared to previous studies, values for total coliform have greatly reduced in all sampled areas but must require some measures to bring back the water quality to Class A. The environmental awareness survey indicated only at moderate level and has some policy implications on the residential, commercial, and industrial activities. Stringent implementation of the environmental laws is highly recommended. Extensive Information Education (IEC) campaign should also be done along with seminars on capacity building. Stringent implementation of barangay ordinances is recommended as well.    Keywords: Environmental awareness, water quality, sustainable intervention    INTRODUCTION    Rivers are among the most important resources that cater to the basic needs ofthe growing populations. However, they also respond to changes with the passing of time and socio-economic development. Lubos (2010) has been a witness to these environmental changes through his studies that showed positive progression in the level of pollution load in Cagayan de Oro River. Zoleta (2012) had the same findings for the same river as indicated by consistently higher coliform values (27,000-566,000 MPN/100 ml) above the standard for Class A waters as stipulated in DAO 34. The higher values were detected in the downstream portion of the river. Survey results on environmental awareness from areas that are situated directly along the riverbank showed moderate awareness only.    Dowell and Wilcock (2008) provided evidence on the effects of different pastoral animals on water quality. He stressed that reduction of water quality tended to have significant effects on the ecosystem of streams, toxicity to aquatic life and loss of habitat due to sedimentation, among others. This contention was inferred from the analysis of 38 studies conducted since 1975. Another study in Australian rivers by Boulton et al. (2010) revealed changes on river flows. text:
Intro Dumping garbage in the river has magnified threat on human health and ecosystem. Drishti Foundation Trust has taken a one-year project for cleaning River Sabarmati (5.665 km). Initial 4 months has been focused on removing solid waste as study found that concentration of antibiotic-resistant E.coli bacteria due to untreated sewage. Due to floating garbage our cleanliness drive didn't last long. Thus, community inclusive awareness sessions started along with tree plantation in river side and through rigorous efforts in 2 months we have cleaned 300 tons of garbage from the river bed and restored 130 bird species in the river belt. Objective of the practice Rivers play a pivotal role in maintaining the livelihood, economy and culture of a particular geographical area. Their significance can be measured by certain ways of utilization like, domestic usage, inland transportation, tourism and agriculture. Sabarmati is one of the primary west flowing rivers of India. It has also a special Gandhian element attached to it. The rising industrialization in Ahmadabad concurrently increased the pollutants levels in the river. A study of physico-chemical and biological characteristics of Sabarmati river in 2016 showed that the pH levels, biological oxygen demand (BOD), dissolved oxygen and total coliform organism levels were considerably high.
Our aims are to make the river free of solid waste and coliform organism. The presence of coliform can cause serious illness and it is evident that potential health hazard since the river water is used for drinking purpose. We are committed to reduce the health hazard in the vicinity. While removing the plastic, metal, construction debris from the river, the project also concentrates on building up a green environment in terms of air quality and preserving animal life by an afforestation drive. The afforestation includes plantation of tree saplings like Banyan, Mango, Peepal etc. the project tries to improve the life of local communities by improving the water quality of a natural resource and also advancing to maintain the regional climate (mass afforestation). Moreover, our objectives transcend into the sphere of infrastructure and awareness. Activities like cleaning the pumping stations, powerhouses are also integral part of Swachh Sabarmati project.
In India, dumping waste in the river is sort of habit which need immediate attention in context to change in the behaviour of the Citizens, which need aggressive awareness campaigning. The Swachh Sabarmati project is intended to mitigate this problem and aligned with Goal 6, 11, 13 and 15 of the Sustainable Development Goal. Partners To implement the agenda of sustainability, need cooperation among government, civil societies, private sectors and other stakeholders to mitigate the socio-economic-environmental challenges. The Swachh Sabarmati project touches various spheres of society. Local communities includes people living in vicinity are the key participants. Primary CSR partner is Oil and Natural Gas Corporation (ONGC), District Administration Ahmedabad, Irrigation Department Ahmedabad, Ahmedabad Municiapl Corporation (AMC) and Forest Department Ahmedabad. The role of AMC and forest department is vital for the project as they conduct research based on field study and also provided workers from the AMC for facilitating the activities in cleaning Sabarmati. Implementation of the Project/Activity The implementation of the project activities are listed below Month 1 Cleaning Drive in the Area from French Well (Sardar Patel Ring Road) Up-Stream of Sabarmati River to Indira Bridge (Up-Stream of Sabarmati River) Cleaning of Garbage from River belt along with the floating garbage from the Sabarmati River. Month 2 Cleaning Driver in the Area from Indira Bridge (Up-Stream of Sabarmati River) to Koteshwar Mahadev Temple (Up-Stream of Sabarmati River) Month 3 Cleaning Drive in the Area from Koteshwar Mahadev Temple (Up- Stream of Sabarmati River) to Pumping Station (Up Stream of Sabarmati River) Behind River Side school on one side and on the other side i.e. Back Side of Motera Stadium. Month 4 Cleaning Drive in the Area from Pumping station (Up-Stream of Sabarmati River) behind River Side School on One Side and on the other Side would be back side of S.P.Stadium –Motera to Torrent Power House (Up-Stream of Ahmedabad River Front) Rest of the years Tree Plantation by Different Schools and Communities with Banyan,Cheeku,Mango,Jamun,Peepal and Badaam Trees.Monthly meetings with various communities,forest, and school visits and inspections for spreading awareness. Through our rigorous efforts from the initial efforts in the first 60 days has removed the garbage from river belt along with floating garbage from the Sabarmati River. We have removed more than 250 Tons of Garbage from the River Bed.As the river witnessed Three Major festivals i.e Ganpati Pooja,Diwali and Chatt Pooja during this duration and have faced most of the garbage. Disposal of Garbage removed from the River Bed with the help of Ahmedabad Municipal Corporation. Results/Outputs/Impacts Sabarmati has been the home for sewage dumping since a long time, going by figures a total of 225 MLD worth of untreated sewage is being dumped into the river. Through the rigorous efforts in the past 60 days we have cleaned 300 tons of garbage from the river bed. One of the major challenges was that the location is surrounded by temples and people often perform religious ceremonies there , and end up throwing plastic bags and leftovers in the river from a bridge leading to a lot of garbage being accumulated on daily basis . To fight this back we have requested the Dist. Collector and commissioner to cover the sides of the bridge with high railings so as to control the amount of garbage being dispersed. In the longer perspective we not only aim the clean the river bed but also plant trees along the river side so as to create a better environment in the longer run . In order to create awareness we have asked students to come upfront in tree plantation. There have been 1000 trees planted on the river side till now . Weekly school club meetings, monthly meetings with various communities, forest, and school visits is also being introduced . We also intend to introduce Green Ahmadabad parties to celebrate every year’s achievements and recognize the most active members and stuff as a way of motivation. Enabling factors and constraints The pathway of the project also contains some inevitable challenges. Firstly, major religious festivals involve religious practices which contaminates river. Secondly, the river is surrounded by many temples and crematoriums which also acts as a catalyst when it comes to sources of pollution. These are behavioral problems, to tackle these problems awareness programs at educational institutions are considered in the project. Sustainability and replicability Sustainability is a balancing act.Sustainability is one the newest degree subjects that attempts to bridge social science with civic engineering and environmental science with the technology of the future. When we hear the word “sustainability” we tend to think of renewable fuel sources, reducing carbon emissions, protecting environments and a way of keeping the delicate ecosystems of our planet in balance. Hence, this project is very much sustainable and resilience. Conclusions DFT intended to take up the removal of plastic waste, metal waste, dead wood and leaves, debris collection and its removal from the river. We planned to clean river water by removing plastic and other floating waste. From a long span of time the risk of dumping untreated sludge into our river was neglected in our government policies. Now, the risk has become huge which started impacting our environment. There have been presence of antibiotic- resistance E.Coli bacteria in high concentration at the riverfront beside Sabarmati Gandhi Asharam. A thorough investigation conducted by the Ahmedabad Municipal Corporation (AMC) had witnessed six major and 10 minor outlets in the city that surround the city’s sewage treatment facilities.
We have faced multiple challenges, as the river is surrounded by the various Crematoriums and Temples and most of the people there performs the pooja near the river and throws Plastic Packing Material and Polythene Bags in the river from Indira Bridge and average One Tons of Additional Garbage coming back to the river nearly daily which actually required a lot of effort from our side.
To clean up River Sabarmati, we had taken numerous concrete steps in the same regard. Cleaning the garbage from river belt along with floating garbage from the Sabarmati River. We also removed more than 250 Tons of Garbage from the river bed. Disposal of Garbage removed from the river bed with the help of Ahmedabad Municipal Corporation.
The Cleanliness Drive provided and impacted a better life for the people living in the city, helping the environment in every possible way to grow naturally which eventually helps the city a better place to survive. Other sources of information

A study of physico-chemical and biological characteristics of Sabarmati river in 2016 showed that the pH levels, biological oxygen demand (BOD), dissolved oxygen and total coliform organism levels were considerably high.
Our aims are to make the river free of solid waste and coliform organism. The presence of coliform can cause serious illness and it is evident that potential health hazard since the river water is used for drinking purpose. We are committed to reduce the health hazard in the vicinity. While removing the plastic, metal, construction debris from the river, the project also concentrates on building up a green environment in terms of air quality and preserving animal life by an afforestation drive. The afforestation includes plantation of tree saplings like Banyan, Mango, Peepal etc. the project tries to improve the life of local communities by improving the water quality of a natural resource and also advancing to maintain the regional climate (mass afforestation). Moreover, our objectives transcend into the sphere of infrastructure and awareness. Activities like cleaning the pumping stations, powerhouses are also integral part of Swachh Sabarmati project.
In India, dumping waste in the river is sort of habit which need immediate attention in context to change in the behaviour of the Citizens, which need aggressive awareness campaigning. The Swachh Sabarmati project is intended to mitigate this problem and aligned with Goal 6, 11, 13 and 15 of the Sustainable Development Goal. Partners To implement the agenda of sustainability, need cooperation among government, civil societies, private sectors and other stakeholders to mitigate the socio-economic-environmental challenges. The Swachh Sabarmati project touches various spheres of society. Local communities includes people living in vicinity are the key participants. Primary CSR partner is Oil and Natural Gas Corporation (ONGC), District Administration Ahmedabad, Irrigation Department Ahmedabad, Ahmedabad Municiapl Corporation (AMC) and Forest Department Ahmedabad. The role of AMC and forest department is vital for the project as they conduct research based on field study and also provided workers from the AMC for facilitating the activities in cleaning Sabarmati. Implementation of the Project/Activity The implementation of the project activities are listed below Month 1 Cleaning Drive in the Area from French Well (Sardar Patel Ring Road) Up-Stream of Sabarmati River to Indira Bridge (Up-Stream of Sabarmati River) Cleaning of Garbage from River belt along with the floating garbage from the Sabarmati River. Month 2 Cleaning Driver in the Area from Indira Bridge (Up-Stream of Sabarmati River) to Koteshwar Mahadev Temple (Up-Stream of Sabarmati River) Month 3 Cleaning Drive in the Area from Koteshwar Mahadev Temple (Up- Stream of Sabarmati River) to Pumping Station (Up Stream of Sabarmati River) Behind River Side school on one side and on the other side i.e. Back Side of Motera Stadium. Month 4 Cleaning Drive in the Area from Pumping station (Up-Stream of Sabarmati River) behind River Side School on One Side and on the other Side would be back side of S.P.Stadium –Motera to Torrent Power House (Up-Stream of Ahmedabad River Front) Rest of the years Tree Plantation by Different Schools and Communities with Banyan,Cheeku,Mango,Jamun,Peepal and Badaam Trees.Monthly meetings with various communities,forest, and school visits and inspections for spreading awareness. Through our rigorous efforts from the initial efforts in the first 60 days has removed the garbage from river belt along with floating garbage from the Sabarmati River. We have removed more than 250 Tons of Garbage from the River Bed.As the river witnessed Three Major festivals i.e Ganpati Pooja,Diwali and Chatt Pooja during this duration and have faced most of the garbage. Disposal of Garbage removed from the River Bed with the help of Ahmedabad Municipal Corporation. Results/Outputs/Impacts Sabarmati has been the home for sewage dumping since a long time, going by figures a total of 225 MLD worth of untreated sewage is being dumped into the river. Through the rigorous efforts in the past 60 days we have cleaned 300 tons of garbage from the river bed. One of the major challenges was that the location is surrounded by temples and people often perform religious ceremonies there , and end up throwing plastic bags and leftovers in the river from a bridge leading to a lot of garbage being accumulated on daily basis . To fight this back we have requested the Dist. Collector and commissioner to cover the sides of the bridge with high railings so as to control the amount of garbage being dispersed. In the longer perspective we not only aim the clean the river bed but also plant trees along the river side so as to create a better environment in the longer run . In order to create awareness we have asked students to come upfront in tree plantation. There have been 1000 trees planted on the river side till now . Weekly school club meetings, monthly meetings with various communities, forest, and school visits is also being introduced . We also intend to introduce Green Ahmadabad parties to celebrate every year’s achievements and recognize the most active members and stuff as a way of motivation. Enabling factors and constraints The pathway of the project also contains some inevitable challenges. Firstly, major religious festivals involve religious practices which contaminates river. Secondly, the river is surrounded by many temples and crematoriums which also acts as a catalyst when it comes to sources of pollution. These are behavioral problems, to tackle these problems awareness programs at educational institutions are considered in the project. Sustainability and replicability Sustainability is a balancing act.Sustainability is one the newest degree subjects that attempts to bridge social science with civic engineering and environmental science with the technology of the future. When we hear the word “sustainability” we tend to think of renewable fuel sources, reducing carbon emissions, protecting environments and a way of keeping the delicate ecosystems of our planet in balance. Hence, this project is very much sustainable and resilience. Conclusions DFT intended to take up the removal of plastic waste, metal waste, dead wood and leaves, debris collection and its removal from the river. We planned to clean river water by removing plastic and other floating waste. From a long span of time the risk of dumping untreated sludge into our river was neglected in our government policies. Now, the risk has become huge which started impacting our environment. There have been presence of antibiotic- resistance E.Coli bacteria in high concentration at the riverfront beside Sabarmati Gandhi Asharam. A thorough investigation conducted by the Ahmedabad Municipal Corporation (AMC) had witnessed six major and 10 minor outlets in the city that surround the city’s sewage treatment facilities.
We have faced multiple challenges, as the river is surrounded by the various Crematoriums and Temples and most of the people there performs the pooja near the river and throws Plastic Packing Material and Polythene Bags in the river from Indira Bridge and average One Tons of Additional Garbage coming back to the river nearly daily which actually required a lot of effort from our side.
To clean up River Sabarmati, we had taken numerous concrete steps in the same regard. Cleaning the garbage from river belt along with floating garbage from the Sabarmati River. We also removed more than 250 Tons of Garbage from the river bed. Disposal of Garbage removed from the river bed with the help of Ahmedabad Municipal Corporation.
The Cleanliness Drive provided and impacted a better life for the people living in the city, helping the environment in every possible way to grow naturally which eventually helps the city a better place to survive. Other sources of information

text: Abstract  Bacterioplankton community compositions in the Dongjiang River were characterized using denaturing gradient gel electrophoresis (DGGE) and 16S rRNA gene clone library construction. Water samples in nine different sites were taken along the mainstem and three tributaries. In total, 24 bands from DGGE gels and 406 clones from the libraries were selected and sequenced, subsequently analyzed for the bacterial diversity and composition of those microbial communities. Bacterial 16S rRNA gene sequences from freshwater bacteria exhibited board phylogenetic diversity, including sequences representing the Alphaproteobacteria, Betaproteobacteria, Gammaproteobacteria, Actinobacteria, Bacteriodetes, Verrucomicrobia, and candidate division TM7. Members of Betaproteobacteria group were the most dominant in all sampling sites, followed by Gammaproteobacteria, Alphaproteobacteria, and Actinobacteria. DGGE profiles and the ∫-libshuff analysis revealed similar patterns of bacterial diversity among most sampling sites, while spatial distribution variances existed in all sites along the river basin. Statistical analysis showed that bacterial species distribution strongly correlated with environmental variables, such as nitrate and ammonia, suggesting that nitrogen nutrients may shape the microbial community structure and composition in the Dongjiang River. This study had important implications for the comparison with other rivers elsewhere and contributed to the growing data set on the factors that structure bacterial communities in freshwater ecosystems.                      Introduction  Microbial communities are recognized as important players in biogeochemical cycling of fundamental elements (e.g. C, N, P, and S) in aquatic ecosystems (Azam & Worden, 2004). The biotic transformation may alter the makeup of carbon and other nutrients in rivers (Winter et al., 2007). In turn, the pelagic microbial communities in rivers adapt to changes in the concentration and composition of organic matter (Kirchman et al., 2004) and nutrients (Cebron et al., 2003, 2004). Consequently, the understanding of the diversity, composition, and structure of microbial communities is necessary for us to predict and/or experimentally determine their ecosystem functions. Considerable interest for determining the structure and function of microbial communities in various aquatic environments such as marine (Giovannoni et al., 1990; Fuhrman et al., 1992; Crump et al., 1999; Stevens & Ulloa, 2008), estuary (Stehr et al., 1995; Crump et al., 1999; Sekiguchi et al., 2002; Hewson & Fuhrman, 2004), and freshwater environments (Ovreas et al., 1997; Crump et al., 1999; Böckelmann et al., 2000; Battin et al., 2001; Zwart et al., 2002; Gaidos et al., 2004; Li et al., 2006, 2008; Lemke et al., 2009) showed the diversity and spatial distribution of microbial populations (Sekiguchi et al., 2002; Herfort et al., 2007; Goh et al., 2009). Moreover, typical freshwater bacterioplankton taxa were proposed to describe the microorganisms using 16S rRNA gene sequences (Zwart et al., 2002; Newton et al., 2011); Betaproteobacteria were numerically the most abundant group in freshwater rivers like the Elbe River of Germany (Böckelmann et al., 2000), the Rotmoos stream in the Austrian Alps (Battin et al., 2001), the Ipswich River in Massachusetts (Crump & Hobbie, 2005), and the Songhua River in China (Li et al., 2008). Current endeavor has been concentrated on the link between the freshwater bacterioplankton dynamics and the environmental changes. Crump et al. found that high similarity in the communities in the Ipswich and Parker Rivers were influenced by temperature and river flow rate (Crump & Hobbie, 2005); the communities in the six rivers of pan-Arctic watershed shifted synchronously over time (Crump et al., 2009). All these researches improved our understanding of the role of freshwater bacterioplankton in global biogeochemical processes in the aquatic ecosystems (Zehr & Ward, 2002; Mason et al., 2009). The Dongjiang River is the major source of drinking water supply for Hong Kong and several main cities of the Pearl River Delta in Guangdong province, China. The rapid economic development of the watershed, especially in the Pearl River Delta, was inevitably leading to the deterioration of water quality in the mainstream and the tributaries by introducing inorganic and organic pollutants in recent decades. Previous studies evidenced that various forms of nitrogen concentrations increased, and organic contaminants (such as polychlorinated biphenyls and polycyclic hydrocarbon) have been detected in the river (Ho & Hui, 2001; Jin, 2001; Jin et al., 2001). From the upstream to the downstream, the concentrations of pollutants in the water and sediment showed an increasing trend, which was correlated with the economic development gradient along the basin. Fortunately, the overall water quality of this river is still keeping acceptable in most time, which could be due to the high pollutant transformation efficiencies of the microorganisms in the river. However, little information about the structures and functions of bacterioplankton communities in the Dongjiang River was reported so far. To understand the diversity and distribution of microbial community and their responses to the environmental changes in the Dongjiang River, the denaturing gradient gel electrophoresis (DGGE) approach and 16S rRNA genes clone library analysis combined with multivariate statistical methods were applied to investigate the bacterioplankton community compositions (BCC) from the water samples in nine different sites along the mainstem and three tributaries of the river in this study. Our analyses exhibited that an ecological coherence presented in the diversity, composition, and structure of microbial communities with heterogeneous variations spatially and indicated that N nutrient (nitrate and ammonia) was strongly correlated with BCC in the Dongjiang River.                    Materials and methods                      Sites description and sampling  The Dongjiang River is a primary drinking water supply in south China. The watershed covers a total area of 35,340 km2, with an annual runoff of 32.4 billion m3 and the length of mainstem about 562 km. Water samples were collected from nine sites along the Dongjiang River (Fig. 0001) during the mid-summer in 2008. Six of the nine sites located in the mainstem, and the others located in its main branches. At each site, 3 L water sample was collected at about one-third of the total depth below the water surface. All samples were stored at 4 °C. For the microbial sample processing, water from each site was filtered, and the filters were stored at −30 °C until DNA extraction.                        Locations of sampling stations at the mainstem and the tributaries of the Dongjiang River. Number 1–9 for sampling site Longchuan, Heyuan, Guzhu, Huizhou, Qiantou, Shilong, Xinfengjiang River, Xizhi River, and Danshui River, respectively.                       Water chemical analysis  Water samples were analyzed for temperature, pH, dissolved oxygen (DO), ammonia, nitrite, and nitrate. The temperature, pH, and DO were measured by the Universal Pocket Meter Multiline P4 (Universal-Taschenmebgerat, Germany). Ammonia, nitrite, and nitrate were determined on a DU 640 UV/Visible Spectrophotometer (Beckman) using Nessler's reagent colorimetric method (420 nm), molecular absorption spectrometric method (540 nm, according to the ISO 6777-1984), and spectrophotometric method with phenol disulfonic acid (410 nm), respectively.                    DNA extraction  Three liters of water from each site was filtered through 10 μm hydrophilic polycarbonate filters (Shanghai, China) and then filtered through 0.22 μm hydrophilic polycarbonate filters (Shanghai, China) to collect microorganisms. DNA was isolated according to the protocol reported previously (Liu et al., 2011). Briefly, filters were cut into small pieces and placed in a tube containing 2 mL of DNA extraction buffer and lysozyme. The tubes were first incubated at 37 °C for 30 min, then incubated with the addition of sodium dodecyl sulfate (SDS, 1.5 , w/v) at 65 °C for 60 min. DNA was extracted from the aqueous phase with phenol–chloroform–isoamyl alcohol (25 : 24 : 1), precipitated with isopropanol, washed with ethanol, and purified with TIANquick Maxi Purification Kit (Tiangen, China).                    DGGE assay  The nearly full-lengthened 16S rRNA gene was used as template to amplify the V3 region of 16S rRNA gene with the primers 338F (5′-ACTCCTACGGGAGGCAGCAG-3′ Lane, 1991) with a GC clamp (CGCCCGCCGCGCCCCGCGCCCGGCCCGCCGCCCCCGCCCC) at the 5′-end (Muyzer et al., 1993) and 518R (5′-ATTACCGCGGCTGCTGG-3′ Lane, 1991). A DCode Universal Mutation Detection System (Bio-Rad) was used to perform DGGE analysis. A gradient of 30–60  denaturant (100  of denaturation corresponds to 7 M urea and 40  formamide) was constructed in an 8  polyacrylamide gel. Samples containing approximately equal amounts of PCR products were loaded in wells of the gel. Electrophoresis was run at 60 °C for 10 h at a constant voltage of 100 V in 1 × TAE. After electrophoresis and staining with goldview, gels images were captured using ImageQuant 350 (GE Healthcare). DGGE profiles were analyzed using Quantity One software (Bio-Rad). The bands were detected by the band-searching algorithm of the software. Band patterns were analyzed with the Dice coefficient using 1  position tolerances and 0.5  optimization for the band migration distance. Similarity matrix and dendrogram of the Clustering patterns were performed by unweighted pair-group method average (upgma) in the Quantity One software package. The richness (S) was determined from the number of bands in each lane, and the Shannon index (H) was calculated from H = ∑PilnPi (Shannon & Weaver, 1963), where Pi is the importance probability of the bands in a lane, calculated from Ni/N, where Ni is the peak height of a band and N is the sum of all peak heights in the densitometric curve. Evenness (E) was calculated as E = H/lnS (Pielou, 1969). Bands of interest (designated with numbers) were excised and rinsed in 0.2 mL sterile deionized water. Each band in gel was crushed with a sterile pipette tip and resolved in 20 μL sterile deionized water overnight at 4 °C. DNA solution was used as a template for reamplification with the primer 338F and 518R. The PCR products were cloned into pMD18-T Simple vector (TaKaRa, Dalian, China). Clones were screened, detected, and sequenced as described above.                    Clone library of 16S rRNA genes  The nearly complete 16S rRNA gene was amplified on a Mastercycler thermocycler (Eppendorf, Germany) with bacterial universal primers 27F (5′-AGAGTTTGATCMTGGCTCAG-3′) and 1492R (5′-TACGGHTACCTTGTTACGACTT-3′ Gurtler & Stanisich, 1996). Each PCR mixture (25 μL) contained 2.5 μL 10× PCR reaction buffer, 200 μM of each deoxyribonucleoside triphosphate, 1 μM each of the forward and reverse primer, and approximately 20 ng of DNA. The PCR was incubated for 5 min at 94 °C, followed by 30 cycles of 30 s at 94 °C, 30 s at 55 °C, and 90 s at 72 °C, with a final extension of 72 °C for 7 min. The PCR products were purified using EZ Spin Column PCR Product Purification Kit (Sangon Inc., Shanghai, China) before ligated into the pMD18-T Simple vector (TaKaRa). The ligation products were transformed into E. coli TOP10 competent cells through heat shock. White colonies were selected randomly and inoculated into glass test tubes containing 1.5 mL of LB-ampicillin broth. Plasmid DNA of each selected clone was extracted and quantified, subsequently screened by PCR using primers M13f (5′-AGGGTTTTCCCAGTCACGACG-3′) and M13r (5′-GAGCGGATAACAATTTCACACAGG-3′). PCR products were checked by 1  agarose gel electrophoresis. Clones with correct-sized insert were sequenced using ABI 3730 automated sequencer.                    Comparative sequence analysis  Sequences of both excised DGGE bands and clones were manually checked and modified with BioEdit v7.0.9 (Hall, 1999) and then compared with the GenBank database by the blast (Altschul et al., 1990). Chimeric sequences were detected using the Bellerophon (version 3) function on the Greengenes web server (DeSantis et al., 2006). The division level groupings were determined by taxonomic assignment performed by the Ribosomal Database Project 10.0 Classifier tool ( rdp.cme.msu.edu) with 80  confidence (Cole et al., 2009). Multiple sequence alignments for each sample were made with ClustalX; phylogenetic analyses were conducted using mega (molecular evolutionary genetics analysis) program version 4 (Tamura et al., 2007). The tree topology was inferred with a Kimura 2-parameter correction model (Kimura, 1980) and with 1000 bootstrap replications. The aligned sequences in the clone libraries were analyzed with dotur (Schloss & Handelsman, 2005) to determine OTUs at a 3  dissimilarity cutoff. And dotur was also used to estimate Shannon's diversity index, the richness indices ACE and Chao1 (Chao & Bunge, 2002).                    Statistical analyses  Statistical T-test was calculated using spss 16 software, and difference was considered significant at P < 0.05. The geochemical parameters were normalized and transformed to carry out canonical correspondence analysis (CCA) and partial canonical correspondence analysis (pCCA) using statistical software package canoco 4.5 (ter Braak & Šmilauer, 2002), and the variance inflation factors was calculated with 999 Monte Carlo permutations as described by Xu et al. (2010), environmental variables with variance inflation factors (VIF) < 20 were selected for the following forward selection to avoid the multicollinearity with other variables, and the variation partitioning analysis was performed on the basis of CCA and pCCA (ter Braak & Šmilauer, 2002). Differences in community composition between pairs of libraries were estimated using the ∫-libshuff program (Schloss et al., 2004), and 10 000 randomizations were run to determine the significance (P = 0.05) of overlapping coverage based on the Bonferroni method. Briefly, sequences were aligned, and evolutionary distances were calculated using the Jukes–Cantor algorithm. The resulting distance matrix was then used to compute the statistical significances of differences in the compositions of each two libraries. The critical P-value was calculated for the Bonferroni correction of libraries comparisons, if the P-value at or below the critical P-value, the libraries can be considered different statistically with 95  confidence.                    Nucleotide accession numbers  All of 24 sequences from DGGE gel have been submitted to GenBank under accession numbers GU553108–GU553131. Sequences of the 16S rDNA clones are available under GenBank accession numbers JF429150–JF429389.                    Results                      Water chemical properties  Environmental parameters including pH value, DO, ammonia, nitrite, and nitrate of the nine sites in the Dongjiang River were summarized below. The pH values of all water samples were neutral (pH 7 ± 0.3). The concentrations of DO at all sites ranged from 3.25 to 8.36 mg L−1, near DO saturation phenomenon was embodied in site like Xinfengjiang River where the water temperature was the lowest in the sampling season (about 20 °C). The low DO values were observed in Danshui River (3.25 mg L−1), Xizhi River (3.82 mg L−1), and Shilong (3.87 mg L−1), the highest DO values was in Xinfengjiang River (8.36 mg L−1) and more than 5 mg L−1 in the other sites. The samples showed high variations in ammonia (-N) contents, from the lowest concentration in Xinfengjiang River (0.51 mg L−1) to the highest one in Danshui River (6.35 mg L−1). The concentrations of nitrate and nitrite were relatively low in all samples (data no shown). Notably, the water quality was slightly getting worse from upstream to downstream along the mainstem (the DO contents gradually decreased and the ammonia contents increased from upstream to downstream).                    Bacterial DGGE profiles  Bacterial diversity and composition of the nine sampling sites were screened by PCR-DGGE fingerprinting with a substantial resolution (Fig. 0002). The DGGE data were transformed in relative quantities based on the intensity of individual bands from the gel image. The Shannon index (H) calculated from DGGE gels ranged from 2.60 to 3.20 showed that high diversity of bacterial community in whole basin (data not shown). In the mainstem, there was relative lower diversity at sites from the upstream of the river (lane 1–3, average H value was 2.75), while higher diversity in the mid- and downstream (lane 4–6, average H value was 3.12), and the significant difference between them was observed statistically (P = 0.03). The dendrograms calculated with upgma showed that Longchuang and Heyuan were clustered together, while Huizhou and Qiaotou were clustered closely (Fig. 0002). The similarity matrix revealed all samples shared similar bacterioplankton communities (42.2–71.4  similarity values) though with variance in the community pattern (Table 0001). The similarity among different sites implied an ecological coherence presented in the diversity and structure of microbial communities along the river. The clones were classified into 167 operational taxonomic units (OTUs) using DOTUR based on 97  sequence similarity. For relative comparison of these libraries, indices of H, Chao1, and 1/D were calculated to descript the equitability of the OTU distribution, nonparametric estimation of OTU richness, and dominance of the OTU abundance, respectively (Table 0003). Chao 1 richness was about 2–8 times higher in Qiaotou than the other sites. The 1/Simpson's index (1/D) showed that Huizhou had the lowest diversity, while Qiaotou had the highest diversity of the nine sites. Rarefaction curves of the clone libraries showed that all libraries had captured roughly the same level of the extant diversity using evolutionary distance of 3 . ∫-libshuff estimation detected no significant differences (P < 0.0001) in the bacterial community composition in the paired sites expect for Shilong vs Danshui River (Table 0004), and other two p values revealed that Guzhu was different from Longchuan and Shilong; Xizhi River was different from Huizhou. Overall, Library comparison based on the ∫-libshuff analysis demonstrated that the bacterioplankton compositions changed in similar pattern along the Dongjiang River. In all sampling sites, five bacterial phyla (Proteobacteria, Actinobacteria, Bacteriodetes, Verrucomicrobia, and candidate division TM7) were identified, with the dominant phylum of Proteobacteria (85.0 ). Phylogenetic analysis revealed that the representative clones were affiliated with cultured isolates and uncultured bacteria clones retrieved from various freshwater habitats (Fig. 0003). The majority of the sequences (74.1  of the total) were related to the Betaproteobacteria subphylum, including family Comamonadaceae, Burkholderiaceae, Burkholderiales_incertae_sedis, Methylophilaceae, Rhodocyclaceae, and the most abundant family was Comamonadaceae with the range from 32.0  to 46.7  in the libraries. Most sequences (58.9  of the total) belong to 39 genera, and the most commonly found species were related to the genera Curvibacter, Hydrogenophaga, Polynucleobacter, Aquabacterium, and Zoogloea. In addition, Actinobacteria were found in all sites but Guzhu; no Verrucomincrobia were detected in the clone libraries from Guzhu, Huizhou, and Xinfengjiang River; no Bacteriodetes were retrieved from Longchuan, Guzhu, and Shilong. The relative abundances and distribution patterns of different phylogenetic bacteria groups in the libraries were calculated for all nine samples (Fig. 0004). Similar to the result showed by DGGE technique, the spatial distribution patterns of bacterial communities in the clone libraries also indicated a dynamic of ecological succession in the whole basin. As Betaproteobacteria was the frequently detected and dominated groups in the river, detailed subdivisions and distribution of families were analyzed further. Families Comamonadaceae, Burkholderiales_incertae_sedis, Methylophilaceae, and Rhodocyclaceae were common in all sampling sites (Fig. 0005). The most abundant typical freshwater taxa Comamonadaceae contains the representatives of betI (Zwart et al., 2002; Newton et al., 2011), e.g. sequences similar to Curvibacter and Limnohabitans curvus (Hahn et al., 2010), and sequences affiliated with the betII lineage such as Pnec (Polynucleobacter necessaries; Heckmann & Schmidt, 1987; Jezbera et al., 2011) within Betaproteobacteria were present in most sites (Table 0005). The high abundance of Betaproteobacteria has been documented in the studies of other rivers, such as the Elbe River of Germany (Böckelmann et al., 2000), the Rotmoos stream in the Austrian Alps (Battin et al., 2001), the Ipswich River in Massachusetts (Crump & Hobbie, 2005), and the Songhua River in China (Li et al., 2008). The phylogenetic compositions of the clone libraries shared the dominant functional taxa with a variation on presence/absence and abundance from the upper to lower reach of the river (Table 0005). variables  The relationships of microbial patterns to environmental variables were summarized in a CCA ordination plot using canoco software. Among all environmental variables, five parameters – water temperature, pH, DO, ammonia, and nitrate – were selected to perform CCA by CCA-based variance inflation factor (VIF) with 999 Monte Carlo permutations. The five environmental variables explained 58.4  of total variance in the bacterial composition the total variance, and the first two CCA dimensions explained 39.5  of the variance. Of the parameters, nitrate, ammonia, and DO appeared to be the most important environmental parameters, and these three parameters explained 38.8  variations of microbial communities, leaving 61.2  of the variation unexplained. Variation partitioning analysis showed that nitrate, ammonia, and DO separately explained 19.8  (P = 0.098), 12.6  (P = 0.457), and 11.8  (P = 0.544) of the variation, respectively. The interactions between pairs of these variables explained smaller proportions of the variation (Fig. 0006).                       The five geochemical variables were also examined by CCA for correlation with the Betaproteobacteria community composition (Fig. 0007). The first axis explained 23.2  of the microbial diversity observed, and the second axis explained 16.2  of the diversity, describing 39.4  of the total variation. Qiaotou, Shilong, Xizhi River, and Danshui River clustered into a group, Longchuan, Heyuan, and Huizhou clustered together, while Xinfengjiang River and Guzhu were located independently. Guzhu did not cluster with either group. The bacterial diversity present in Qiaotou, Shilong, Xizhi River, and Danshui River appears to be strongly affected by the ammonia concentrations, as indicated by their proximity to those arrows. The community structure in Xinfengjiang River appears to be mainly affected by the DO concentration. Longchuan, Heyuan, and Guzhu are not close to any of the geochemical arrows, indicating that unmeasured factors are likely to be the important controllers of microbial diversity in these sites. The CCA ordinations of the microbial patterns (total bacteria and Betaproteobacteria) and environmental variables demonstrated that N nutrient (nitrate and ammonia) was strongly correlated with the bacterial communities in the Dongjiang River. Discussion  Microbial communities are fundamental in the functioning of river ecosystems. However, the roles of most microorganisms in natural systems are unclear because most of them are uncultivated by the conventional culturing methods currently (Amann et al., 1995). Fortunately, the advent of culture-independent molecular methods has shed light on the determination of community compositions and laid the foundation for deeper understanding of aquatic microbial ecology. Studies demonstrated that DGGE technique is capable of identifying and comparing the dominant members of these communities (Muyzer et al., 1993; Diez et al., 2001; de Araujo & Schneider, 2008; Kobayashi et al., 2009). 16S rRNA gene clone library method has widely used in bacterial communities analysis in various environments (Hiorns et al., 1997; Zwart et al., 1998; Wu et al., 2007). In our study, DGGE approach was used to characterize the bacterial composition in nine sampling sites along the Dongjiang River. In addition, with respect to the DNA fragment sequences obtained from the DGGE bands were not long enough to predict the species level (Ogino et al., 2001), clone library analysis was employed as a complementary method to obtain more precise taxonomic information of microbial communities. The bacterioplankton communities analyzed in current study included free-living microorganisms and particle-associated microorganisms (diameter range from 0.22 to 10 μm). Based on the sequence analysis, the results showed that phyla Proteobacteria, Actinobacteria, Bacteriodetes, and Verrucomincrobia were present in both DGGE and clone library analyses. The phyla Firmcutes and Nitrospirae found in bacterial DGGE gel were not presented in the clone libraries; alternatively, phylum TM7 was unique in the library. These might just reflect the different sections of the community that were amplified. Consistently, Proteobacteria was the predominant phylum embodied in both DGGE (58.3 ) and clone library analyses (85 ), which indicated that the phylum outnumbered other microorganisms in quantitatively in the Dongjiang River. The variation in the percentages may be due to the lower resolution of DGGE assay and (or) the magnifying proportion of dominant groups during random colony selecting in cloning library. As two popular approaches in revealing the microbial community composition individually, DGGE and clone library construction methods were compared by the percentages of bacterial divisions using spss 16. T-test result showed that there was no significance difference between them (P > 0.05). Considering the laborious and time-consuming characteristics of clone library construction method (Sanz & Kochling, 2007), and even the phylogenetic/taxonomic resolution of almost complete 16S rRNA sequences is not sufficient to distinguish between taxa significantly differing in ecological adaptations (Simek et al., 2010; Jezbera et al., 2011), DGGE technique may be a more rapid and straightforward alternative choice for tracking genotypic community changes in the Dongjiang River. Although the limitations that there might be the much shorter sequences or lower qualities taxa information obtained from DGGE bands, DGGE method can give a good microbial overview with medium phylogenetic resolution in the river over time. It was noted that Betaproteobacteria were predominant group frequently in the Dongjiang River (Fig. 0004), and this result was agreed with previous studies on rivers (Böckelmann et al., 2000; Battin et al., 2001; Crump & Hobbie, 2005; Li et al., 2008), lake (Newton et al., 2006), and reservoirs (Simek et al., 2001, 2005). Previous studies showed that the betIand betII lineages represented the most sequences of Betaproteobacteria and distributed widely in the freshwater environments (Zwart et al., 2002; Newton et al., 2011). The most abundant typical freshwater taxa Comamonadaceae contains the representatives of betI (Glockner et al., 2000; Zwart et al., 2002), which is a fast-growing and nutrient-loving group. The wide distribution of Betaproteobacteria in freshwater habitats may primarily ascribe to the well adaption capacity in most environments, and abundance in the molecular determination might partially because some of them belong to high nucleic acid containing bacterial group (Simek et al., 2005). Furthermore, in freshwater mesocosm and isolation studies, some members of the Betaproteobacteria were observed to respond quickly to nutrient additions (Burkert et al., 2003; Hahn, 2003; Simek et al., 2005) and recognized as autotrophic ammonia oxidizers, which contribute to ammonia removal (Head et al., 1993; Teske et al., 2002). Members of Alphaproteobacteria and Gammaproteobacteria were present in equal proportions in the Dongjiang River; this result is similar to that of the water column of the Selenga River estuary (Maksimenko et al., 2008) and Ipswich River (Crump & Hobbie, 2005). As common groups in aquatic ecosystems, they were involving in the balance of global nitrogen budget through nitrogen fixation (Xie & Yokota, 2006) or denitrification (Patureau et al., 2000). Actinobacteria are Gram-positive bacteria that represent a most abundant group (50–70 ) of total bacteria in various freshwater habitats (Glockner et al., 2000; Sekar et al., 2003; Warnecke et al., 2004; Lemke et al., 2009). Researchers reported that members of Actinobacteria contributed to glucose assimilation and heterotrophic nitrification in freshwater (Witzel & Overbeck, 1979; Brierley & Wood, 2001; Elifantz et al., 2005) and played a key role in nutrient and energy cycling in aquatic habits (Elifantz et al., 2005). These suggested that ecological functions might enable a global distribution of these microorganisms in freshwater habitats (Hiorns et al., 1997; Zwart et al., 1998; Burkert et al., 2003; Eiler & Bertilsson, 2004). Interestingly, the diversity, composition, and structure of bacterial communities varied in different clone libraries. For example, Actinobacteria were found in all sites but Guzhu; no Verrucomincrobia were detected in the clone libraries from Guzhu, Huizhou, and Xinfengjiang River; no Bacteriodetes were retrieved from Longchuan, Guzhu, and Shilong (Fig. 0004). These suggested that the coverage of clone library is not sufficient to exhaust the true diversity of environmental samples, or these microorganisms are not ubiquitous to all aquatic habitats as well as previous study (Lemke et al., 2009). Although relatively undersampled, the rarefraction curves showed that all 16S rRNA genes clone libraries had captured roughly the same level of the extant diversity (data not shown). The spatial distribution patterns of these bacterial communities showed a dynamic of ecological succession in the whole basin. The result of CCA confirms that nitrogen is an important environmental factors to alter the microbial community structure significantly by serving as essential nutrients for the growth of river microorganism, which is consistent with the finding that trophic types have profound effects on microbial communities (Allen et al., 2005; Davidson et al., 2007). In conclusion, this study presented preliminary data on the composition of aquatic microbial communities in the Dongjiang River by DGGE and clone libraries. The results indicated that the members of Betaproteobacteria dominated along the whole watershed. The spatial biodiversity of bacterioplankton was documented in the river niches, and the overall bacterial community composition and structure were different from those of the other rivers. Furthermore, nitrogen is an essential nutrient correlated with the spatial distribution of the microorganisms. However, our understanding about the composition, diversity, and structure of the bacterial community in the freshwater is still limited. High-throughput molecular tools such as pyrosequencing and functional gene array, may provide a further understanding for the spatial and temporal changes of microbial community composition in the future study.
