text: Não obstante toda polêmica que envolve o rio São Francisco, muito pouco tem sido dito sobre o rio Sergipe. Nos seus aproximados 210 Km de extensão, desde sua nascente, no município de Nossa Senhora da Glória até sua foz no Oceano Atlântico, entre as cidades de Aracaju e Barra dos Coqueiros, esse rio assiste em sua bacia hidrográfica 1.010.523 habitantes, ou 56,6  da população sergipana. FREDERICO LISBÔA ROMÃO A campanha eleitoral tem trazido à tona discussão sobre a urgência da revitalização do Velho Chico. Ataques, acusações e números, muitas vezes carentes de confirmações isentas, são apresentados ao cidadão eleitor. É uma discussão que a despeito de todos os exageros e afirmações aterrorizadoras, hegemoniza, ao menos, um elemento de positividade: O RIO SÃO FRANCISCO NÃO PODE SER TRANSPOSTO ANTES QUE OCORRA SUA REVITALIZAÇÃO. Não obstante toda polêmica que envolve o rio São Francisco, muito pouco tem sido dito sobre o rio Sergipe, no entanto, a publicação do livro Rio Sergipe: Importância, vulnerabilidade e preservação, reunindo pesquisas sob a organização de Alves (2006) dão conta que este rio genuinamente sergipano falece rapidamente em muitos dos seus sinais vitais. É urgente que a discussão avance para o rio Sergipe. Nos seus aproximados 210 Km de extensão, desde sua nascente, no município de Nossa Senhora da Glória até sua foz no Oceano Atlântico, entre as cidades de Aracaju e Barra dos Coqueiros, esse rio assiste em sua bacia hidrográfica 1.010.523 habitantes, ou 56,6  da população sergipana. Suas águas drenam 16,7  das terras do estado, atingindo 26 municípios, nos quais se localizam 47  do total de estabelecimentos industriais cadastrados (Rocha, 2006). Não obstante ser elemento vital para a maioria da população de Sergipe, abastecendo, via água encanada, 85,2  ou 116.689 dos domicílios existentes na sua bacia, o balanço hídrico ao longo da sua bacia explicita atualmente um déficit na grande maioria da sua extensão. A demanda de água desta bacia para os mais variados usos é de 259.351 m3/dia, entretanto, a mesma tem capacidade de gerar apenas 54,9 mil m3/dia, conformando um déficit em torno de 80 . Permanecendo a forma de uso atual a perspectiva é de ampliação desse déficit. Atualmente a falta de água é suprida pela transposição do rio São Francisco através do sistema de adutoras (Rocha, 2006). Os números apresentados denotam por si só a importância do rio Sergipe que generosamente tem fornecido água e alimento para inúmeras gerações, mas recebe em troca dejetos, descuido e deszelos. Desde maio de 1925, quando foi de uma vez por todas esclarecido que o rio a separar a nova capital Aracaju do povoado Barra dos Coqueiros era o Sergipe e não o Cotinguiba, como se pensava até então (Alves, 2006), ele vem sendo impactado negativamente pela resultante das ações do homem no seu projeto modernista. Dos domicílios que abastece, apenas 38,7  possuem rede de esgoto, com o agravante de parte significativa desse esgotamento não passar por tratamento adequado (Rocha, 2006; Araújo, 2006). O efluente do Distrito Industrial de Aracaju (DIA) foi abandonado a mais de 15 anos sendo despejado diretamente no rio Poxim (Alves e Garcia, 2006). Soma-se a isso o fato de não haver tratamento apropriado para os resíduos sólidos que são depositados em grandes lixeiras concorrendo para contaminação dos cursos d’ água. Contribui ainda para a degradação da bacia, uma urbanização apressada, ecologicamente insustentável, especialmente em Aracaju, acelerando a instável situação da sua barra ou embocadura. Ao longo de quase dois séculos o rio viu sua foz se transformar por três vezes até assumir a formação atual. Muitos com certeza se admirarão em saber que no ano de 1823, ano do registro cartográfico mais antigo, esse rio desaguava nas proximidades do Hotel Beira Mar. Essa instabilidade, característica marcante da foz do rio Sergipe, implicou entre outras coisas, na necessidade de contínuas dragagens realizadas de fins do século XIX ate o ano de 1972. Do ponto de vista urbanístico a mais impactante mudança foi o Projeto de Urbanização da Coroa do Meio (Wanderley, 2006). Em 1977, na Coroa do Meio, durante a administração do então prefeito João Alves Filho, foram aterrados e terraplanados canais de mangues, restinga, manguezal e construído um cais à margem direita do rio. Essa abrangente intervenção, em local ecologicamente frágil, associada ao atraso na implementação de medidas compensatórias (Wanderley, 2006), foi responsável em grande medida, pela desfiguração ambiental e gasto elevado de recursos do estado. O resultado de tamanho descalabro não poderia ser outro se não a degradação desse ambiente hídrico. Diversos indicadores demonstram que rapidamente o rio Sergipe deixa de ser fonte de beleza e vida se transformando em veiculo de doenças e contaminação. Análises realizadas no rio do Sal, rio Poxim e Rio Sergipe, na região estuarina no entorno de Aracaju, apresenta níveis preocupantes no tocante a oxigênio dissolvido, nitrogênio e surfactantes, todos parâmetros indicadores de poluição. No tocante ao oxigênio, os três rios apresentam sinais de poluição, particularmente o rio do Sal e o Poxim. O primeiro com níveis de oxigênio acima do recomendado (a jusante da Estação de Tratamento de Esgoto de Aracaju – ETE). O segundo com problema inverso, níveis de oxigênio próximos de zero (anoxia) na região sob influência dos dejetos do DIA (Alves e Garcia, 2006). Em relação à presença de nitrogênio (N-amoniacal) os valores do rio do Sal e Poxim denotam ambientes poluídos em processo de eutrofização. Quanto aos surfactantes os rios Sergipe e do Sal apresentam as mais altas concentrações. O rio Poxim atinge níveis considerados letais a vida aquática (Alves e Garcia). Afora os indicadores químicos, marcadores biológicos também apontam sinais evidentes de poluição. Pesquisas no estuário do Rio Sergipe entre os anos de 1977 e 2002 apresentam sinais claros de deterioração. Em 1977/1978 análises de amostras de plâncton detectaram valores dentro da normalidade com predominância dos Copepoda (organismos holoplanctônicos, importantes para cadeia trófica), em torno de 50 . Entretanto, as amostras de plâncton pesquisadas entre os anos de 2001 e 2002 revelaram a presença de protozoário Favella ehrenbergii em valores próximos a 80  e uma diminuta presença dos Copopeda, menos que 10 , indicador de ambiente poluído (Araújo, 2006). Esses dados do estuário são por demais preocupantes. Por sua riqueza biótica e complexidade ecossistêmica, os estuários são grandemente responsáveis pela sustentação de conjuntos de espécies de peixes (ictiofauna), algumas exclusivas desse ecossistema (Araújo, 2006; Alcântara, 2006). Estudos anteriores da fauna de peixes do estuário do rio Sergipe explicitam sua riqueza, comportando 136 espécies, agrupadas em 50 famílias, indicadores elevados mesmo quando comparados a outros ambientes (Alcântara, 2006). Infelizmente a riqueza da ictiofauna do seu estuário tem sido duramente atingida. Desde 2004 ocorre mortandade em massa de peixes no rio do Sal. Amostragens de locais diversos dessa ictiofauna, realizadas em janeiro de 2004 apresentaram diferentes espécies de peixes com erosão das nadadeiras, um sinal de estresse crônico, cuja evolução pode acarretar sua destruição completa (Alcântara, 2006). Outro elemento denunciador das agressões sofridas pelo rio Sergipe é os manguezais presentes no seu estuário. Nunca é demais destacar a enorme importância do mangue para a fauna e flora dos estuários, águas costeiras e como fonte de alimento e renda para as populações em seu entorno. Infelizmente, a exemplo dos outros aspectos relatados anteriormente, os manguezais têm sido destruídos pela conjugação da ação imobiliária e poluição (Landim e Guimarães, 2006). O cheiro fétido, a morte de árvores do mangue pela ação de algas e os níveis elevados de contaminação por coliforme fecais, presentes na água e ostras, na Praia 13 de Julho, evidenciam o descaso ambiental. Colocam em risco não só a riqueza biótica do estuário e faixa costeira, como inviabiliza uma importante fonte econômica e de proteína, potencialmente geradora de trabalho, renda, e lazer. (Landim e Guimarães, 2006). Todas as informações que emergem em função da publicação dessas pesquisas tornam público a premente necessidade da substituição de um certo modelo de desenvolvimento megalomaníaco, socialmente injusto e ecologicamente insustentável. No exato momento em que o governador João Alves combate corretamente, a transposição do rio São Francisco, ele se esquece de dizer que ela já ocorre. Diariamente as adutoras transpõem 206.755 m3 de água do São Francisco para diversos municípios sergipanos. E no que depender das ações do governo estadual a intenção é ampliar essa transposição: Do contrario como explicar a propalada estrutura que existe sob a ponte Aracaju – Barra dos Coqueiros, especificamente para receber uma adutora? É tão incorreto construir novas transposições do Velho Chico como ampliar as que já existem. É preciso fundamentalmente revitalizar os rios, avançando no uso sustentável dos corpos d’ água. Os dados apresentados são incontestáveis. O rio Sergipe morre um pouco a cada dia e não é por falta de informação e recursos, mas por falta de vontade política, ou melhor dizendo, pela presença de uma ação de governo monolítica e míope que aposta unicamente na engenharia quando o problema é essencialmente de pedagogia. Revitalizar nos recursos hídricos, especialmente a bacia hidrográfica do rio Sergipe, é algo que diferentemente do rio São Francisco, está a altura do governo estadual que nesse quesito deixa muito a desejar. No momento em que a tecnologia avança para tratamentos de efluentes visando a retirada de contaminantes não eliminados pelos métodos convencionais, em Sergipe sequer ocorre de forma satisfatória o tratamento básico. Por fim, fica evidente; mais do que discurso vãos, precisa haver VONTADE DE FATO. Uma ação integrada do governo estadual, instituições de pesquisas, iniciativa privada e população, poderá em tempo curto restabelecer os parâmetros de vida ao nosso rio Sergipe, contribuindo verdadeiramente, com a tão propagandeada revitalização do rio da unidade nacional. *Doutor em Ciências Sociais pela UNICAMPfredericoromao@uol.com.br
text_en: Despite all the controversy surrounding the São Francisco River, very little has been said about the Sergipe River. In its approximately 210 km length, from its source in the municipality of Nossa Senhora da Glória to its mouth in the Atlantic Ocean, between the cities of Aracaju and Barra dos Coqueiros, this river is home to 1,010,523 inhabitants in its watershed, or 56.6% of the population of Sergipe. FREDERICO LISBÔA ROMÃO The electoral campaign has brought to the fore the discussion about the urgency of revitalizing the Velho Chico. Attacks, accusations and numbers, often lacking unbiased confirmation, are presented to the voting public. It is a discussion that, despite all the exaggerations and terrifying statements, at least one element of positivity prevails: THE SÃO FRANCISCO RIVER CANNOT BE CROSSED BEFORE ITS REVITALIZATION OCCURS. Despite all the controversy surrounding the São Francisco River, very little has been said about the Sergipe River. However, the publication of the book Rio Sergipe: Importância, Vulnerância e Preservação (Sergipe River: Importance, Vulnerability and Preservation), a collection of research organized by Alves (2006), shows that this genuinely Sergipe river is rapidly dying in many of its vital signs. It is urgent that the discussion move on to the Sergipe River. In its approximately 210 km length, from its source in the municipality of Nossa Senhora da Glória to its mouth in the Atlantic Ocean, between the cities of Aracaju and Barra dos Coqueiros, this river supports 1,010,523 inhabitants in its watershed, or 56.6% of the population of Sergipe. Its waters drain 16.7% of the state's land, reaching 26 municipalities, where 47 of the total registered industrial establishments are located (Rocha, 2006). Despite being a vital element for the majority of the population of Sergipe, supplying 85.2 or 116,689 of the households in its basin with piped water, the water balance along the basin currently shows a deficit in the vast majority of its extension. The demand for water in this basin for the most varied uses is 259,351 m3/day, however, it has the capacity to generate only 54,900 m3/day, forming a deficit of around 80%. If the current form of use continues, the prospect is for this deficit to increase. Currently, the lack of water is supplied by the transposition of the São Francisco River through the adductor system (Rocha, 2006). The figures presented show in themselves the importance of the Sergipe River, which has generously provided water and food for countless generations, but in return receives waste, neglect and neglect. Since May 1925, when it was once and for all clarified that the river separating the new capital Aracaju from the town of Barra dos Coqueiros was the Sergipe and not the Cotinguiba, as previously thought (Alves, 2006), the city has been negatively impacted by the result of human actions in its modernist project. Of the homes it supplies, only 38.7 have a sewage system, with the aggravating factor that a significant part of this sewage does not undergo adequate treatment (Rocha, 2006; Araújo, 2006). The effluent from the Aracaju Industrial District (DIA) has been abandoned for over 15 years and is dumped directly into the Poxim River (Alves and Garcia, 2006). Added to this is the fact that there is no appropriate treatment for solid waste that is deposited in large landfills, contributing to the contamination of waterways. The basin's degradation is further contributed to by hasty, ecologically unsustainable urbanization, especially in Aracaju, accelerating the unstable situation of its mouth. Over the course of almost two centuries, the river's mouth has changed three times until it assumed its current shape. Many will surely be surprised to know that in 1823, the year of the oldest cartographic record, this river flowed into the vicinity of the Beira Mar Hotel. This instability, a striking characteristic of the mouth of the Sergipe River, has led, among other things, to the need for continuous dredging since the end of the century.XIX until 1972. From an urbanistic point of view, the most impactful change was the Coroa do Meio Urbanization Project (Wanderley, 2006). In 1977, in Coroa do Meio, during the administration of then mayor João Alves Filho, mangrove channels, sandbanks, and mangrove swamps were filled in and leveled, and a pier was built on the right bank of the river. This comprehensive intervention, in an ecologically fragile location, associated with the delay in implementing compensatory measures (Wanderley, 2006), was largely responsible for the environmental disfigurement and high expenditure of state resources. The result of such a disaster could only be the degradation of this water environment. Several indicators demonstrate that the Sergipe River is rapidly ceasing to be a source of beauty and life, becoming a vehicle for diseases and contamination. Analyses performed on the Sal River, Poxim River and Sergipe River, in the estuarine region around Aracaju, show worrying levels of dissolved oxygen, nitrogen and surfactants, all parameters that indicate pollution. Regarding oxygen, the three rivers show signs of pollution, particularly the Sal River and the Poxim. The first has oxygen levels above the recommended level (downstream of the Aracaju Sewage Treatment Plant - ETE). The second has the opposite problem, with oxygen levels close to zero (anoxia) in the region under the influence of DIA waste (Alves and Garcia, 2006). Regarding the presence of nitrogen (ammoniacal N), the values ​​of the Sal River and Poxim indicate polluted environments in the process of eutrophication. Regarding surfactants, the Sergipe and Sal Rivers have the highest concentrations. The Poxim River reaches levels considered lethal to aquatic life (Alves and Garcia). In addition to chemical indicators, biological markers also indicate clear signs of pollution. Research in the Sergipe River estuary between 1977 and 2002 showed clear signs of deterioration. In 1977/1978, analyses of plankton samples detected values ​​within the normal range, with a predominance of Copepoda (holoplanktonic organisms, important for the food chain), around 50 . However, plankton samples researched between 2001 and 2002 revealed the presence of the protozoan Favella ehrenbergii at values ​​close to 80 and a tiny presence of Copopeda, less than 10 , indicating a polluted environment (Araújo, 2006). These data from the estuary are extremely worrying. Due to their biotic richness and ecosystem complexity, estuaries are largely responsible for sustaining a number of fish species (ichthyofauna), some of which are exclusive to this ecosystem (Araújo, 2006; Alcântara, 2006). Previous studies of the fish fauna of the Sergipe River estuary demonstrate its richness, comprising 136 species, grouped into 50 families, high indicators even when compared to other environments (Alcântara, 2006). Unfortunately, the richness of the ichthyofauna of this estuary has been severely affected. Mass fish mortality has occurred in the Sal River since 2004. Sampling of this ichthyofauna from various locations, carried out in January 2004, showed different species of fish with fin erosion, a sign of chronic stress, the progression of which can lead to their complete destruction (Alcântara, 2006). Another element that reveals the damage suffered by the Sergipe River is the mangroves in its estuary. It is important to emphasize the enormous importance of mangroves for the fauna and flora of estuaries, coastal waters and as a source of food and income for the populations in their surroundings. Unfortunately, as with the other aspects reported above, mangroves have been destroyed by the combination of real estate development and pollution (Landim and Guimarães, 2006). The foul odor, the death of mangrove trees due to the action of algae and the high levels of contamination by fecal coliforms, present in the water and oysters, at Praia 13 de Julho, are evidence of environmental neglect. Cnot only put the biotic wealth of the estuary and coastal strip at risk, but also make an important economic and protein source unviable, potentially generating jobs, income, and leisure (Landim and Guimarães, 2006). All the information that emerges as a result of the publication of these studies makes public the pressing need to replace a certain megalomaniacal, socially unjust, and ecologically unsustainable development model. At the very moment that Governor João Alves is rightly fighting the transposition of the São Francisco River, he forgets to say that it is already happening. Every day, the adductors transpose 206,755 m3 of water from the São Francisco River to several municipalities in Sergipe. And if it depends on the actions of the state government, the intention is to expand this transposition: Otherwise, how can we explain the much-touted structure that exists under the Aracaju-Barra dos Coqueiros bridge, specifically to receive a adductor? It is as incorrect to build new transpositions of the Velho Chico as it is to expand the ones that already exist. It is fundamentally necessary to revitalize the rivers, advancing in the sustainable use of water bodies. The data presented is indisputable. The Sergipe River is dying a little each day and this is not due to a lack of information and resources, but rather due to a lack of political will, or rather, due to the presence of a monolithic and short-sighted government action that relies solely on engineering when the problem is essentially one of pedagogy. Revitalizing water resources, especially the Sergipe River basin, is something that, unlike the São Francisco River, is up to the state government, which in this regard leaves much to be desired. At a time when technology advances in effluent treatment aimed at removing contaminants not eliminated by conventional methods, in Sergipe, basic treatment is not even being carried out satisfactorily. Finally, it is clear that more than empty talk, there needs to be REAL WILL. An integrated action by the state government, research institutions, private initiative and the population could, in a short time, reestablish the parameters of life on our Sergipe River, truly contributing to the much-touted revitalization of the river of national unity. *PhD in Social Sciences from UNICAMP fredericoromao@uol.com.br

text: Organizaciones sociales de Perú han unido esfuerzos para salvar el río Mantaro, que agoniza a causa de los pesticidas, aguas residuales y desechos de la actividad minera que se vuelcan en su cauce. El Mantaro, que corre en la sierra central de este país a una altitud que varía de los 4.300 a los 3.400 metros sobre el nivel del mar, es una de las principales fuentes de agua para riego y generación de energía eléctrica.   Pero arrastra una carga de metales pesados como cobre, hierro, plomo y zinc, según estudios de organismos estatales y no gubernamentales. Lo amenazan no sólo las explotaciones mineras, sino también la intensa producción agrícola de la zona.   Desde julio de 2006, organizaciones sociales de las seis provincias que el moribundo río atraviesa intentan revertir la situación. Activistas de Chupaca, Concepción, Huancayo, Jauja, Junín y Yauli-La Oroya han lanzado la campaña "El Mantaro revive".   El proyecto contempla el control de la cuenca, tanto en lo que se refiere al agua como al suelo y el aire, con la asistencia de la estadounidense Universidad Saint Louis de Missouri, el cuidado de la salud y la educación ambiental de las poblaciones ribereñas afectadas y la instalación de mesas de diálogo para acordar una agenda común.   [related_articles]  Los resultados de los estudios de control se conocerán en unas pocas semanas, a partir de la firma de convenios con instituciones gubernamentales que avalen los resultados y que, sobre todo, se comprometan a tomar medidas para solucionar el problema.   La cuenca del Mantaro alberga 17 explotaciones mineras en actividad, además de decenas ya abandonadas que causan un grave daño ambiental y a la salud de las personas, según el Ministerio de Energía y Minas.   Además, cerca de él se encuentra la planta metalúrgica de la compañía estadounidense Doe Run, responsable por la contaminación de la ciudad andina de La Oroya y la alta concentración de plomo en la sangre de sus habitantes.   La Comisión Interamericana de Derechos Humanos (CIDH) solicitó al Estado peruano el 31 de agosto la aplicación de medidas cautelares urgentes para proteger la salud, la integridad y la vida de los pobladores de La Oroya.   El agua del Mantaro, según un estudio de la Dirección General de Salud Ambiental, realizado entre enero y marzo de este año, sobrepasó los límites aceptables de plomo y coliformes termotolerantes, bacterias de origen fecal.   El análisis detectó 0,37 microgramos de plomo por litro de agua, cuando el máximo aceptable, según las normas nacionales, es de 0,1. La concentración de coliformes supera en ocho veces el tope tolerable, a consecuencia de las aguas residuales y la basura que se arrojan al río.   Un estudio de 1997, a cargo de consultoras internacionales por pedido del Ministerio de Energía y Minas, indicó que la concentración de metales pesados en el río superaba los límites permitidos tanto por Perú como por las normas ambientales del Banco Mundial.   En 1999, un informe de la Contraloría General de la República, basado en 17 auditorías realizadas ese año, advirtió sobre la pérdida de una cadena de lagunas y el daño a la biodiversidad de la cuenca por la descarga de aguas ácidas y el depósito de desechos de la actividad minera.   Según ese estudio, se generaron "cambios severos en los ecosistemas adyacentes, pérdida de flora, fauna y del recurso agua, y riesgo potencial de afectar aguas subterráneas".   A eso debía sumarse, advirtió el documento, "la polución ácida que se dispersa por efecto de los vientos, degradando los suelos y pastos".   Casi nada cambió desde entonces.   En 2006, un informe de la no gubernamental Unión para el Desarrollo Sustentable de la Provincia de Yauli-La Oroya (UNES), destacó que "los vertimientos líquidos de la actividad minera continúan afectado la calidad de las aguas del río Yauli (que forma parte de la cuenca del Mantaro), no siendo aptas para su uso para riego y bebida de animales".   Uno de los puntos más críticos sigue siendo la zona del túnel Kingsmill, construido para eliminar las aguas de las minas y extraer los metales de los yacimientos. La UNES indica que el Mantaro recibe por esa vía cobre, hierro, zinc y sólidos totales en suspensión.   La compañía Perú Copper, a pedido del gobierno, se encuentra corrigiendo un estudio de factibilidad para construir una planta de tratamiento de estas aguas ácidas.   "El Mantaro en realidad nace muerto", dijo a IPS el secretario de la Mesa de Diálogo Ambiental de Huancayo, Washington Mori. El lago Junín en Cerro de Pasco, que da origen al Mantaro, es el depósito de desechos mineros que marcan el inicio de esta cadena de contaminación.   La contaminación del aire resulta también alarmante, porque según el gubernamental Consejo Nacional del Medio Ambiente (Conam) la chimenea principal del complejo metalúrgico de Doe Run lanza a la atmósfera en promedio 1,5 toneladas de plomo por día.   Además, la planta expulsa 810 toneladas de dióxido de azufre cada 24 horas, más de cuatro veces el nivel máximo permitido por la legislación peruana, según el Ministerio de Energía y Minas.   El Conam sostiene que la fundición es causante de 99 por ciento de los gases tóxicos que respiran los pobladores de La Oroya y que a su vez ocasionan graves enfermedades respiratorias y deficiencias de aprendizaje en los niños.   Estudios de la no gubernamental CooperAcción en 1999 y 2003 y de la Universidad de Saint Louis en 2005 revelaron que la mayoría de los menores de seis años de edad tenían más de 40 microgramos de plomo por decilitro de sangre (mg/dcl), cuatro veces más de los 10 mg/dcl que establece como límite la Organización Mundial de la Salud.   "Por esta situación y debido a la ausencia de monitoreos permanentes, decidimos generar estos estudios técnicos para conocer la verdadera dimensión del problema y empezar a afrontar el reto", señaló a IPS la ingeniera Paula Meza, directora de "El Mantaro revive".   También se preparan papillas nutritivas para 1.600 niños con altos niveles de plomo en sangre y se les entregan dosis de vitamina C, para aminorar los efectos nocivos.   Las mesas de diálogo con dirigentes vecinales y autoridades locales en las seis provincias ribereñas del Mantaro, para discutir una agenda que contribuya a afrontar el problema y sea considerada por las autoridades del gobierno central, es otro aspecto clave.   El 27 de septiembre se logró establecer una de estas mesas en Yauli-La Oroya. Fue un logro, a causa de la poca aceptación a iniciativas ambientales por el respaldo mayoritario que goza Doe Run, motor de la economía local.   "El Mantaro revive" cuenta con un presupuesto de 1,32 millones de dólares para su año y medio de funcionamiento, provenientes del Fondo Ítalo Peruano, además de una contrapartida de otros 500.000 que aporta la Iglesia Católica.   "Quedan muchas cosas pendientes, pero nos damos cuenta de que organizados podemos hacer algo desde la sociedad fortaleciendo capacidades locales. El mayor problema sigue siendo la falta de apoyo a nivel político", señaló Meza.   Sin embargo, esto no debe significar que estas iniciativas tengan que "reemplazar las obligaciones del Estado, porque hay que tener claro que son esfuerzos complementarios", destacó el gerente regional de Recursos Naturales y Gestión del Medio Ambiente de Junín, Iván Lanegra.   Éste es uno de los funcionarios más comprometidos con la campaña contra la contaminación en la zona y considera que uno de los mayores obstáculos es "un esquema nacional fragmentado y por lo tanto también de responsabilidades en el tema social y ambiental".   "Planteamos una figura más centralizada, mediante la articulación de actores nacionales y regionales. Por ejemplo, deberíamos tener un real organismo ambiental independiente, en el que los gobiernos regionales sean los brazos operativos de la fiscalización", concluyó. (FIN/IPS/ms/jsp/la en he cs dv md pr pn sl/07)
text_en: Social organizations in Peru have joined forces to save the Mantaro River, which is dying because of pesticides, waste water and mining waste that are dumped into its bed. The Mantaro, which runs through the central mountains of this country at an altitude that varies from 4,300 to 3,400 meters above sea level, is one of the main sources of water for irrigation and electricity generation. But it carries a load of heavy metals such as copper, iron, lead and zinc, according to studies by state and non-governmental organizations. It is threatened not only by mining operations, but also by the intense agricultural production of the area. Since July 2006, social organizations from the six provinces that the dying river runs through have been trying to reverse the situation. Activists from Chupaca, Concepción, Huancayo, Jauja, Junín and Yauli-La Oroya have launched the campaign "El Mantaro revives." The project involves control of the basin, both in terms of theThe aim is to improve the quality of the water, soil and air, with the assistance of the American Saint Louis University of Missouri, the health care and environmental education of the affected riverside populations and the installation of dialogue tables to agree on a common agenda. [related_articles] The results of the control studies will be known in a few weeks, after the signing of agreements with government institutions that endorse the results and, above all, commit to taking measures to solve the problem. The Mantaro basin is home to 17 active mining operations, in addition to dozens already abandoned that cause serious environmental damage and damage to people's health, according to the Ministry of Energy and Mines. In addition, nearby is the metallurgical plant of the American company Doe Run, responsible for the contamination of the Andean city of La Oroya and the high concentration of lead in the blood of its inhabitants. The Inter-American Commission on Human Rights (IACHR)On August 31, the IACHR requested that the Peruvian State apply urgent precautionary measures to protect the health, integrity and life of the inhabitants of La Oroya. According to a study by the General Directorate of Environmental Health, carried out between January and March of this year, the water from the Mantaro River exceeded the acceptable limits for lead and thermotolerant coliforms, bacteria of fecal origin. The analysis detected 0.37 micrograms of lead per liter of water, when the maximum acceptable level, according to national standards, is 0.1. The concentration of coliforms exceeds the tolerable limit by eight times, as a result of the waste water and garbage dumped into the river. A 1997 study, carried out by international consultants at the request of the Ministry of Energy and Mines, indicated that the concentration of heavy metals in the river exceeded the limits permitted by both Peru and the environmental standards of the World Bank. In 1999, a report by the Comptroller General's OfficeThe report, based on 17 audits carried out that year, warned of the loss of a chain of lagoons and the damage to the biodiversity of the basin due to the discharge of acid water and the deposit of waste from mining activity. According to this study, "severe changes in the adjacent ecosystems, loss of flora, fauna and water resources, and potential risk of affecting groundwater" were generated. To this should be added, the document warned, "the acid pollution that is dispersed by the effect of the winds, degrading the soil and pastures." Almost nothing has changed since then. In 2006, a report by the non-governmental Union for Sustainable Development of the Province of Yauli-La Oroya (UNES), highlighted that "liquid discharges from mining activity continue to affect the quality of the waters of the Yauli River (which is part of the Mantaro basin), making it unsuitable for use for irrigation and animal drinking." One of the most critical points continues to be the areaThe Mantaro is a mine that is located in the north of the state of Huancayo, in the state of Guanacaste ...The smelter is the maximum level permitted by Peruvian law, according to the Ministry of Energy and Mines. Conam maintains that the smelter is responsible for 99 percent of the toxic gases breathed by the inhabitants of La Oroya, which in turn cause serious respiratory illnesses and learning disabilities in children. Studies by the non-governmental organization CooperAcción in 1999 and 2003 and by Saint Louis University in 2005 revealed that the majority of children under six years of age had more than 40 micrograms of lead per decilitre of blood (mg/dcl), four times more than the 10 mg/dcl established as the limit by the World Health Organization. "Due to this situation and due to the lack of permanent monitoring, we decided to carry out these technical studies to understand the true dimension of the problem and begin to face the challenge," engineer Paula Meza, director of "El Mantaro revive", told IPS. Nutritious baby food is also prepared for 1,600 children with high levels of lead.Lead is injected into the bloodstream and they are given doses of vitamin C to lessen the harmful effects. The roundtable discussions with neighborhood leaders and local authorities in the six provinces bordering the Mantaro River, to discuss an agenda that contributes to addressing the problem and is considered by the central government authorities, is another key aspect. On September 27, one of these roundtables was established in Yauli-La Oroya. It was an achievement, due to the low acceptance of environmental initiatives due to the majority support enjoyed by Doe Run, the engine of the local economy. "El Mantaro revives" has a budget of 1.32 million dollars for its year and a half of operation, from the Italian-Peruvian Fund, in addition to a counterpart of another 500,000 provided by the Catholic Church. "There are still many things pending, but we realize that organized society can do something by strengthening local capacities. The biggest problem continues to be the lack of resources, and the lack of resources is a major problem.""We are looking for a more centralized system, through the articulation of national and regional actors. For example, we should have a real independent environmental agency, in which the regional governments are the operational arms of the inspection," he concluded. (END/IPS/ms/jsp/la en he cs dv md pr pn sl/07)

trans_snippet: Dec 21 2013 — Asunción alone throws 3.2 million liters of sewage and industrial waste into its stream every hour without any type of processing, according to...
text: El Río Paraguay, uno de los grandes sistemas acuíferos de Suramérica y fuente clave de agua para el consumo y el riego, recibe cada hora millones de litros de residuos urbanos sin tratar de ciudades de Brasil, Argentina y Paraguay, y una creciente carga de productos químicos usados en agricultura.                                    Solo Asunción arroja a su corriente 3,2 millones de litros de basura cloacal e industrial cada hora sin ningún tipo de procesamiento, según dijo a Efe Osmar Sarubbi, presidente de la Empresa de Servicios Sanitarios del Paraguay (Essap). La capital de Paraguay, cuya área metropolitana, con más de 2,6 millones de personas, es el mayor núcleo demográfico bañado por el río, y también su mayor agente pestilente, pues todos sus desperdicios cloacales van directamente a sus aguas. La degradación del río es también común a su paso por Brasil, su lugar de nacimiento, desde donde recorre 2.625 kilómetros que le llevan por Bolivia, Paraguay y Argentina. Elías Díaz, hidrólogo y coordinador del grupo ecologista paraguayo Sobrevivencia, citó en especial la contaminación generada en las ciudades brasileñas de Corumbá (unos 100.000 habitantes), y Cuiabá (con algo más de medio millón), asentada sobre el río del mismo nombre, que es afluente del Paraguay. El río recibe una nueva carga de desperdicios en la urbe argentina de Formosa (unos 230.000 habitantes), que, como las dos anteriores, adolece de un sistema de tratamiento de los efluentes cloacales, que son expulsados en crudo al río. "Tiran todos sus desechos cloacales sin tratamiento al río Paraguay. Entonces tenemos mucha carga de contaminantes", dijo a Efe Díaz. A su paso por Asunción el río forma una bahía, que cuenta con un paseo muy popular, por debajo del cual pasan cuatro vertientes cloacales, y una playa donde nadie puede nadar por el alto nivel de "coliformes fecales" detectado. Otras 12 vertientes evacúan las descargas de la ciudad directamente en la corriente principal del río, según Sarubbi. "La mayoría son desperdicios domésticos e industriales, que por ley deberían ser tratados. Pero lo cierto es que no hay plantas de tratamiento", dijo Sarubbi. La situación se repite en el lago Ypacarai, una de las "postales" de Paraguay y uno de los lugares de veraneo de la capital, a unos 50 kilómetros. Los veraneantes tampoco podrán disfrutar está temporada del lago, conectado con el Paraguay por el río Salado, ya que las autoridades locales han prohibido su uso recreativo tras la invasión de cianobacterias, unas algas originadas por los vertidos de los mataderos y empresas de curtientes. Planta de tratamiento Sarubbi indicó que la situación mejorará en Asunción con la construcción de su primera planta de tratamiento, que costará 85 millones de dólares, En enero se abrirá la licitación para su fase inicial, indicó. "Sería la primera de un total de cuatro plantas para el Gran Asunción que estarían funcionando en cuatro años y tendrán un presupuesto de 584 millones de dólares". Según Sarubbi, con esas plantas en funcionamiento se trataría hasta un 98 por ciento de las aguas cloacales que el Asunción metropolitano arroja al río Paraguay. "Es una necesidad arrastrada desde hace veinte años y estamos pagando las consecuencias con la contaminación de los acuíferos", dijo Sarabbi, que añadió que para 2014 está previsto que se eliminen los cuatro colectores que desembocan en la bahía. Pese a la polución, el río Paraguay sigue siendo el principal abastecedor del agua consumida en Asunción, lo que se explica gracias a sus humedales, que funcionan como filtros descontaminantes. "Ejercen como tratamiento natural, son un elemento purificador, procesadores biológicos de la contaminación y la principal garantía para mantener la calidad de agua del río", dijo Díaz. La cuenca del Paraguay tiene, desde su desembocadura en el Paraná, que le adentra en Argentina, más de un millón de kilómetros cuadrados de superficie, el 30 por ciento de los cuales son humedales. Deforestación Sin embargo, Díaz alertó sobre su constante deterioro, amenazados por la deforestación y el drenaje para la habilitación de tierras agrícolas. "El ecosistema de Cerrado, en el Mato Grosso, y el Pantanal del Alto Paraguay, están siendo transformados en campos para el cultivo de arroz y soja, para lo cual se utilizan químicos tóxicos" que terminan en el río, indicó. El Pantanal, repartido entre el sur de Brasil, Paraguay y norte de Bolivia, está considerado el ecosistema de humedad tropical más grande del mundo. "Los humedales son los pulmones del río. Sin ellos el río se muere", dijo Díaz. EFE
text_en: The Paraguay River, one of the largest aquifer systems in South America and a key source of water for consumption and irrigation, receives millions of liters of untreated urban waste every hour from cities in Brazil, Argentina and Paraguay, and a growing load of chemicals used in agriculture. Asunción alone dumps 3.2 million liters of sewage and industrial waste into its stream every hour without any type of processing, Osmar Sarubbi, president of the Paraguayan Sanitation Services Company (Essap), told Efe. The capital of Paraguay, whose metropolitan area, with more than 2.6 million people, is the largest population center bathed by the river, and also its greatest pestilential agent, since all its sewage waste goes directly into its waters. The degradation of the river is also common as it passes through Brazil, its birthplace, from where it travels 2,625 kilometers that take it through Bolivia, Paraguay and Argentina. Elias Diaz, a hydrologist and coordinator of the Paraguayan environmental group Sobrevivencia, cited in particular the pollution generated in the Brazilian cities of Corumba (about 100,000 inhabitants) and Cuiaba (with just over half a million), located on the river of the same name, which is a tributary of the Paraguay. The river receives a new load of waste in the Argentine city of Formosa (about 230,000 inhabitants), which, like the two previous cities, lacks a system for treating sewage effluents, which are expelled raw into the river. "They dump all their sewage waste into the Paraguay River without treatment. So we have a lot of pollutants," Diaz told Efe. As it passes through Asuncion, the river forms a bay, which has a very popular promenade, under which four sewage drains pass, and a beach where no one can swim due to the high level of "fecal coliforms" detected. Another 12 springs evacuate the city's waste directly into the main stream of the river, according to Sarubbi. "Most of it is domestic and industrial waste, which by law should be treated. But the truth is that there are no treatment plants," said Sarubbi. The situation is repeated at Lake Ypacarai, one of Paraguay's "postcards" and one of the capital's summer resorts, some 50 kilometers away. Vacationers will not be able to enjoy the lake this season, connected to Paraguay by the Salado River, as local authorities have prohibited its recreational use following the invasion of cyanobacteria, algae caused by discharges from slaughterhouses and tanning companies. Treatment plant Sarubbi indicated that the situation will improve in Asunción with the construction of its first treatment plant, which will cost 85 million dollars. The tender for its initial phase will open in January, he said. "It would be the first of a total of four plants for Greater Asunción that would be operational in four years and will have a budget of 584 million dollars." According to Sarubbi, with these plants in operation, up to 98 percent of the sewage that metropolitan Asunción dumps into the Paraguay River would be treated. "It has been a necessity for twenty years and we are paying the consequences with the contamination of the aquifers," said Sarabbi, who added that by 2014 it is planned to eliminate the four collectors that flow into the bay. Despite the pollution, the Paraguay River continues to be the main supplier of water consumed in Asunción, which is explained by its wetlands, which function as decontaminating filters. "They act as a natural treatment, they are a purifying element, biological processors of contamination and the main guarantee to maintain the quality of the river's water," said Díaz. The Paraguay basin has, from its mouth in the Paraná, which enters Argentina, more than one million square kilometers of surface, 30 percent of which is100 percent of which are wetlands. Deforestation However, Díaz warned about their constant deterioration, threatened by deforestation and drainage for the development of agricultural land. "The Cerrado ecosystem, in Mato Grosso, and the Pantanal of Alto Paraguay, are being transformed into fields for the cultivation of rice and soybeans, for which toxic chemicals are used" that end up in the river, he indicated. The Pantanal, spread across southern Brazil, Paraguay and northern Bolivia, is considered the largest tropical humid ecosystem in the world. "The wetlands are the lungs of the river. Without them the river dies," said Díaz. EFE

text: Es el más contaminado de Córdoba por falta de saneamiento desde las Sierras hasta Mar Chiquita donde ya se perciben impactos. De 1 6 millones de habitantes sólo el 37  cuenta hoy con cloacas. En una década por las obras en Capital subiría al 87 . Punilla sigue sin avances. Sin vueltas, el río Suquía es el más contaminado de Córdoba. El mayor impacto que recibe es uno de los que, según los especialistas, más fácilmente se podrían revertir, aunque lleva décadas de degradación acumulada. No lo afecta la contaminación industrial sino, sobre todo, la que proviene de la falta de tratamiento de los líquidos cloacales de 25 pueblos y ciudades ubicadas en todo su recorrido, con la Capital como fuente principal.  El Suquía (o Primero) se ha transformado en un desagüe cloacal, desde su nacimiento en las sierras de Punilla hasta su final en la laguna Mar Chiquita. Su degradado estado tendría solución si durante años se hicieran las obras de saneamiento en sus 200 kilómetros de recorrido. ¿Cuántas cloacas faltan en toda su travesía?, ¿qué obras están en marcha para reducir el impacto?   El Suquía nace en el Valle de Punilla, de la unión de los ríos Cosquín y San Antonio y de los arroyos Los Chorrillos y Las Mojarras. Todos se juntan en el embalse San Roque. Todos llegan allí ya con síntomas de degradación por falta de tratamiento cloacal. En el San Roque se acentúa el problema. Luego, atraviesa la ciudad capital (donde vive el 40 por ciento de los cordobeses), con una insuficiente red cloacal y una planta de tratamiento desbordada. Aguas abajo de la ciudad de Córdoba es donde se miden los síntomas más graves de contaminación por materia fecal. Luego, queda el mayor recorrido hasta que entrega sus aguas a la Mar Chiquita, la quinta laguna salada más grande del mundo. Pero en ese tramo (que atraviesa el departamento Río Primero) sólo pasa por tres pueblos que apenas representan el uno por ciento del total de habitantes de toda la cuenca que recorre el río.  En números, esa cuenca suma 185 mil habitantes en 21 localidades de Punilla; 1,4 millones en Córdoba capital, y los apenas 17 mil que viven, aguas abajo, en Capilla de los Remedios, Río Primero y Santa Rosa de Río Primero. De todo ese mapa, están en marcha obras para optimizar el tratamiento cloacal en la ciudad de Córdoba, y para crearlo en Río Primero y Santa Rosa. En Punilla, área clave de origen, nada pasa por ahora. Si las obras de cloacas en marcha en Capital se terminan, hacia 2030 se duplicaría la cantidad de usuarios con cobertura potencial.  Hoy, escaso porcentaje de habitantes con redes A la mar  Un reciente informe de La Voz dio cuenta de los primeros indicios del impacto del río Suquía sobre la Mar Chiquita. Aunque se admite que restan estudios más puntuales, varios trabajos científicos han anticipado que en la Laguna del Plata, el estuario en el que desemboca el río, se percibe ya una degradación. En ese punto –una porción muy menor de la enorme laguna–, se detectó una alta presencia de cianobacterias (algas), la más clásica consecuencia de la presencia del fósforo y nitrógeno que aportan, sobre todo, los líquidos cloacales. Esa porción del estuario ya tiene un parecido con el dique San Roque. La cuestión es relevante porque implicaría la señal de degradación de un reducto que parecía a salvo del impacto y, además, porque Mar Chiquita está a punto de transformarse en el más nuevo parque nacional de Argentina. Esa categoría requerirá un alto grado de preservación ambiental.  En Punilla Un informe publicado por este diario concluyó hace un año que de los 185 mil personas que habitan las 21 localidades vinculadas a la cuenca del río Suquía en Punilla, sólo el 21 por ciento tiene redes cloacales disponibles. Sin embargo, el número real de conectados sería aún menor: que pase la red no implica que los vecinos sean usuarios del sistema. El San Roque es el reservorio donde se acumula ese problema. En su cuenca, hoy, no hay ninguna obra de cloacas en marcha ni licitada. Quedan, sí, promesas por venir. Cuenca alta. Comprende a La Falda, Huerta Grande, Valle Hermoso y Villa Giardino. Según sus municipios, tienen un 55 por ciento promedio de cobertura en cloacas, pero con problemas de funcionamiento. Matías Montoto, intendente de Huerta Grande, graficó que, aunque la red circula por la mitad del pueblo, sólo el 10 por ciento está conectado. "Pesa el alto costo de la conexión, acá es de unos 25 mil pesos por frentista", marcó. Montoto confirmó que, la semana pasada, el Ministerio del Interior de la Nación les anunció que este año licitaría la obra para que esas cuatro localidades lleguen al 100 por ciento de cloacas. Por ahora no hay proyecto ni presupuesto definido. Montoto insistió en que además de tender redes "habrá que ver cómo se logra que la gente se conecte". Cuenca media. En 2016, el Gobierno provincial anunció que con un crédito del exterior, por 366 millones de pesos, construiría el sistema cloacal base para Cosquín, Santa María, Bialet Massé y Siquiman. En febrero pasado, se anunció el llamado a licitación, agregando la cobertura para Tanti. Pero el proceso no registra avances. Alberto Bresciano, secretario de Servicios Públicos de la Provincia, explicó que la licitación se postergó "porque falta cerrar el financiamiento". Señaló que "el proyecto está listo, tiene la audiencia pública hecha y el permiso de vuelco al dique San Roque; lo que falta es definir de dónde saldrán los fondos". Bresciano apuntó que una gestión de créditos ante fondos árabes se complicó por el nuevo escenario financiero nacional, y que se reiniciaron las gestiones de la Provincia por recursos ante el Ente Nacional de Obras Hídricas y Saneamiento (Enhosa). Para esa obra, en 2016 el Gobierno nacional había prometido aportar el 67 por ciento, con el 33 restante a cargo de la Provincia. Pero hoy no hay certezas. En otras obras de cloacas con similar compromiso y ya iniciadas (en Capital, Río Cuarto y San Francisco), la Provincia asevera que la Nación aún no giró su parte. Mientras, el costo se reactualiza: según Bresciano, la obra costaría ahora unos 800 millones, más otros 300 millones para agregar a Tanti. El funcionario precisó que el proyecto provincial involucra la infraestructura básica y más costosa: “el caño máximo colector, la planta depuradora, las estaciones de bombeo y la descarga”. Esa obra, no licitada aún, tendrá un plazo de ejecución de dos años. Y las redes domiciliarias posteriores deberán ser gestionadas luego por cada municipio, con el aporte de sus frentistas. Aun acelerando, llevará varios años cubrir esa área con el servicio. Cuenca sur. Ninguna de las comunas ubicadas sobre el río San Antonio tiene ni un metro de cloacas. Icho Cruz, Cuesta Blanca, Tala Huasi, Mayu Sumaj y San Antonio están en ese lote. "Esa zona es la que está más demorada", admitió Bresciano. "Ahora estamos armando el proyecto, que en unos seis meses estará listo", acotó. Pero nadie habla aún de licitación ni de plazos, y menos aún de financiamiento. Villa Carlos Paz. Representa casi la mitad de la población de la cuenca de Punilla. Tiene una planta cloacal inaugurada en 2007 (fue hecha con fondos nacionales), con capacidad para toda la ciudad. Pero sólo tendió redes en el 28 por ciento de la zona urbana y se estima que en esa área más del 20 por ciento de los usuarios no está conectado. El año pasado, tras varios días de ofrecer una patética imagen de deterioro el dique San Roque, el municipio anunció que, con aval provincial, gestionaría un crédito ante la Nación para ampliar esa red. Pero no hubo avances hasta ahora. Emilio Iosa, hasta hace un mes secretario de Políticas Saludables de Carlos Paz, planteó que "la situación es de alerta, por la presencia probada de bacterias coliformes fecales medidas en varios sectores del lago, por encima del tope admitido para su uso recreativo". También advirtió de que "resultados de laboratorio muestran ya indicios de esa presencia también en el río San Antonio", y aclaró que sobre el Cosquín (el otro afluente) no hubo análisis de ese municipio. El médico Iosa marcó que la gestión del crédito ante la Nación sigue en trámite: "Eran 192 millones de pesos, para completar sólo el primer anillo, con lo que se llegaría quizá a cubrir el 50 por ciento de la ciudad", precisó. "Una lástima tan poco avance, teniendo una planta ya hecha para tratar el 100 por ciento de la ciudad", remató Iosa. Aguas abajo, tres pueblos Entre la ciudad de Córdoba y la laguna Mar Chiquita está el mayor recorrido del río. Pero, a la vez, donde se genera el menor impacto. Hay sólo tres localidades en esa extensión: Capilla de los Remedios (mil habitantes, a 35 kilómetros de la Capital), Río Primero (ocho mil pobladores, a 58 kilómetros de Córdoba) y Santa Rosa (ocho mil habitantes, a 90 kilómetros). Para las dos mayores, la Provincia ya licitó y adjudicó las obras básicas de cloacas. En ambos casos, anunció su finalización para 2019. Luego, pasarán algunos años más hasta que la red urbana llegue a la mayoría de las viviendas en ambas. En todo el departamento Río Primero, que el río Suquía atraviesa, sólo el 2,7 por ciento de los habitantes está hoy conectado a redes de saneamiento cloacal. De 1.600.000 vecinos, sólo 600 mil con cloacas Es la población que habita hoy en la cuenca del río Suquía. Son 25 los pueblos y ciudades ubicados sobre el río. De ellos, hoy, sólo 600 mil (el 37 por ciento) cuentan con redes de cloacas disponibles. Pero el número real de conectados al servicio es menor. En el Valle de Punilla viven 185 mil personas (sin contar turistas) y tiene redes el 21 por ciento. En la Capital, cuenta con redes el 40 por ciento de sus 1,4 millones de habitantes. Y en la cuenca baja (departamento Río Primero) no hay pueblos con redes por ahora.
text_en: It is the most polluted river in Córdoba due to the lack of sanitation from the mountains to Mar Chiquita, where the impacts are already being felt. Of the 1.6 million inhabitants, only 37% have sewers today. In a decade, due to the works in the Capital, the number would rise to 87%. Punilla continues to have no progress. Without a doubt, the Suquía River is the most polluted river in Córdoba. The greatest impact it receives is one of those that, according to specialists, could be most easily reversed, although it has been degraded for decades. It is not affected by industrial pollution, but, above all, by the pollution that comes from the lack of treatment of sewage from 25 towns and cities located along its entire course, with the Capital as its main source. The Suquía (or Primero) has been transformed into a sewage drain, from its source in the mountains of Punilla to its end in the Mar Chiquita lagoon. Its degraded state would be solved if, over the years, sanitation works were carried out along its 200 kilometers of course. How many sewers are missing along its entire journey? What works are underway to reduce the impact? The Suquía is born in the Punilla Valley, from the union of the Cosquín and San Antonio rivers and the Los Chorrillos and Las Mojarras streams. They all join together in the San Roque reservoir. They all arrive there already with symptoms of degradation due to lack of sewage treatment. The problem is accentuated in the San Roque. Then, it crosses the capital city (where 40 percent of the people of Córdoba live), with an inadequate sewage network and an overflowing treatment plant. Downstream of the city of Córdoba is where the most serious symptoms of contamination by fecal matter are measured. Then, there is the longest journey until it delivers its waters to the Mar Chiquita, the fifth largest salt lake in the world. But in that section (which crosses the Río Primero department) it only passes through three towns that barely represent one percent of the total inhabitants of the entire basin that the river runs through. In numbers, that basin has 185 thousand inhabitants in 21 localities of Punilla; 1.4 million in Córdoba capital, and the barely 17 thousand who live downstream in Capilla de los Remedios, Río Primero and Santa Rosa de Río Primero. Of all that map, there are works underway to optimize sewage treatment in the city of Córdoba, and to create it in Río Primero and Santa Rosa. At that point – a very minor portion of the enormous lagoon – a high presence of cyanobacteria (algae) was detected, the most classic consequence of the presence of phosphorus and nitrogen, which are mainly provided by sewage. That portion of the estuary already bears a resemblance to the San Roque dam. The issue is relevant because it would imply the sign of degradation of a redoubt that seemed safe from the impact and, in addition, because Mar Chiquita is about to become the newest national park in Argentina. That category will require a high degree of environmental preservation. In Punilla A report published by this newspaper a year ago concluded that of the 185 thousand people who live in the 21 localities linked to the Suquía River basin in Punilla, only 21 percent have sewage networks available. However, the real number of those connected would be even lower: the fact that the network is connected does not imply that the neighbors are users of the system. The San Roque is the reservoir where this problem accumulates. In its basin, today, there are no sewage works underway or tendered. There are, yes,promises to come. Upper Cuenca. It includes La Falda, Huerta Grande, Valle Hermoso and Villa Giardino. According to their municipalities, they have an average of 55 percent coverage in sewers, but with problems of operation. Matías Montoto, mayor of Huerta Grande, illustrated that, although the network runs through half of the town, only 10 percent is connected. "The high cost of the connection weighs, here it is about 25 thousand pesos per frontage," he said. Montoto confirmed that, last week, the Ministry of the Interior of the Nation announced that this year it would tender the work so that these four localities reach 100 percent sewers. For now there is no project or defined budget. Montoto insisted that in addition to laying networks "we will have to see how to get people connected." Middle Cuenca. In 2016, the provincial government announced that with a foreign loan of 366 million pesos, it would build the basic sewage system for Cosquín, Santa María, Bialet Massé and Siquiman. Last February, the call for tenders was announced, adding coverage for Tanti. But the process has not made progress. Alberto Bresciano, Secretary of Public Services of the Province, explained that the tender was postponed "because the financing has yet to be closed." He pointed out that "the project is ready, the public hearing has been held and the permit to overflow into the San Roque dam has been obtained; what is missing is to define where the funds will come from." Bresciano pointed out that the management of credits with Arab funds was complicated by the new national financial scenario, and that the Province's efforts for resources with the National Entity for Water Works and Sanitation (Enhosa) were restarted. For this project, in 2016 the national government had promised to contribute 67 percent, with the remaining 33 percent to be covered by the Province. But today there are no certainties. Meanwhile, the cost is being updated: according to Bresciano, the work would now cost about 800 million, plus another 300 million to add to Tanti. The official specified that the provincial project involves the basic and most expensive infrastructure: “the main collector pipe, the treatment plant, the pumping stations and the discharge.” This work, not yet tendered, will have a two-year execution period. And the subsequent residential networks must then be managed by each municipality, with the contribution of its front-line contractors. Even accelerating, it will take several years to cover that area with the service. Southern Basin. None of the communities located on the San Antonio River has even a meter of sewers. Icho Cruz, Cuesta Blanca, Tala Huasi, Mayu Sumaj and San Antonio are in that lot. "That area is the one that is taking the longest," Bresciano admitted. "We are now putting together the project, which will be ready in about six months," he added. But no one is talking about bidding or deadlines yet, and even less about financing. Villa Carlos Paz. It represents almost half of the population of the Punilla basin. It has a sewage plant inaugurated in 2007 (it was built with national funds), with capacity for the entire city. But it only laid networks in 28 percent of the urban area and it is estimated that in that area more than 20 percent of the users are not connected. Last year, after several days of offering a pathetic image of the deterioration of the San Roque dam, the municipality announced that, with provincial backing, it would manage a loan with the Nation to expand that network. "It is a shame so little progress, having a plant already built to treat 100 percent of the city," Iosa concluded. There are only three towns in that extension: Capilla de los Remedios (one thousand inhabitants, 35 kilometers from the Capital), Río Primero (eight thousand inhabitants, 58 kilometers from Córdoba) and Santa Rosa (eight thousand inhabitants, 90 kilometers). text: QUALIDADE DA ÁGUA E INCIDÊNCIA DE DOENÇAS DE TRANSMISSÃO HÍDRICA NO CANAL SÃO GONÇALO, PELOTAS/RS              Código              XXIII-SBRH0600                            Autores              Carolina Faccio Demarco, Robson Andreazza, Josiane Farias, Thays França Afonso, Maurizio Silveira Quadro, Cassia Brocca Caballero                                        Tema              07 - Qualidade da água                                        Resumo              O canal São Gonçalo é responsável pela ligação da Lagoa dos Patos com a Lagoa Mirim e vêm sofrendo alterações em suas características físicas, químicas e biológicas devido ao lançamento de efluentes sem tratamento. Para a avaliação da qualidade da água, foi utilizado o Índice de Qualidade da Água, de acordo com a metodologia de APHA (2005). A determinação da concentração de coliformes fecais foi realizada pelo método de tubos múltiplos com meio de cultura A-1. Foram realizadas 10 coletas de água no período de 2013 à 2015, em cinco pontos amostrais ao longo do Canal São Gonçalo. No período monitorado, a água do Canal São Gonçalo recebeu três classificações de qualidade de água: 54,54  obteve valor de IQA correspondentes a qualidade de água aceitável, 36,36   qualidade ruim e 9,09  qualidade boa. Pode-se dizer que a água do Canal São Gonçalo vem sofrendo grandes interferências ocasionando a degradação de qualidade da água. O valor elevado de coliformes fecais encontrado em alguns pontos pode ser relacionado à contribuição de despejos de esgotos sanitários provenientes do centro urbano de Pelotas, representando uma ameaça à população devido à possível disseminação de doenças.
text_en: WATER QUALITY AND INCIDENCE OF WATERBORNE DISEASES IN THE SÃO GONÇALO CANAL, PELOTAS/RS Code XXIII-SBRH0600 Authors Carolina Faccio Demarco, Robson Andreazza, Josiane Farias, Thays França Afonso, Maurizio Silveira Quadro, Cassia Brocca Caballero Theme 07 - Water quality Abstract The São Gonçalo canal is responsible for connecting Lagoa dos Patos with Lagoa Mirim and has been undergoing changes in its physical, chemical and biological characteristics due to the release of untreated effluents. The Water Quality Index was used to assess water quality, according to the APHA methodology (2005). The determination of fecal coliform concentration was performed by the multiple tube method with A-1 culture medium. Ten water samples were collected between 2013 and 2014.015, at five sampling points along the São Gonçalo Canal. During the monitoring period, the water from the São Gonçalo Canal received three water quality classifications: 54.54 obtained an IQA value corresponding to acceptable water quality, 36.36 poor quality and 9.09 good quality. It can be said that the water from the São Gonçalo Canal has been suffering major interferences, causing degradation of water quality. The high value of fecal coliforms found at some points may be related to the contribution of sewage discharges from the urban center of Pelotas, representing a threat to the population due to the possible spread of diseases.
