Nitratos                          La cantidad de nitratos          fluctuó entre 0,225 y 1,40 ppm. La norma chilena para agua potable, establece          un límite máximo de 10 ppm, aún cuando el Ministerio de Salud puede aceptar          un contenido mayor. El valor es similar al establecido por la EPA en Estados          Unidos. Cuando el nitrato está presente en aguas de pozo, significa que          existe en exceso en el área por acción directa o indirecta de la agricultura,          fertilización de césped o tanques sépticos.                        N-amoniacal                          El nitrógeno amoniacal          presentó valores entre 0,02 y 1,18 ppm. El valor máximo siempre estuvo          en las estaciones de muestreo 6-8, que son las más cercanas a los colectores          de alcantarillado y zonas productoras de hortalizas. Cantidades superiores          a 1ppm son indicadoras de contaminación sensible.           Sólidos suspendidos                          Valores mayores a          25 y menores a 50 ppm corresponden a concentraciones asignadas a clase          3 de aguas que están relacionadas con zonas inferiores de ciertos ríos          de premontaña y llanura, que presentan una buena situación. La mayor parte          de los valores están muy cercanos a los rangos señalados con la excepción          de la estación de muestreo 8 correspondiente al puente de Carahue en la          estación de verano con 248 ppm.           Aluminio                          El aluminio presentó          concentraciones entre 0,002 y 0,055 ppm.  Las cuales se encuentran por          debajo de las 5 ppm  establecidas como norma para aguas de regadío en          Chile y por debajo de 0,2 ppm  establecidas en España en relación con          la estructura de aguas naturales para aguas potables (MOPT,          1992).           Cobre                          Los ríos estudiados          presentaron concentraciones de cobre entre 0,17 y 0,63 ppm. Sin antecedentes          previos, esta diferencia se puede atribuir a características propias de          la geología del río, sin embargo no se puede establecer en forma definitiva          con la información originada por un periodo muy corto, por lo que se debe          mantener un monitoreo permanente con el fin de captar las variaciones          específicas del sistema. La norma de calidad de aguas para regadío en          Chile establece valores de 0,20 ppm, en cambio los valores patrones para          calidad de aguas en España de acuerdo con MOPT (1992)          es de 100 ppb. Las concentraciones de cobre superiores a 3000 ppb pueden          producir sabores astringen tes y coloraciones. Cu siendo un metal esencial          para los organismos, cuando sobrepasa ciertas concentraciones, puede producir          efectos tóxicos, principalmente trastornos gastrointestinales y hepáticos.           Magnesio                          Las concentraciones          fluctuaron entre 0,95 y 1,82 ppm. El contenido de magnesio en las aguas          superficiales varía entre 1 y 40 ppm, sobrepasando a veces los 100 ppm          en las aguas que pasan por terrenos ricos en sales de magnesio. De igual          forma las concentraciones de magnesio son inferiores a la Norma Chilena          de Calidad de Agua de regadío (0,20 ppm).           Cinc                          El cinc no se considera          tóxico, aunque confiere al agua un sabor desagradable. Los valores encontrados          fueron entre 0,02 y 0,14  ppm. La norma chilena para agua potable acepta          hasta 5 ppm. En aguas saladas y dulces es muy estable.            Hierro                          Los ríos estudiados          presentaron concentraciones de hierro que oscilaron entre los 0,21 y 0,56          ppm.  Las concentraciones son inferiores al estándar de calidad de aguas          de regadío (0,5 ppm), según Norma Chilena 1333 (1978),          e inferiores a los niveles patrón y concentraciones máximas admisibles          exigidos para aguas de riego en España (200 ppb) (MOPT,          1992).           El hierro puede aparecer          en el agua en sus distintos estados de oxidación, no se considera tóxico          para el hombre aunque puede dar origen a problemas de olor o sabor, incluso          a bajas concentraciones. El hierro puede depositarse como hidróxido y          obturar las branquias de los organismos, disminuyendo su potencial respiratorio.          Los huevos y las larvas cultivadas son más sensibles a estos metales,          produciéndose entonces su muerte.           El hierro en el medio          acuático no es nocivo al estar en bajo contenido, pero suele serlo en          presencia de altas concentraciones. Para las truchas, con valores de pH          en agua de 6,5 a 7,5 y concentraciones de 0,9 ppm de hierro, es de efecto          mortal (debe ser oxidado).           Los metales pesados          pueden presentarse en forma de trazas en las aguas de abastecimiento superficiales,          su toxicidad puede llegar a ser alta y es aumentada por diversos factores,          entre ellos  principalmente el pH, el oxígeno disuelto y la temperatura.          El ingreso a los cultivos se produce a través del agua de abastecimiento          y como consecuencia de operaciones industriales efectuadas por el hombre(          papeleras, extracción de minerales, curtiembres, etc.)  o bien porque          son producto del arrastre de las aguas. El principal problema radica en          que son bioacumulables, afectan el sistema neuromuscular y pueden llegar          a ser letales.           Boro                          Se encuentra en cantidades          de 0,01 a 0,06 ppm no presentando problemas para su uso como agua para          riego, por cuanto la Norma Chilena acepta como límite máximo 0,75 ppm.                      El boro es esencial          para los vegetales, en especial para los frutales; sin embargo, presenta          la característica de funcionalidad ambivalente, puesto que, por sobre          un nivel crítico de disponibilidad en el agua de riego, genera un efecto          de toxicidad limitante al desarrollo de la especie, dependiendo de la          concentración de boro disponible y de la sensibilidad y tolerancia que          presenta cada especie.           DBO5           La demanda bioquímica          de oxígeno, se presentó con un rango de 0,44 a 2,41 ppm. Si se considera          que corresponde a la cantidad de oxígeno disuelto en el agua, necesario          para la oxidación bioquímica aeróbica de las sustancias orgánicas presentes          en el agua, la DBO5 es por tanto un buen indicador de la calidad          general del agua y concretamente de la contaminación orgánica. Valores          de la DBO5 superiores a 10 ppm, son característicos de aguas          muy contaminadas y valores menores  de 3 ppm indicarían una contaminación          muy débil. Por lo anterior se trata de aguas muy débilmente contaminadas.           DQO                                       La DQO que es la cantidad          de oxígeno  ocupado para oxidar toda la materia orgánica oxidable, tanto          la orgánica como la mineral. Existe una cierta relación entre la DQO y          la DBO5, siendo esta última una fracción de la DQO comprendida          entre el 2 y el 70 . Los ríos presentaron valores entre 2 y 406. Este          valor mas alto correspondió a la estación de muestreo cercana a la desembocadura.                          Las aguas no contaminadas          tienen valores de DQO de 1 a 5 ppm, o algo superiores. Las aguas residuales          domésticas suelen contener entre 250 y 600 ppm (Orrego,          2002). El valor de la DQO es siempre superior al de DBO5 porque muchas          sustancias orgánicas pueden oxidarse químicamente, pero no biológicamente.           Indicadores microbiológicos                          El anteproyecto de           norma de calidad para la protección de las aguas continentales superficiales,          establece para coliformes fecales en las aguas que se utilicen en actividades          con contacto directo y el riego de frutas y hortalizas que se desarrollan          a ras de suelo y que habitualmente se consumen sin proceso de cocción          un máximo de 1000 coliformes fecales/100 mL, y 2000 coliformes totales/100          mL. Las distancias entre las estaciones          están expresadas como disimilaridad entre 0 y 1. La medida de distancia          corresponde al índice City Block y grupo promedio como método de agrupación.    "v:shapes="_x0000_s1073">           La norma secundaria          de calidad ambiental para la protección de las aguas continentales perficiales           chilenas,  en  su  artículo  cuarto dice relación con las aguas aptas          para la protección y conservación de las comunidades acuáticas y los usos          prioritarios  contemplan para coliformes totales y fecales cinco categorías          que van desde clase de excepción hasta clase 4, en un rango desde 10 a          menos de 10000 NMP por 100 ml. (CONAMA, 2000). Los ríos          presentaron en coliformes totales un mínimo de 33 y un máximo de 5400          expresado como NMP/100ml. En cuanto a coliformes fecales se presentó un          mínimo de 2 y un máximo de 790 NMP/100 ml. Lo anterior permite señalar          que existen tres estaciones en las cuales se superaron los valores máximos          de coliformes totales, convirtiéndolas en agua no apta para actividades          con contacto directo y para riego de frutas y hortalizas.           Análisis estadístico                          Utilizando las bases          de datos de calidad de aguas, se realizó un Análisis de Cluster,  el cual          permite mostrar las relaciones intergrupos indicando el nivel de disimilaridad          entre las estaciones de muestreo en función del perfil físico químico          (Field et al., 1982). Se utilizó como medida de distancia          el índice  City Block (STSC, 1989) y el método jerárquico          UPGMA como método de agrupación.            Se puede observar          en las figuras 2 y 3, que las estaciones           muestreos  6, 7 y 10 se diferencian del resto a un nivel de 50  de similaridad          tanto en verano como invierno. La estación 6 corresponde al sector de          Ragñin-tuleufu situada a la salida de Temuco, posterior a las descargas          de los colectores de alcantarillado. La estación 7 se ubica en la ciudad          de Imperial influenciada por las descargas urbanas. En cambio la estación          10 corresponde a la desembocadura del río con influencia marina.                                        CONCLUSIONES                          A partir de los resultados          mostrados, de su análisis y de su discusión, se puede obtener las siguientes          conclusiones:           1.- Las aguas de los          ríos Cautín e Imperial no presentan problemas, de acuerdo a las especificaciones          contempladas en las Normas Chilenas Oficiales, ya que todos los parámetros          evaluados están dentro de los rangos o límites permitidos.           2.- Las concentraciones          de iones presentes en las muestras, tanto cationes como aniones y específicamente          metales pesados se encuentran muy por debajo de los límites establecidos          en las normas (NCh,1333-78 y otras normas internacionales).          Los resultados generales son los esperados para este tipo de ríos andinos          del tipo ritrón en el Sur de Chile, comparados con los 30 ríos estudiados          por Campos (1985).           3.- Los resultados          microbiológicos, aún cuando están bajo los límites establecidos en las          Normas Chilenas permiten predecir que una disminución mayor del caudal          de los ríos a la que se presenta normalmente en el estiaje provocará una          modificación mayor del ecosistema de los ríos, que hoy ya muestran los          resultados de la ausencia de un  plan de manejo integral adecuado.                       AGRADECIMIENTOS           Los autores agradecen          al Proyecto Plan Ambiental para la Provincia de Cautín, a la  Dirección          de Investigación y postgrado de la UCT y a los colegas Teresa Rueda y          José Luis Barahona, por su valiosa colaboración.                       REFERENCIAS           Campos,          H. Muñoz-Pedreros2 and P. Mejias1 Catholic University of Temuco, Fac. of Sciences, (1) Department of Biological Sciences and Chemistry, (2) School of Environmental Sciences, Casilla 15-D, Temuco-Chile (e-mail: nrivera@uct.cl) Abstract The objective of this work was to establish the descriptive water quality of the Cautín and Imperial rivers that make up the Imperial River watershed located in the IX Region of Araucanía-Chile. The physicochemical and microbiological characterization was carried out by setting up ten sampling stations. The results show that the waters of these rivers do not present physicochemical problems, according to official Chilean standards. In the microbiological part, a high count of total coliform bacteria was found in some sampling stations, which makes them unsuitable for activities with direct contact and for the irrigation of vegetables and fruits that grow at ground level. It can be predicted that a decrease in the flow of the rivers during the dry season will cause the greatest modification of the ecosystem, a situation that is made more critical by the lack of an adequate integral management plan. Abstract The objective of this work was to establish the descriptive water quality of the Cautín and Imperial rivers which form the Imperial River hydrographic basin in the IX Region of Araucanía, Chile. Physicochemical and microbiological evaluations were made at ten sampling stations. Physicochemical parameters measured in these rivers did not exceed the legally established Chilean water criteria. Microbiological testing showed high counts of coliform bacteria at some stations, exceeding water quality criteria for use in direct contact activities as well as for watering fruits and vegetables that develop at ground level. It can be predicted that reductions in river flow volume during dry periods will produce further modifications in this environment, which at present is not regulated by an appropriate integral management plan. Keywords: water quality, water chemistry, microbiological tests, environmental management INTRODUCTION Nowadays, it is as important to know the quality of water for human consumption as it is for irrigating crops, for industrial use in boilers, for the manufacture of pharmaceutical products, for the issuance of environmental licenses, to design and execute monitoring programs in environmental assessments, to adapt it to the multiple analytical applications of laboratories and to regulate and optimize the operation of treatment plants, among many other purposes (Cárdenas, 2003). The IX Region of Araucanía, located in the southern part of Chile and extending between 37º35 and 39º35 South latitude and from 70º50 West longitude to the Pacific Ocean, with an area of ​​31,858.4 km2, is not immune to the problems of deterioration of water courses. The IX Region has two important hydrographic basins, which are fully developed within it, these are: the Imperial River and the Toltén. In addition, the Biobio River is born in the region, which occupies a territory of 1,000 hectares.commerce of its basin in the Araucanía region. There is also a small part of the Valdivia River, corresponding to the upper part of the Cruces River. Finally, the coastal basins stand out, those that drain directly to the sea in the coastal mountain range. The Imperial River basin occupies a total area of ​​approximately 12,900 km2, bordered to the north by the Biobio basin, to the east by the Biobio and Toltén river basins, to the west by small coastal basins, and to the south by the Toltén river basin. In this region, the main problem of river pollution is associated with the cities located on their banks, with a significant population increase, as is the case of Lautaro, Temuco, Nueva Imperial and Carahue. These urban centers pour their wastewater directly into the waterways, without prior treatment. The most direct example is the Cautín River, which receives wastewater from Temuco, Padre Las Casas and Lautaro, which discharge an untreated flow of 407.1 L/s (12,842,462 m3/year), with an organic load, BOD5 of 2,569 t/year. Curacautín discharges an untreated wastewater flow of 10.5 L/s into the Loncopira River, with an organic load, BOD5 of 66 t/year (Orrego, 2002). Downstream, Vilcún discharges an untreated wastewater flow of 4 L/s into the Vilcún River, with an organic load, BOD5 of 1 t/year. Carahue discharges an untreated wastewater flow of 9.7 L/s into the Imperial River, with an organic load, BOD5 of 61 t/year. In this section, there are also pig slaughterhouses and meat factories, about whose discharges there is no information (Orrego, 2002). The total discharges of wastewater, through various rivers and streams, and with various degrees and types of treatment, to the Imperial River basin, reach 515.9 L/s, which is equivalent to 16,270,798 m3/year, with a total BOD5 organic load of 2,943 t/year. The total discharges of wastewater in the basins of Region IX reach 603.2 L/s, which is equivalent to 19,022,644 m3/year, with a total BOD5 organic load of 3,336 t/year. Sewage contamination in Region IX corresponds to one of the current lowest levels of sewage treatment coverage in relation to the population (568,263 inhabitants) in the country, which in 2001 reached 9%, with projections by the Empresa de Servicios Sanitarios de la Araucanía, Sociedad Anónima (ESSAR, S.A.) of reaching 13% in December 2002, and 81.4% in 2005. A relevant aspect that cannot be ignored is the one related to the contribution of fecal phosphorus in sewage, which is in the order of 1 to 2 g/inhabitant/day. The contribution of ammonium ion through urea can also be mentioned with 30 g/inhabitant/day (Rivera, 1992). On the other hand, the Imperial River is the continuation of the Cautín River, which receives water from the city of Nueva Imperial (200 km downstream from Temuco) and Carahue (30 km downstream from Nueva Imperial). The contribution made by the estuaries and tributary rivers of the Cautín and Imperial Rivers that carry domestic, industrial and agricultural waste from the various localities located on their banks should not be overlooked. In general, chemical substances can produce a bad taste or color in the water, but this is quite noticeable if the salt or mineral substances are in large quantities, other times they are capable of reacting to form compounds with aAltered toxicity. These substances include arsenic, barium, cadmium, cyanide, hexavalent chromium, silver, lead, selenium and fluoride, which give water toxic properties when present in concentrations higher than the limits established in Chilean Standards. This explains the importance of water quality monitoring systems (Rivera et al., 2002). In this region, the contamination of these rivers by industrial waste originates in the dairy industry, tanneries and slaughterhouses in the case of liquid waste, and meat processing plants and sawmills (sawdust) in the case of solid waste. Agroindustry is another productive activity with great responsibility for the contamination of water with extremely dangerous chemical products that can have major effects on human health and aquatic biota in general, even in very small quantities. Many of these agrochemicals should simply not be used, because once they enter the hydrological cycle, they spread over great distances, are very difficult to detect and, due to their presence at a practically molecular level, it is not possible to filter or neutralize them once in the environment, causing harmful effects on the environment (Orrego, 2002). ESSAR, S.A. has carried out an exhaustive monitoring campaign of liquid industrial waste, which is discharged into the public sewage system. The results that appeared in public reports allow us to deduce from the discharge volumes that the greatest impacts come, according to the uniform international industrial classification (UN, 1988), from: CIIU 31111 (slaughter of cattle), CIIU 62536, which corresponds to service stations (sale of fuel, lubricants, washing services, greasing, etc.) and CIIU 31115 (preparation of cold cuts, sausages and canned meat). Water quality is relevant due to the various roles it plays, outside the river course (domestic, agricultural and industrial use), within the river course (recreation and aesthetics) and as a means for aquaculture and wildlife management in general. The Cautín and Imperial rivers are a resource of primary importance that must maintain their original characteristics in order to be used on a sustained basis. The objective of this work was to determine the physicochemical and microbiological quality of the waters of the Cautín and Imperial rivers, which will allow the construction of an adequate baseline for environmental impact studies and other determinations at the governmental, business and other levels. MATERIALS AND METHODS Study area The hydrological regime of the rivers in the Araucanía Region is pluvial, that is, the water resource comes from rainfall. This characteristic is associated with the fact that the Andes mountain range is normally low in height in this region, so not much snow accumulates. The Cautín River rises east of the Lonquimay volcano in a west-south direction to the city of Lautaro, Chile (38º32S; 72º27W), where it turns south to the city of Temuco (38º43S; 72º35W. Along its course it receives contributions from the Sierra Nevada and the Raíces mountain range, as well as the contribution of a large number of tributaries of varying importance, among which we can highlight the Blanco, Muco and Quepe rivers. Downstream the Cautín heads west where it flows into the Sierra Nevada and the Raíces mountain range.It forms the Imperial River when it joins the Chol-Chol River (as seen in Figure 1). In this way, the river occupies the intermediate depression, for about 174 kilometers, with an average slope of the channel of 1 . (Rivera and Muñoz-Pedreros, 1999). The Imperial River is short, since it is formed by the confluence of two large tributaries such as the Cautín and Chol-Chol rivers, just below the city of Nueva Imperial. Throughout its territory, the river receives small tributaries, the Ranquilco stream and the Damas and Moncul rivers being of some importance. The morphometric parameters of the hydrographic basin of the Imperial River indicate that they are rivers with adjacent trumaos soil derived from volcanic ash, rivers of the Ritral and Ritropotamal type, according to the sediment (Table 1). Type of environment Scrubland, regrowth, native forest, and agricultural and livestock activity. Source of origin Precordillera and the Andes mountain range. River classification Third to fifth order. The Chol-Chol River has a basin of 5,439 km2 and drains the entire northern part and some of the extreme north-east of the Imperial River basin. It is born from the confluence of the Lumaco and Quillen rivers, 12 kilometers from Galvarino. Significant parameters for the evaluation For the selection of significant parameters, MOPT (1992) considered the natural and anthropic factors that would condition the composition of the waters of the Cautín and Imperial rivers. The physicochemical parameters that were determined for the evaluation of water quality were: pH, temperature, dissolved oxygen, total dissolved solids, conductivity, sodium, potassium, magnesium, aluminum, iron, copper, boron, zinc, phosphates, ammoniacal nitrogen, nitrite, nitrate, sulfate, total solids, suspended solids, chlorides, alkalinity, BOD5 and COD. The microbiological parameters were total and fecal coliforms. Sampling and preservation Both the physicochemical and microbiological parameters were evaluated in the annual cycle 1998-1999 in winter and summer seasons, with three samples in triplicate in each season of the year. The samples were carried out according to MOPT (1992) and CONAMA (1996), such as: recording them at points far from thethe banks, in homogeneous systems, in adequate quantities for sub-samples and everything that means obtaining representative samples of the total. The samples were immediately sent to the laboratory and stored at 4ºC. To work with the logical sequence of the analyses, they were processed with three parallel replicas for each case. The physicochemical and microbiological characterization was carried out by establishing ten sampling stations from the Lonquimay slope to the Nehuentue reservoir and they were: 1-Lonquimay slope, 2-Curacautín, 3-Aguas frías, 4-Cajón, 5-Santa Rosa, 6-Ragñintuleufu Bridge, 7-Imperial Bridge, 8-Exit to Carahue, 9-Carahue Bridge and 10-Nehuentue Reservoir (figure 1). Each sample was taken from the surface waters of the river, using a metal container with which special glass and plastic bottles were filled for the collection and storage of water samples (CONAMA, 1996). Analytical procedures The following were measured in situ: dissolved oxygen, measured with a portable Hanna oximeter model HI 9142; pH, measured with a portable Hanna digital pH meter model 2041 and conductivity (mS) measured with a HACH conductivity meter model 2041. The microbiological analyses were performed using the most probable number (MPN) technique, according to current Chilean standards. The chemical analyses were performed in the laboratories of the Department of Biological and Chemical Sciences, belonging to the Faculty of Sciences of the Catholic University of Temuco, according to current Chilean standards, and were: - Available phosphate, determined by the modified Olsen method for water. N-ammonia was determined using the Nessler reagent. - Nitrite was determined by diazotization calorimetric method with spectrophotometric measurements on a DR3000. - Nitrate was determined by colorimetric method with Cd reduction, with spectrophotometric measurements. - Iron was determined using the 1-10 phenanthroline colorimetric method, with spectrophotometric measurements. - Chlorides measured (sodium, potassium and calcium) applying the colorimetric method with mercuric thiocyanate were determined with a flame spectrophotometer (Jenway). - Determinations of metallic elements were carried out on a Varian A 200 atomic absorption spectrophotometer. - Total alkalinity was determined by the titration method with 0.1 N hydrochloric acid. - For total hardness the simplified Titriplex method was used. Dissolved solids were determined by the gravimetric method. The flow rate was estimated by calculating the area of ​​the river section and the speed of the current. The speed was estimated by subsurface drifters. The criteria and standards used are those indicated by the Chilean Water Quality Standards (CONAMA, 1996), compared with other international standards (WHO, European Community, USA and Canada). To determine the water quality, the values ​​of the significant parameters measured were used together. RESULTS AND DISCUSSION The average results of the parameters analyzed are presented in tables 2-5. Temperature The probability of finding waters in nature that maintain a constant temperature throughout the year is very high.scarce, even more so in a temperate climate such as this area. The temperature in natural groundwater varies only slightly in its annual average, while in surface water it fluctuates according to the seasons of the year; thus finding for the Cautín River the lowest temperatures in winter with 5.0ºC and the highest in spring-summer with 21.0ºC (Rivera and Muñoz-Pedreros, 1999) Considering the temperature from the point of view of aquatic life, in current water flow, the natural value should not increase by more than 3ºC. As for recreation (with direct contact) a maximum of 30ºC can be tolerated (Rivera and Muñoz-Pedreros, 1999). According to the data in tables 2 and 3, in this study the temperature varied between 7.9 and 25.9ºC. Based on the above, the waters of the Cautín and Imperial rivers meet the minimum requirements for aquatic life and recreation. Conductivity Conductivity is a measure of the degree of mineralization of the waters, as well as the ionic charge present. The values ​​found were 32.4 to 190 Ms/cm, which are within those stipulated by the Chilean Standards for irrigation waters. The reported values ​​are those expected for this type of rivers and as averages are similar to those reported by Figueroa et al. (2003) for a study in the Damas River watershed. pH The pH varies between 7.1 and 8.7 (Tables 2 and 3). These are values ​​that tend to neutral ranges, such as those expected for waters from rhytrón-type rivers. From the point of view of human consumption, a pH range of 7 to 8.5 and a maximum limit of 6.5 to 9.2 are considered; According to the above, the waters of these rivers are within the established norms. Considering the requirement for irrigation waters, according to the Official Chilean Standards (NCh 1333-1978), these must have a pH between 5.5 and 9.0, so the waters of these rivers are suitable for that use. The pH requirements for waters destined for recreation and aesthetics, according to Chilean Standard 1333, are 6.5 to 8.3 and in no case less than 5 or greater than 9, according to this regulation the waters of these rivers are suitable for that use. The requirement for aquatic life is 6 to 9 pH units, fresh waters have a pH between 6.5 and 8.7 so the waters of these rivers do not present a problem. Dissolved oxygen Oxygen concentration is relevant in water quality control, its presence and concentration being essential to sustain higher life forms, as well as to assess the effects of potential contaminating agents, mainly due to the oxygen balance in the system. It is also relevant in the degradation processes contemplated in wastewater treatment and in pipe corrosion processes. The sources of oxygen in water are aeration and algae photosynthesis. Removal is related to plant respiration, chemical oxygen demand of organic materials and sediments, over-saturation and removal of organic matter. The low solubility of oxygen is the main factor that limits the purification capacity of natural waters. Dissolved oxygen ranged from 8.0 to 12.7 ppm, being above the minimum values ​​that allow sustaining aquatic life, which according to current regulations is 5 ppm. ChloridesThe chloride content in river waters was between 1.8 and 111.4 ppm. Therefore, these waters are classified as normal chlorinated. In addition, these waters are below the current limit for drinking water, which is 250 ppm. These concentrations correspond to areas above the ritral zones and free of contamination (MOPT, 1992). The maximum content in irrigation waters is 200 ppm, therefore these waters are suitable for irrigation. For the use of untreated waters in tourist and recreational activities, it must be considered that the normal elimination of chlorides through human urine is approximately in the order of 12 to 1.5 grams daily, being a considerable amount; It should also be noted that a content of 500 ppm of NaCl in river water has a saline taste, but the body cannot tolerate up to 2500 ppm (Rivera et al., 2002). Alkalinity represents the main buffer system of fresh water, and also plays a relevant role in the productivity of natural water bodies, serving as a reserve source for photosynthesis. Excessive alkalinity does not produce harmful effects on the health of consumers but it does impart an unpleasant taste to the water. The alkalinity system has important interactions with the processes of photosynthesis and cellular respiration. Phosphates The quantities of phosphate present in these rivers varied between 0.074 and 0.317 ppm, indicating that these are unpolluted waters and are very unproductive because phosphates are one of the limiting factors in plant growth, this being a common indicator of upper sections of river networks. Campos (1985) found higher values ​​in 30 rivers, with an average of 17.8 and a minimum of 0.9 ppm. The 0.074 to 0.317 ppm found in the study area indicate minimal anthropic influence due to forestry, agriculture and livestock activity. Nitrites The nitrite concentrations at the sampling stations are typical of pure, uncontaminated waters; values ​​between 0.001 and 0.004 ppm do not indicate disturbance of the nitrogen cycle. Nitrates The amount of nitrates fluctuated between 0.225 and 1.40 ppm. The Chilean standard for drinking water establishes a maximum limit of 10 ppm, although the Ministry of Health may accept a higher content. The value is similar to that established by the EPA in the United States. When nitrate is present in well water, it means that there is an excess in the area due to the direct or indirect action of agriculture, lawn fertilization or septic tanks. Ammoniacal NAmmoniacal nitrogen presented values ​​between 0.02 and 1.18 ppm. The maximum value was always at sampling stations 6-8, which are closest to the sewage collectors and vegetable producing areas. Quantities greater than 1 ppm are indicators of sensitive contamination. Suspended solids Values ​​greater than 25 and less than 50 ppm correspond to concentrations assigned to class 3 waters that are related to lower areas of certain foothills and plain rivers, which are in a good situation. Most of the values ​​are very close to the indicated ranges with the exception of sampling station 8 corresponding to the Carahue bridge in the summer season with 248 ppm. Aluminum Aluminum presented concentrations between 0.002 and 0.055 ppm. Which are below the 5 ppm established as a standard for irrigation water in Chile and below 0.2 ppm established in Spain in relation to the structure of natural waters for drinking water (MOPT, 1992). Copper The rivers studied presented copper concentrations between 0.17 and 0.63 ppm. Without previous history, this difference can be attributed to characteristics of the geology of the river, however it cannot be established definitively with the information originated by a very short period, reason why a permanent monitoring must be maintained in order to capture the specific variations of the system. The quality standard for irrigation water in Chile establishes values ​​of 0.20 ppm, on the other hand, the standard values ​​for water quality in Spain according to MOPT (1992) is 100 ppb. Copper concentrations higher than 3000 ppb can produce astringent flavors and colors. Cu being an essential metal for organisms, when it exceeds certain concentrations, it can produce toxic effects, mainly gastrointestinal and liver disorders. Magnesium Concentrations fluctuated between 0.95 and 1.82 ppm. The magnesium content in surface water varies between 1 and 40 ppm, sometimes exceeding 100 ppm in waters that pass through lands rich in magnesium salts. Likewise, magnesium concentrations are lower than the Chilean Quality Standard for Irrigation Water (0.20 ppm). Zinc Zinc is not considered toxic, although it gives the water an unpleasant taste. The values ​​found were between 0.02 and 0.14 ppm. The Chilean standard for drinking water accepts up to 5 ppm. It is very stable in salt and fresh water. Iron The rivers studied presented iron concentrations that ranged between 0.21 and 0.56 ppm. Concentrations are lower than the quality standard for irrigation water (0.5 ppm), according to Chilean Standard 1333 (1978), and lower than the standard levels and maximum admissible concentrations required for irrigation water in Spain (200 ppb) (MOPT, 1992). Iron can appear in water in its different oxidation states; it is not considered toxic to humans, although it can cause odor or taste problems, even at low concentrations. Iron can be deposited as hydroxide and block the gills of organisms, decreasing their respiratory potential. Eggs and cultured larvae are more sensitive to these metals, which then causes their death. Iron in the environmentAquatic iron is not harmful when present in low concentrations, but it is usually harmful when present in high concentrations. For trout, with pH values ​​in water of 6.5 to 7.5 and concentrations of 0.9 ppm of iron, it is lethal (it must be oxidized). Heavy metals can be present in traces in surface supply waters, their toxicity can be high and is increased by various factors, mainly including pH, dissolved oxygen and temperature. They enter crops through supply water and as a consequence of industrial operations carried out by man (paper mills, mineral extraction, tanneries, etc.) or because they are the product of water drag. The main problem is that they bioaccumulate, affect the neuromuscular system and can be lethal. Boron It is found in quantities of 0.01 to 0.06 ppm, presenting no problems for its use as irrigation water, since the Chilean Standard accepts 0.75 ppm as a maximum limit. Boron is essential for plants, especially for fruit trees; however, it has the characteristic of ambivalent functionality, since, above a critical level of availability in irrigation water, it generates a limiting toxicity effect on the development of the species, depending on the concentration of available boron and the sensitivity and tolerance presented by each species. BOD5 The biochemical oxygen demand was presented with a range of 0.44 to 2.41 ppm. If it is considered that it corresponds to the amount of oxygen dissolved in the water, necessary for the aerobic biochemical oxidation of organic substances present in the water, BOD5 is therefore a good indicator of the general quality of the water and specifically of organic pollution. BOD5 values ​​greater than 10 ppm are characteristic of highly contaminated waters, and values ​​less than 3 ppm indicate very weak contamination. Therefore, these are very weakly contaminated waters. COD COD is the amount of oxygen used to oxidize all oxidizable organic matter, both organic and mineral. There is a certain relationship between COD and BOD5, the latter being a fraction of COD between 2 and 70%. The rivers had values ​​between 2 and 406. This highest value corresponded to the sampling station near the mouth. Uncontaminated waters have COD values ​​of 1 to 5 ppm, or slightly higher. Domestic wastewater usually contains between 250 and 600 ppm (Orrego, 2002). The COD value is always higher than BOD5 because many organic substances can be oxidized chemically, but not biologically. Microbiological indicators The draft quality standard for the protection of surface continental waters establishes a maximum of 1000 fecal coliforms/100 mL and 2000 total coliforms/100 mL for fecal coliforms in water used in activities with direct contact and for irrigation of fruits and vegetables that grow at ground level and are usually consumed without cooking. Text box: Fig. 3: Agglomerative hierarchical cluster analysis of the sampling stations in Winter. The distances between the stations are expressed as dissimilarity between 0 and 1. The measure ofdistance corresponds to the City Block index and group average as a grouping method. The secondary environmental quality standard for the protection of Chilean continental superficial waters, in its fourth article, relates to waters suitable for the protection and conservation of aquatic communities and priority uses, and includes five categories for total and fecal coliforms, from exception class to class 4, ranging from 10 to less than 10,000 MPN per 100 ml (CONAMA, 2000). The rivers had a minimum of 33 and a maximum of 5,400 total coliforms, expressed as MPN/100 ml. As for fecal coliforms, a minimum of 2 and a maximum of 790 MPN/100 ml were present. The above allows us to point out that there are three stations in which the maximum values ​​for total coliforms were exceeded, making them unsuitable water for activities with direct contact and for irrigating fruits and vegetables. Statistical analysis Using the water quality databases, a Cluster Analysis was performed, which allows to show the intergroup relationships indicating the level of dissimilarity between the sampling stations based on the physical-chemical profile (Field et al., 1982). The City Block index (STSC, 1989) was used as a distance measure and the UPGMA hierarchical method was used as a grouping method. It can be seen in figures 2 and 3, that sampling stations 6, 7 and 10 differ from the rest at a level of 50 of similarity both in summer and winter. Station 6 corresponds to the Ragñin-tuleufu sector located at the exit of Temuco, after the discharges of the sewage collectors. Station 7 is located in the city of Imperial influenced by urban discharges. On the other hand, station 10 corresponds to the mouth of the river with marine influence. CONCLUSIONS From the results shown, their analysis and discussion, the following conclusions can be drawn: 1.- The waters of the Cautín and Imperial rivers do not present problems, according to the specifications contemplated in the Official Chilean Standards, since all the parameters evaluated are within the ranges or limits allowed. 2.- The concentrations of ions present in the samples, both cations and anions and specifically heavy metals are well below the limits established in the standards (NCh,1333-78 and other international standards). The general results are those expected for this type of Andean rivers of the ritrón type in southern Chile, compared with the 30 rivers studied by Campos (1985). 3.- The microbiological results, even though they are below the limits established in the Chilean Standards, allow us to predict that a greater decrease in the flow of the rivers than that normally occurs during the dry season will cause a greater modification of the ecosystem of the rivers, which today already show the results of the absence of an adequate integral management plan. text: Sergio Prieta / [email protected]    Si bien es un espacio consolidado y uno de los más atractivos de la ciudad, las mansas aguas del arroyo Napostá se encuentran contaminadas. Y mucho más de lo que todos imaginamos.     Estudios publicados en 2016 por el Comité Técnico Ejecutivo (CTE) del Municipio en el marco del Programa Integral de Monitoreo (PIM) determinaron que se encuentra peligrosamente afectado.   Recibí los Newsletters de La Nueva sin costo       Las colonias de Salmonella y Escherichia coli superan los parámetros que establece la Autoridad del Agua.    Otro problema es que no parece haber medidas de fondo para dar soluciones a ese curso de agua, que termina contaminando el estuario de Ingeniero White.    Al mismo tiempo ponen en riesgo a los cientos de bahienses que habitan en sus zonas aledañas o a quienes durante los fines de semana aprovechan la vera del arroyo a la altura de Paso Vanoli, Puente Canesa, la zona de Urquiza o el Parque de Mayo para tomar mate o incluso pescar.    Precisamente en ese espacio público, ya ni siquiera existe el cartel que hasta hace algunos meses advertía sobre la contaminación del líquido y la prohibición para bañarse.    Durante el verano es común encontrar a chicos y grandes sumergidos en esas aguas, buscando un poco de refresco ante las elevadas temperaturas.     En los últimos meses, a raíz de que se observan especies de bagres y otros peces, algunos aprovechan el Paso Vanoli y el tramo de arroyo que va desde el partidor del parque de Mayo hasta Casanova para despuntar su gusto por la pesca.    El inconveniente es que el último estudio dado a conocer sobre la calidad del líquido que fluye desde Sierra de la Ventana hacia Ingeniero White detectó que las mansas aguas del Napostá y que las que se derivan por el canal Maldonado son los afluentes que mayor aporte de bacterias fecales realizan al estuario.       “Las elevadas concentraciones de Escherichia coli en ambos cursos son reflejo del impacto que reciben a lo largo de sus recorridos, ya que atraviesan la ciudad de Bahía Blanca”, escribieron desde el CTE tras las muestra que se tomaron en 2016 en cercanías al estuario.     El problema no empieza en nuestra ciudad. Estudios de años anteriores determinaron que los primeros indicios de contaminación provienen de campos y chacras que se encuentran fuera de Bahía por las heces de animales.     Una resolución de la Autoridad del Agua establece que para arroyos con fines recreativos como el Napostá, los coliformes fecales no deberían sobrepasar los 126 UFC (Unidades Formadoras de Colonias) cada 100 milímetros de agua.     Las muestras recolectadas por el CTE en la desembocadura del Napostá van desde los 1.500 UFC cada 100 milímetros de agua a las 9.600 colonias, lo que supera con creces los límites establecidos.    Las muestras también detectaron la presencia de Salmonella en elevadas concentraciones.      “Dentro de los metales pesados analizados se comprobó la presencia de mercurio en muy baja concentración”, se informó desde el organismo municipal que se encarga del monitoreo de las aguas y de las empresas del Polo.    Los datos son públicos y se pueden ver en la web de ese organismo municipal. Desde la subsecretaría de Gestión Ambiental confirmaron que por estas horas trabajan para subir los datos recolectados durante 2017.    Pileta en la década del 30    Ante este panorama a nadie se le ocurriría recrear la idea que tuvo en 1933 el intendente Agustín de Arrieta, que mandó a construir un dique para generar una piscina natural en la intersección del arroyo y calle Darwin.    Sin embargo, no pasó mucho tiempo para que aparecieran enfermedades por el agua estancada y se decidió clausurar el lugar.    A pesar de todo, como ocurre en la actualidad, los más incrédulos --o arriesgados-- seguían disfrutando de la “pileta”.    Al final, en diciembre de 1941, el Municipio demolió el dique y la piscina dejó de existir. Hoy esa zona del arroyo se encuentra entubada.    Lo cierto es que ese no fue el único proyecto recreativo que prosperó allí en toda la historia bahiense.    Al asumir como intendente en 2015, Héctor Gay reflotó un viejo anhelo de décadas  y mencionó el deseo de montar una pista de canotaje en cercanías al parque de Mayo y Casanova.     "Tengo un viejo sueño que es establecer un tramo del arroyo Napostá para practicar este deporte. Ensanchando un poco el curso y poniendo una compuerta se puede hacer y así convertiríamos el Parque en un lugar para hacer deporte. Se sumaría al Polideportivo y a Las Tres Villas", reconoció el jefe comunal.    Si bien las palabras del intendente dieron a conocer un proyecto desconocido para muchos jóvenes que disfrutan de esa zona, la promesa de una pista de canotaje viene desde hace varios años.      En 2003 se hizo un amplio y difundido estudio con la idea de sanear los 90 kilómetros del arroyo.    Para ello se tomaron muestras de agua en diferentes puntos, se habló de hacer convenios con el Municipio de Tornquist y finalmente convertir el arroyo –-por lo menos en el tramo bahiense-- en un lugar para la práctica de deportes náuticos y diversión.    En ese entonces se detectó que los primeros indicios de contaminación ocurren por la materia fecal de los animales que existen en los campos aledaños al curso de agua, fuera de los límites de nuestra ciudad.     “Con referencia al arroyo Napostá, nuestros resultados muestran que, a medida que el arroyo atraviesa Bahía, se contamina aún más por la llegada de desechos cloacales y diferentes asentamientos poblacionales ribereños” decían desde el Municipio.     En aquella oportunidad se afirmó que los excrementos de origen animal eran la principal fuente de contaminación, aunque no descartaban aportes de materia fecal humana u otros focos infecciosos.     Pero lejos de manifestar un deseo, los entonces funcionarios municipales pusieron fecha para que el arroyo se convirtiera en un centro de esparcimiento más para los bahienses.     Prometieron que en 2004 comenzarían con el saneamiento de las aguas y que, ese mismo año, el arroyo podría ser utilizado con fines recreativos o para el canotaje.    “Se completarán los análisis iniciados sobre la calidad microbiológica, se realizarán estudios fisicoquímicos del agua y se elaborarán dos proyectos de ordenanza, uno con niveles-guía de calidad de agua para uso recreacional y otro para regular el servicio de desagote de líquidos cloacales”, se dijo.    También se impulsaría la creación de un programa de educación, un convenio con Tornquist para coordinar acciones tendientes a preservar el curso de agua libre de contaminantes, y hasta la creación de un comité de cuenca.    Las tareas quedarían a cargo de un equipo de trabajo interdisciplinario formado por representantes de las distintas secretarías municipales, organizaciones no gubernamentales y escuelas.    El 2004 era un año clave    Por aquel entonces se decía que se trabajaba en la consolidación del mencionado grupo y en el relevamiento de datos sobre las actividades que se desarrollan en predios linderos al arroyo.    También, en la identificación de los propietarios de inmuebles del sector rural lindantes con el curso de agua y en el monitoreo para determinar la calidad bacteriológica del agua.    Asimismo, se pidieron informes sobre las instalaciones sanitarias de las instituciones ubicadas a lo largo del curso y se notificó al directorio de la Autoridad del Agua sobre la contaminación orgánica detectada y las acciones a cumplimentar para evitarla.    En cuanto al sector entubado, se informó acerca de la realización de tareas de control de vectores y limpieza del conducto, junto con medidas tendientes a evitar el aporte de contaminantes por parte de empresas y/o particulares ubicados en las inmediaciones del mismo.    El ingeniero Carlos Ocaña, por entonces secretario municipal de Política Urbano Ambiental, anunció que las acciones tendientes a sanear el arroyo Napostá y posibilitar su uso con fines recreativos comenzarían a instrumentarse en 2004.    "Durante lo que queda de 2003, pensamos terminar el relevamiento técnico de los aportes de posibles contaminantes y, luego, se encararán los trabajos para sanear el lugar", sostuvo.    Ocaña expresó que la contaminación obedecía, principalmente, a la presencia de materia fecal en las aguas y explicó que, una vez reunidas todas las pruebas necesarias, se analizaría un cambio o ampliación de las ordenanzas vigentes.    En cuanto al aspecto recreativo, dijo que “la dirección municipal de Turismo está analizando aquellas zonas del arroyo que potencialmente podrán utilizarse para el mencionado fin”.    Las ideas terminaron de desplomarse cuando el 14 de septiembre de 2003, Jaime Linares perdió las elecciones a manos de Rodolfo Lopes. Algunas intervenciones recientes    A la realizada el año pasado por el Municipio, en el cual se emplearon maquinarias para extraer residuos del fondo del arroyo desde Villa Rosario hasta White, y en la cual se invirtieron 10 millones de pesos, se suman otras pequeñas iniciativas impulsadas por vecinos.     En septiembre de 2015 más de 30 personas se pusieron a limpiar el arroyo Napostá a partir de la convocatoria en Facebook impulsada por la escritora bahiense Liza Porcelli Piussi.    Lo mismo se había hecho meses antes en el lago del parque de Mayo. Es que tanto la vera del arroyo como el lago suelen ser lugares donde la gente tira botellas y otros residuos     En ambas jornadas se encontraron latas, botellas de plástico cortadas por la mitad, vasos, botellas de bebidas alcohólicas, un celular, un pantalón y hasta decenas de preservativos, entre otras cosas.  Sin respuestas oficiales    Este diario se comunicó con la subsecretaria de Gestión Ambiental, Adriana Chanampa, que sostuvo que en los próximos días se darán a conocer los datos recolectados en 2017.     También con el Departamento de Saneamiento Ambiental para saber qué acciones se concretan para mejorar la situación del Napostá, aunque quedaron en devolver el llamado y nunca lo hicieron.
text_en: Sergio Prieta / [ protected] Although it is an established space and one of the most attractive in the city, the calm waters of the Napostá stream are contaminated. And much more than we all imagine. Studies published in 2016 by the Executive Technical Committee (CTE) of the Municipality within the framework of the Comprehensive Monitoring Program (PIM) determined that it is dangerously affected. Receive the La Nueva Newsletters for free Salmonella and Escherichia coli colonies exceed the parameters established by the Water Authority. Another problem is that there do not seem to be any substantive measures to provide solutions to this waterway, which ends up contaminating the Ingeniero White estuary. At the same time, they put at risk the hundreds of people from Bahía Blanca who live in the surrounding areas or who, during the weekends, take advantage of the banks of the stream at Paso Vanoli, Puente Canesa, the Urquiza area or Parque de Mayo to drink mate or even fish. Precisely in that public space, there is no longer even the sign that until a few months ago warned about the contamination of the liquid and the prohibition of bathing. During the summer it is common to find children and adults submerged in these waters, looking for a little refreshment from the high temperatures. In recent months, due to the sighting of species of catfish and other fish, some take advantage of Paso Vanoli and the section of stream that goes from the Parque de Mayo watershed to Casanova to develop their taste for fishing. The problem is that the last study released on the quality of the liquid that flows from Sierra de la Ventana to Ingeniero White detected that the calm waters of the Napostá and those that are derived through the Maldonado canal are the tributaries that contribute the greatest amount of fecal bacteria to the estuary. “The high concentrations of Escherichia coli in both courses are a reflection of the impact they receive throughout their journeys, since they cross the city of Bahía Blanca,” wrote the CTE after the samples that were taken in 2016 near the estuary. The problem does not begin in our city. Studies from previous years determined that the first signs of contamination come from fields and farms that are outside of Bahía due to animal feces. A resolution from the Water Authority establishes that for streams for recreational purposes such as the Napostá, fecal coliforms should not exceed 126 CFU (Colony Forming Units) per 100 millimeters of water. The samples collected by the CTE at the mouth of the Napostá range from 1,500 CFU per 100 millimeters of water to 9,600 colonies, which far exceeds the established limits. The samples also detected the presence of Salmonella in high concentrations. “Among the heavy metals analyzed, the presence of mercury was confirmed in very low concentrations,” reported the municipal agency in charge of monitoring the waters and companies of the Polo. The data is public and can be seen on the website of that municipal agency. The Undersecretary of Environmental Management confirmed that they are currently working to upload the data collected during 2017. Pool in the 1930s Given this panorama, no one would think of recreating the idea that Mayor Agustín de Arrieta had in 1933, who ordered the construction of a dam to create a natural pool at the intersection of the stream and Darwin Street. However, it was not long before diseases began to appear due to the stagnant water and it was decided to close the place.     Despite everything, as it happens today, the most incredulous - or daring - continued to enjoy the "pool".     Finally, in December 1941, the Municipality demolished the dam and the pool ceased to exist. Today that area of ​​the stream is piped.     The truth is that thisIt was not the only recreational project that prospered there in the entire history of Bahía Blanca. When he took office as mayor in 2015, Héctor Gay revived an old desire of decades and mentioned the desire to set up a canoeing track near the Mayo and Casanova park. "I have an old dream which is to establish a section of the Napostá stream to practice this sport. By widening the course a little and putting a floodgate it can be done and thus we would turn the Park into a place to do sports. It would join the Sports Center and Las Tres Villas," acknowledged the communal leader. Although the mayor's words revealed a project unknown to many young people who enjoy that area, the promise of a canoeing track has been around for several years. In 2003 a broad and widespread study was done with the idea of ​​cleaning up the 90 kilometers of the stream. To do this, water samples were taken at different points, there was talk of making agreements with the Municipality of Tornquist and finally converting the stream – at least in the Bahia section – into a place for the practice of water sports and fun. At that time it was detected that the first signs of contamination occur due to the fecal matter of animals that exist in the fields adjacent to the watercourse, outside the limits of our city. “With reference to the Napostá stream, our results show that, as the stream crosses Bahia, it becomes even more contaminated by the arrival of sewage waste and different riverside population settlements” said the Municipality. At that time it was stated that animal excrement was the main source of contamination, although they did not rule out contributions from human fecal matter or other infectious sources. But far from expressing a desire, the municipal officials at the time set a date for the stream to become another recreational center for the people of Bahía Blanca. They promised that in 2004 they would begin cleaning up the water and that, that same year, the stream could be used for recreational purposes or for canoeing. “The analyses initiated on the microbiological quality will be completed, physical-chemical studies of the water will be carried out and two draft ordinances will be drawn up, one with guide levels of water quality for recreational use and another to regulate the sewage drainage service,” it was said. The creation of an education program would also be promoted, an agreement with Tornquist to coordinate actions aimed at keeping the waterway free of contaminants, and even the creation of a watershed committee. The tasks would be carried out by an interdisciplinary work team made up of representatives of the different municipal departments, non-governmental organizations and schools. 2004 was a key year. At that time, it was said that work was being done to consolidate the aforementioned group and to collect data on the activities carried out on properties bordering the stream. Also, work was being done to identify the owners of properties in the rural sector bordering the watercourse and to monitor the bacteriological quality of the water. Likewise, reports were requested on the sanitary facilities of the institutions located along the course and the board of directors of the Water Authority was notified of the organic contamination detected and the actions to be taken to avoid it. As for the piped sector, information was provided on the performance of vector control tasks and cleaning of the conduit, along with measures to avoid the contribution of contaminants by companies and/or individuals located in the vicinity of the stream. Engineer Carlos Ocaña, then municipal secretary of Urban Environmental Policy, announced that actions to clean up the Napostá stream and enable its use for recreational purposes would beginThe project was to be implemented in 2004. “During the remainder of 2003, we plan to complete the technical survey of possible contaminants and then begin work to clean up the area,” he said. Ocaña said that the contamination was mainly due to the presence of fecal matter in the water and explained that once all the necessary evidence was gathered, a change or extension of the current ordinances would be analyzed. Regarding the recreational aspect, he said that “the municipal tourism department is analyzing those areas of the stream that could potentially be used for this purpose.” The ideas finally collapsed when Jaime Linares lost the elections to Rodolfo Lopes on September 14, 2003. Some recent interventions    In addition to the one carried out last year by the Municipality, in which machinery was used to extract waste from the bottom of the stream from Villa Rosario to White, and in which 10 million pesos were invested, there are other small initiatives promoted by neighbors.     In September 2015, more than 30 people began to clean the Napostá stream following a call on Facebook promoted by the Bahian writer Liza Porcelli Piussi.     The same thing had been done months before in the lake in the Parque de Mayo. The fact is that both the banks of the stream and the lake are usually places where people throw bottles and other waste.    On both days, cans, plastic bottles cut in half, glasses, alcoholic beverage bottles, a cell phone, a pair of pants, and even dozens of condoms were found, among other things. No official responses    This newspaper contacted the Undersecretary of Environmental Management, Adriana Chanampa, who said that in the next few days the data collected in 2017 will be released.    It also contacted the Department of Environmental Sanitation to find out what actions are being taken to improve the situation in Napostá, although they agreed to return the call and never did.

title: Wasserqualität Rhein
snippet: Die sehr schlechte Wasserqualität des Rheins machte das Baden im Fluss zu dieser Zeit zu einem absolut gesundheitsgefährdenden Abenteuer. Wasserqualität Rhein: ...
trans_snippet: The very poor water quality of the Rhine made swimming in the river at that time an absolutely dangerous adventure. Water quality Rhine: ...
text: Der Rhein ist der zweitlängste Fluss Deutschlands und fließt auf seinem Weg zur Nordsee durch neun verschiedene Länder. Wichtige Anrainerstaaten sind Frankreich, die Niederlande und Deutschland. Entlang des Rheins liegen Großstädte wie Basel, Köln oder Rotterdam.  Das gesamte Einzugsgebiet des Rheins ist von starker Industrialisierung und intensiver Landwirtschaft geprägt. Bis in die frühen 1980er-Jahre war die Wasserqualität des Rheins insgesamt sehr schlecht.  Hauptverursacher der Verschmutzungen waren Industrieabwässer und fehlende Kläranlagen der angrenzenden Städte und Gemeinden. Hinzu kam noch ein erheblicher Schadstoffeintrag aus Zuflüssen wie Main, Ruhr oder Maas. Die sehr schlechte Wasserqualität des Rheins machte das Baden im Fluss zu dieser Zeit zu einem absolut gesundheitsgefährdenden Abenteuer.   Wasserqualität Rhein: die wichtigsten Fakten  Die Wasserqualität des Rheins hat sich stark verbessert.  Das Wasser des Rheins erreicht heute größtenteils die Güteklasse II.  Lokal und temporär erhöhte Keimbelastungen sind weiterhin ein Problem.   Heutige Wasserqualität des Rheins  Die Wasserqualität des Rheins hat sich bis heute sehr stark verbessert. An einigen Stellen ist sogar das Baden im Rhein wieder erlaubt. Die jährliche Belastung des Rheins mit dem besonders gefährlichen Schwermetall Quecksilber ist gegenüber dem Jahr 1985 um etwa 70   zurückgegangen. Teilweise weist der Rhein aber noch eine erhöhte lokale Belastung mit Colibakterien oder Salmonellen auf.[1] Diese kann besonders in heißen Sommermonaten oder nach Hochwasserlagen stark ansteigen.  Die Wasserqualität von Rhein und anderen Gewässern wird in Deutschland in die Güteklassen I – IV eingeteilt. Güteklasse I gilt als „gering bis unbelastet“ und Güteklasse IV wird als „Abwasserzone“ eingestuft. Die Einstufung in die Güteklassen erfolgt nach mikrobiologischen, biologischen und chemischen Parametern. Der Rhein besitzt heute vielerorts die Güteklasse II („mäßig belastet“). In den Uferbereichen des Rheins wird von einigen Wasserwerken Trinkwasser entnommen. Trinkwasser unterliegt in Deutschland der Trinkwasserverordnung. Diese kann nicht mit den Gewässergüteklassen gleichgesetzt werden.   Wasserqualität und Wasseranalyse  Trinkwasser aus rheinnahen Brunnen kann mitunter mit Schwermetallen, anderen Schadstoffen und Keimen belastet sein. Dies gilt besonders für private Entnahmestellen, die keinen Laborkontrollen durch die großen Wasserwerke unterliegen.  Eine professionelle Wasseranalyse verschafft dem Brunnenbetreiber Klarheit über eine mögliche Belastung des Trinkwassers.     Referenzen zu Wasserqualität Rhein:  [1] Informationsblatt des Landesamtes für Umwelt, Wasserwirtschaft und Gewerbeaufsicht Rheinland-Pfalz
text_en: The Rhine is the second longest river in Germany and flows through nine different countries on its way to the North Sea. Important riparian states are France, the Netherlands and Germany. Major cities such as Basel, Cologne and Rotterdam are located along the Rhine. The entire catchment area of ​​the Rhine is characterized by strong industrialization and intensive agriculture. Until the early 1980s, the water quality of the Rhine was very poor overall. The main causes of pollution were industrial wastewater and the lack of sewage treatment plants in the neighboring towns and communities. In addition, there was a significant amount of pollutant input from tributaries such as the Main, Ruhr and Maas. The very poor water quality of the Rhine made bathing in the river an absolutely health-endangering adventure at that time. Water quality of the Rhinen: the most important facts The water quality of the Rhine has improved greatly. The water in the Rhine now largely reaches quality class II. Local and temporary increased bacterial contamination is still a problem. Current water quality of the Rhine The water quality of the Rhine has improved greatly to date. In some places, bathing in the Rhine is even permitted again. The annual contamination of the Rhine with the particularly dangerous heavy metal mercury has fallen by around 70% compared to 1985. In some parts, however, the Rhine still has an increased local contamination with coliform bacteria or salmonella.[1] This can increase sharply, particularly in hot summer months or after floods. The water quality of the Rhine and other bodies of water in Germany is divided into quality classes I - IV. Quality class I is considered "low to uncontaminated" and quality class IV is classified as a "wastewater zone". The classification into quality classes is based onmicrobiological, biological and chemical parameters. The Rhine now has quality class II ("moderately polluted") in many places. Drinking water is extracted from some waterworks on the banks of the Rhine. Drinking water in Germany is subject to the Drinking Water Ordinance. This cannot be equated with the water quality classes. Water quality and water analysis Drinking water from wells near the Rhine can sometimes be contaminated with heavy metals, other pollutants and germs. This is especially true for private extraction points that are not subject to laboratory tests by the large waterworks. A professional water analysis provides the well operator with clarity about possible contamination of the drinking water.   References to water quality in the Rhine: [1] Information sheet from the State Office for the Environment, Water Management and Trade Supervision Rhineland-Palatinate
