To illustrate this data, we can say that, assuming a river that would have a flow rate as high or even higher than that of the Niger but which would be afflicted with a geomorphology less favorable to flooding (for example a steep or dammed bed), the biotic production and, in particular, the fish production would be much lower. 91Another determining element is constituted by the amplitude of the seasonal variation. In the current state of knowledge, it is accepted that this variation plays a favorable role through the dynamics of interaction that it creates between dry spaces and aquatic ecosystems, this dynamic constituting a factor of enrichment of the latter in nutrients (see above the enrichment model by the "flood pulse" Junk et al., 1989, cited in footnote no. 7). Thus, between two ecosystems whose water surfaces "averaged over the year" would be identical, the one which presents a wider seasonal variation (with a strong contrast between the period of high water and thelow water period) will have the highest biotic productivity, particularly in fish, because it is the one that interacts the most with the surrounding land areas. Moreover, even if we consider the case of a lake ecosystem (reservoir lakes for example), the existence of a wide seasonal variation in water surface area with annual flooding of large riverside strips constitutes a positive point for biotic production10. 92Beyond these two main features, namely the importance of water as a volume and especially as a surface area and the importance of the seasonal variation of this surface area, other more detailed elements can be put forward from the detailed analysis of the life traits of fish. 93Thus, it appears that the annual sequence of hydroclimatic events is all the more profitable for fish as there is a favorable phasing between the flood cycle and the temperature cycle. Because of the thermal requirements of fish for reproduction, a high availability of water (in quantity or surface area) in the cold season would not present the same advantages for their reproduction11. Basic research is still underway on these points, but it can already be stated that, for most species, the current phasing of the hydraulic cycle with that of temperatures (which is "good" over most of the river's course as it crosses Mali) plays an important role. Some authors (Welcomme and Halls, 2002) also believe that the phasing with the rainy season may play a role: if the flood occurs just after the rains, when the soils are not dried out and the young herbaceous shoots have already emerged, the conditions are more favourable for the survival of eggs, larvae and juvenile fish. This is what is happening today on the middle course of the river. 94Another fine element to take into account is that the favourable phase (flood and high water) is, at present, not only very predictable and gradual in its occurrence, but also quite long in its annual duration: it extends over 4 to 6 months (depending on the location and the way of counting) and, above all, it is continuous, i.e. made up of a "single block". It can reasonably be assumed that several flood phases of shorter duration that would be spread over two, three or four times during the year would not be as well exploited by the majority of fish species since their young cannot reach sufficient sizes (i.e. a size giving them a sufficient level of robustness to face unfavourable conditions) in a time of less than two or three months. Similarly, a rise in water levels that is too rapid, or worse, an unpredictable or non-progressive rise (a succession of rises and falls in water levels without a fixed schedule) would undoubtedly hinder fish reproduction, with the risk of losing their spawn. 95The final element to be drawn from knowledge of the fish cycle is that several living spaces are used by fish during their lives and during the annual cycle: at flood time, on very specific dates, fish must be able to invade the plains and, at the recede a few months later, they must be able to return to the river or lakes (Bénech, 2002). In other words, the possibility of spatial mobility constitutes an essential component of the adaptive strategy of most species. If this mobility based on the continuity of the aquatic space (at least at certain times of the year) is prevented, it is certain that negative consequences will result in terms of the level of population renewal. 96Finally, one last obvious element (because it is general and not specific to fish in the Niger River) is that fish not only need water to live but they need awater of suitable quality, that is, not too loaded with pollutants or other products harmful to their survival and the life of their prey. This presence of harmful chemical substances could be particularly damaging when it occurs in flood plains at the time of flooding, where larvae and juveniles live, or at the time of lowest water (in April-May) when fish are already facing difficult natural conditions (little water, little oxygen, etc.). Another cause of deterioration in water quality is the possible presence of significant surface plant cover (for example, water hyacinths) which prevents the penetration of light and makes the water column dark and, consequently, more or less anoxic (Akinyemiju, 1987; Dembélé, 1994). However, these two types of phenomena (pollution and invasion by macrophytes) are not very present today on the river stricto sensu, at least in its Malian portion. But they are more so in the large neighboring irrigated areas, for example in the canals and outlets (fala) of the Office du Niger. 97In other words, the requirements of fish for the renewal of their populations can be summarized in six points: sufficient extension of the annual flood, resulting from the product of a factor "magnitude of the water supply in flood" by a "geomorphological factor favoring flooding" (existence of a network of gaps and channels leading to low plains); maintenance of a broad seasonality (strong contrast between flood and low water) favoring the "flood pulse" effect; good coincidence between the trophically and thermally favourable periods, i.e. between the flood or high water on the one hand and the hot or non-cold season on the other; regularity of the cycle: calendar predictability, gradual rise and fall of the water, sufficient duration of the favourable phase ("in a single block"); continuity (or existence of communication routes) between the portions of the aquatic space, at least in flood and high water; water quality, particularly in terms of the absence of anoxia and no concentration of pesticides. 98Each of the six preceding elements can constitute, to varying degrees, a point of vulnerability to human manipulation and their direct or indirect effects. Natural water (and fish) movement requirements for successful fishing 107The general study of fishermen’s activity shows that water and fish movements are largely used to catch fish efficiently. 108The basic condition for these movements is that there is an alternation between high and low water periods, i.e. a marked and regular hydraulic seasonality. By examining the techniques deployed in more detail, we observe that several types of hydraulic conditions play an important role in promoting capture. 109During the receding and flooding periods, the change in level must be regular and predictable, for several reasons: so that the trap dams can be set up and operated without (bad) surprises. Indeed, a sudden rise in water levels can allow fish to pass over the traps; so that migrating schools of pelagic fish (particularly tineni Brycinus leuciscus) remain well formed and do not disintegrate, which would harm their capture in the river by drift netsts. 110During the low water period, the level must be very low, at least in the ponds and in some branches, to allow the organization of real depletion fishing and to allow the gear to access almost all of the biomass present12. It is also necessary, during this same season, that the water level of the river does not experience sudden rises (generally due to releases) because these, if accompanied by gusts of wind, can dislocate the dams. 111Among these hydraulic conditions favorable or unfavorable to the capture, a distinction must be made between those that are structuring (with the existence of a seasonality13) and those that play a rather accessory role and act as a hazard on the daily success of the activity. In the latter case, one can wonder whether the grievances of the fishermen should be considered as real problems at the global level. Indeed, in a situation where exploitation is intensive (see Figure 9), the fish that is not caught today due to unfavourable circumstances will be caught tomorrow or the day after by the same fisherman or more probably by another. Depending on the day, a given fisherman wins or loses in this little game and, while it is normal for his mood to be affected at the time, it is likely that the effect of such hazards on the production of a campaign, even for a given household, is generally very low or zero. This must be effective in the major bed during the entire fishing season in order to allow both the circulation of migrant pinnaces (in particular the return movements towards the upstream villages which begin in April-June) and also the evacuation of fishery products by the collector traders. This requirement is now becoming increasingly strong with the development of fresh marketing, which requires a daily passage of collector pinnaces, while the evacuation of smoked fish could withstand certain delays and therefore go hand in hand with the use of less easy routes. In June 1999, a virtual halt in the flow (as well as a significant drop in the prices paid to fishermen) occurred in the Batamani area following the drop in the flow in the river caused by the incident in the management of the Sélingué structure (Morand et al., 2002a). Other needs of fishermen with regard to environmental management in general 113Until now, Malian fishermen, whether from the Inner Niger Delta or from the entire valley, have always favoured a strategy of spatial mobility and/or flexibility of activity (juggling the fishing/agriculture ratio) to cope with hydroclimatic and economic variations. Any development policy that has the direct or indirect implication of hindering this strategy of mobility and flexibility will require a very significant adaptation effort from these fishermen with an uncertain final result. Among these policies, two are currently relevant: decentralization, which, by giving significant power to manage natural resources to "registered" indigenous populations, can have the consequence of creating difficulties for groups whose professional activity is based on migration (such as fishermen) by making their access to resources more difficult; heavy hydro-agricultural developments (large gravity-fed irrigation perimeters) which, due to the investments made, will lead to favoring a policy of allocating plots (cages) only to households capable of providing continuous agricultural work throughout the year, or almost, with two crops per year (which, at the same time, largely excludes peasant-fishermen whose annual calendar isl is based on the alternation of agricultural and fishing activities). 114In both cases, particular attention must be paid to finding solutions that allow the perpetuation of fishing activity as a means of existence (for fishermen) and as a source of protein (for the country). Pastoralism in the Inner Niger Delta The importance of the Inner Niger Delta in Malian livestock farming 115The Inner Niger Delta plays a very special role in the organization and economy of livestock farming in Mali. The Malian cattle herd is estimated at 7.6 million head (OIE, 2003), including nearly 1.6 million in the Mopti region. It is difficult to estimate precisely the number of cattle currently frequenting the pastures of the Inner Niger Delta. However, old aerial counts dating from the 1980s estimated the number of cattle frequenting these pastures at 1.4 million head. At that time, this figure represented nearly 30 of the Malian cattle herd, which was estimated at 4.8 million head. It is likely that the number of animals seasonally hosted in the delta was, at that time, close to the maximum and that this figure has probably not been exceeded today. In this hypothesis, the inner Niger delta would still currently host, on an area of ​​less than 20,000 km2 (1.5 of the national territory), nearly 20 of the Malian cattle herd. The importance of the inner delta is marked by this high concentration, which is due to the exceptional productivity of its flooded pastures. The richest of them, the bourgoutières, have a productivity that can be placed between twenty and thirty tons of dry matter per hectare, that is to say fifteen to twenty times that of a good Sahelian pasture. In this respect, the inner Niger delta therefore appears to be a unique area in West Africa. The principles of livestock farming in the inner delta 116It also seems necessary to briefly outline the principles on which the organization of livestock farming in the inner delta of the Niger is based. This organization is the result of the meeting, exceptional in many respects, of assets and constraints linked to the physical environment and particular historical circumstances. 117Physical assets and constraints, first of all, can be summarized in a few sentences. The annual rhythm of the flood makes the pastures of the inner delta impassable for at least five months in the year. The animals must by regulation have evacuated the delta by August 15 at the latest, but this is also a physical constraint: in fact, beyond this date, the rising waters would risk drowning them. During the entire duration of the high waters, from August to November-December, the pastures are too deeply submerged for the animals to be able to feed there. Furthermore, the sanitary conditions there become very difficult (in particular the multiplication of biting insects and parasites) and the rare animals that remain in the delta to ensure a minimum of milk production for the families of breeders are, in a way, sacrificed animals. In order to avoid submersion, the herds then leave the inland delta for a long transhumance towards the pastures of the Sahel and only return when the floodwaters, well underway, begin to uncover the pastures. 118The exceptional richness of the pastures and the rhythm marked by the flood therefore constitute both the assets and the constraints of the environment. But the originality of the delta also lies in the existence of a pastoral land infrastructure – also unique in many respects – whose creation is the work of a Fulani political power at a particular historical moment. The Fulani breeders gradually invested the inland delta from the 15th century onwards but remain nomadic pastoralists. It was at the beginning of the 19th century14 (1818), under the leadership of a Fulani sovereign, Cheikou Ahmadou, that these nomads became sedentary.during a historical episode known as the "Diina". The Diina regulated the lives of the men of the inner delta according to a very strict code of dependence for the benefit of the politically and militarily dominant Fulani group, the other groups becoming slaves or subjugated. It also created an original organization of space, divided into agro-pastoral territories, the leyde, with a very strict pastoral land code. 119This organization still survives today and constitutes the land framework of the pastoral space. In 1982, the delta had 32 leyde and an infrastructure of pastoral tracks and shelters of astonishing complexity: more than 3,600 km of pastoral tracks internal to the delta (59 main tracks with very many branches) and more than 1,000 shelters which allow animals to exploit the pastures. If we stick to a few average values, the inner delta would have 1 km of track for 4 km2 and one lodge for 16 km2. Each leyden, with its pastures, tracks and lodges is collectively appropriated by a Fulani clan, represented by its shepherd chief: the Jowro. 120Historically, the creation of the leydens of the delta concretized the search for a double balance between pastoral exploitation and agricultural exploitation on the one hand, and between grazing and the herd on the other hand. The balance between pastoralism and agriculture was achieved, under the Diina, by the fact that the pastures, cultivated lands and farmers were managed by dominant groups of herders and for their sole benefit, a situation often heavy with oppression for the other social groups. The balance between pasture and herd was achieved by limiting foreign herds by imposing a tax, the Tollo, collected by the Jowro, chief shepherd and master of the leydi pastures. This tax was then distributed among the men of the family responsible for managing the land. 121Currently, this double balance sought by the organization of the Diina no longer exists. The causes are multiple: the rise of agriculture, first of all, with a net growth rate close to that of the population and a mobility of rice fields exacerbated by the low floods, then the increase in herds, due in large part to veterinary care, while the agricultural rise operates a very significant reduction in pastoral space. In 1958, Jean Gallais (1984) estimated the cattle herd in the delta at 200,000 head, to which were added another 200,000 head belonging to Sahelian herders accompanying the delta herders during the return from transhumance when the waters receded. In 1970, he estimated the herds in the delta at 480,000 head of large cattle and the "foreign" herds at 560,000 head, a total exceeding one million (excluding small livestock). In the early 1980s, counts carried out by aerial surveys indicated a total, for cattle alone, of 1,200,000 head in a delta that had become a refuge from the Sahelian drought. 122The disruption of the balances desired by the Diina is also linked to the modification of livestock ownership structures highlighted by various authors (Cissé, 1982; Turner, 1992). The reconversion of financial liquidity generated by fishing, agriculture, trade or employee savings most often takes place in cattle breeding. As a result, a growing number of herd owners are no longer breeders, while conversely, a growing number of traditional breeders who lost the majority of their animals during the droughts that have had a strong impact on the hydrology of Niger have become salaried shepherds of landowners. At the same time, the Tollo, although banned by the Malian government, continues to be collected clandestinely, often for the sole benefit of the Jowro. The Tollo, which originally served to mark power and control the management of the land, is a form of income tax.ion of pastures becomes a source of personal or family enrichment and the temptation is then great to admit as many animals as possible to the pastures of the leydi. 123Moreover, the dynamics of the land has largely escaped the former Fulani masters. Under the pressure of clearing, the pastoral infrastructure is now seriously threatened. As a result, the very foundation of the socio-territorial organization in leyden (economic and political domination of a group of breeders, ownership of a large herd, control of an agro-pastoral space by means of a land code) is largely called into question to varying degrees by the political, economic and social evolution of the region. The organization of transhumance 124During high water, the herds and their shepherds carry out a long transhumance (it can exceed 300 km) in a radiating manner around the delta. Three main directions are favored. The first is the northwest, towards the Malian and Mauritanian Sahel. Some take it directly from the pastoral territories of the north of the delta, while others first head west, towards the lands of the Office du Niger which are then bypassed to the north. The other two directions go, one, east towards Gourma, the other towards the southeast to reach the pastures of Séno Mango by bypassing the Bandiagara plateau to the south. Finally, for several years, herds have spent the winter in the southern part of the delta, at the edge of the flood. 125The return of the herds takes place gradually around the month of October. The herds scattered in the Sahel will concentrate in waiting areas on the periphery of the flood while waiting to be able to enter the delta in order to return to their original leydi. 126The entry of herds into the delta is conditioned by the flood of the year (water height, speed of withdrawal). The bourgoutières can be considered accessible when the water reaches the climax level (660 cm) minus two meters, i.e. the level of 460 cm in Mopti. The entries into the delta (table 10) are made by fords controlled by the breeders' associations and by the police. Table 10 - Main entry points into the circles127Each year, the official services set the dates of the main crossings. As the flood recedes from the southwest and spreads slowly towards the north, the pastures are only accessible very gradually, the bourgoutières in the north only being opened about three months after the first crossing in the south (that of Diafarabé generally opens the calendar). The dates chosen attempt to reconcile three imperatives: the scarcity of pastures in the peripheral waiting areas, the drop in water in the delta which makes the tracks and shelters passable and the date of the last rice harvests in order to try to avoid conflicts between farmers and herders. Until the 1980s, the average date for southern entries into the delta was around December 20. The public authorities also regulate the dates from which the northern bourgoutières are officially accessible. A second transhumance, internal to the delta, generally takes place from March, with the herds confined to the south of the delta moving up towards the northern pastures. The year 1994 illustrates this double shift (waiting area/delta pastures in November-December and southern delta pastures/northern pastures in March-April) which represent crucial periods for the herders and their herds. The 1994 flood of 642 cm was the first good year since the early eighties. The calendar for the 1994-95 season began with the "deggal" (crossing) of Diafarabé which took place on December 17, 1994 followed by the crossings of Dia-Bozo, Sofara, Koubi and Soye between the 19th and 24th of the month. The lastThe first official crossings, opening access to the northern pastures, took place between March 15 and April 8, 1995. 128The herds progressed along pastoral tracks, the animals resting at night on exposed mounds, the shelters also allowing them to graze in the surrounding area during the day. Tracks, shelters and pastures were appropriated by the Fulani clan holding the leyde. The herds of the different “owners” of each leydi were organized into a collective herd, the eggirgol, led by the Jowro, the chief shepherd, who regulated the route and the rhythms of the progression. He authorized or not foreign herds, in particular those belonging to Sahelian herders, to join his own eggirgol. Some eggirde can exceed 20,000 head of cattle and, in reality, the herds follow each other at a certain distance according to an order of precedence codified by custom. The Jowro herd leads the way, followed by those of the various owners of the leyden, then by the herds of the neighbours who have to cross the leyden to reach theirs, then by the herds of the breeders foreign to the delta. Pastoralism and water use 129Pastoralists are not, in the strict sense and except for watering, users consuming the resource. But, like fishermen, they nevertheless depend very closely on the annual flood, the magnitude of which directly conditions the existence and productivity of the plant formations that constitute the fodder resource. Pastoralists need a flood of high magnitude accompanied by a long duration of submersion. A strong and prolonged flood directly conditions the extension of the flood, therefore that of the pastures as well as their productivity. On the other hand, it also encourages compliance with the rules governing pastoral organisation. 130The low floods of the 1980s precipitated the pastoral crisis of the inland delta that the economic and socio-political developments of Mali had already hinted at. 131The social organization of transhumance, inherited from the Diina, was based on a hegemonic political power of the Fulani shepherds, a power that no longer exists today and would be completely anachronistic. However, this organization has endured thanks to the often ambiguous action of the public authorities and to agreements between Fulani clans or lineages. However, conflicts have become common between shepherds and farmers, between neighboring shepherds from Leyden fighting to be the first to reach the pastures, between shepherds from Leyden and shepherds from outside the delta, many of whom, since Mali's independence and the laws on land nationalization, consider the delta's pastures to be freely accessible. 132The theme of the crisis in the organization of space in the delta has been developed by several authors (Turner, 1992; Barrière and Barrière, 1995). However, two conclusions can be drawn from the previous data: the beginning of the 1980s corresponds to a situation that combines a maximum number of animals and the high occurrence of low floods reducing the productivity of pastures. At the same time, the duration of the flood decreases and entry into the delta is earlier. We can add to this the very obvious fact that low floods make it possible not to respect the network of tracks and shelters most often located on the high points of the landscape. In bad years, large areas are discovered early and herds foreign to the delta or those from another leydi can easily bypass the shelters controlled by the Jowro of the leydi and not respect precedence. The maximum number of animals and the low floods that reduce the productivity of the rangelands and leave a great latitude in the non-respect of customs are the main factors that lead to maximum disorder in the functioning of the pastoral organization. These disorderswhich are taking place against a backdrop of a crisis of power (denial of Fulani power, which has long since lost its political base, failure to respect state power, which, moreover, often takes contradictory initiatives, rapid changes in the ownership of livestock capital) form the constituent elements of a deep crisis. At this stage, it is still too early to know whether the decentralization that has led to a territorial reorganization of Mali – and therefore of the delta – by creating rural communes vested with powers in the area of ​​natural resource management and the promulgation of the recent pastoral code will be able to provide a satisfactory response to the disorders currently affecting the organization of livestock farming in the delta. 133This conflictual disorder is further aggravated by the rise of agriculture. In 1989, the last date for which we have comprehensive information, flooded rice cultivation occupied 159,000 hectares in the delta. This is nomadic rice farming with yields (on average 900 kg/ha) that are among the lowest in the world. If we compare the situation in 1958-59 with that of 1989, we see that the areas under rice have doubled in thirty years while the available per capita, in the best case15, would have remained more or less constant (0.45 ha/person in 1989 compared to 0.47 ha/person in 1957-58). In other words, this nomadic rice farming (rice farmers move their rice fields according to the expected flood each year) is evolving with a growth rate that follows that of population growth. 134From the beginning of the 1980s, the low floods forced farmers to plant their rice fields in deeper plant formations which were then cleared. However, these formations correspond to the best pastures: the bourgoutières. While in 1952 the bourgoutières were very rarely cleared, in 1989, 51,252 ha of bourgoutières were cleared and transformed into rice fields, the most affected areas being located around Mopti and Ténenkou, in Yongari-Mangari to the south, and along an axis that goes from Mourra to Sormé crossing the territory of Togoro Kotia. At that date, a quarter of the bourgoutières had therefore been cleared with a very marked distribution of the phenomenon since the clearing rates, if we replace them within the current limits of the new rural communes that will have to manage the problem, range from 0 to 81.9 depending on the commune. The most worrying cases concern communes around Ténenkou, Kewa, to the south, and communes around Mopti, notably Socoura and Sio. This situation is worrying for two reasons: on the one hand, it represents a significant loss of pasture for pastoralists and for livestock farming in general (and here, as we have said previously, we are talking about pastures with the highest productivity of all tropical pastures) and, on the other hand, these areas represent highly contested areas and sources of conflict. 135At the same time, pastoral infrastructure (tracks and shelters) is seriously threatened. In 1989 (we do not have more recent information), 242 shelters out of the 1,014 in the delta were cultivated and inaccessible to livestock farmers. Cultivated shelters represent approximately 24 of all the shelters in the delta, a percentage very close to the surface area of ​​cleared bourgoutières. Cultivated shelters in the delta are mainly found: in the region of Ténenkou, the historic Maasina; in the south of Mopti; along the eastern edge of the delta between Mopti in the south and Konna in the north; on an arc of a circle on the tracks of Wuro Ali leading to the basin of Yongari Mangari; along an axis which starts from Moura, crosses the leydens Salsalbe and Sossobe and continues along the Burtol of Jallube Burgou leading to Débo. 136The preceding observations lead us to believe that the evolution of rice cultivation hast pursued until now, posing increasingly serious threats to the pastoral organization and thus hampering its capacity to maintain a very significant part of Mali's livestock. Conservation of ecosystems 137The Inner Niger Delta contains a wide variety of aquatic habitats (marshes, lakes, pools, plains and floodplain forests) which host part of the year or all year, colonies of fish, reptiles, mammals and aquatic birds which find, here, favorable conditions for their reproduction and feeding. While the Inner Niger Delta shares this role with several other wetlands in Sahelo-Sudanese Africa, including the Senegal Delta (Djoudj), the Hadejia-Nguru plain in Nigeria, all the floodplains dependent on Lake Chad, the Logone and the Chari, and the Sudd marshes in Sudan, it is the largest of these wetlands in West Africa. However, the various authors agree on the fact that the floodable forests of the delta could have suffered a sharp decline since the end of the 1970s. Let us recall that there are two types of floodplain forests in the inner delta: the Acacia seyal and Acacia Nilotica forests, which are slightly floodable (between 0 and 60 cm) and which constitute highly developed acacia plantations in the high plains of Farimaké to the northwest of Débo, and the heavily flooded Acacia Kirkii forests (between 2.80 and 4 m). We do not share the opinion of the researchers of the "Wetlands" project for whom the inland delta must have been, originally, mainly covered with one or the other category of these two large families of flooded forests, forests which would have greatly receded under the effect of clearing. It seems to us, on the contrary, that the great majority of the plant formations of the delta are, on the contrary, grassy formations devoid of trees. 149In any case, all observers agree in recognizing the fact that these forests have been seriously threatened for about thirty years. Three sets of causes contribute to this regressive development: drought and low floods from the end of the 1970s, population growth which increases human pressure on resources and the destruction of common management rules by local communities of breeders, fishermen and farmers, this destruction being, to a large extent, attributable to land laws and the dysfunction of the supervisory administrations, in particular the Water and Forests Department (Marie, 1989; Moorehead, 1997). However, and this is very regrettable, the greatest uncertainty reigns over the real extent of the decline of these forest formations. The problem seems crucial for deep flooded forests with Acacia Kirkii because of the weakness of their spatial extent and the very important role they play in the reproduction of nesting waterbirds. Indeed, during the flood, the half-flooded canopy forms a quasi-impenetrable tangle which offers a refuge to nesting colonies of waterbirds. Until the end of the 1970s, colonies of several tens of thousands of birds could be observed, while no other colony of this size is known elsewhere in West Africa (which highlights the unique nature of the inland delta). The very strong pressure on the flooded forests resulted, in the early 1980s, in significant clearing in order to create rice fields whose depth would compensate for the insufficient flooding. In most cases, rice farmers obtained only very mediocre results and these rice fields, following the return of good flooding from 1994, have now been abandoned. 150As early as 1985, the IUCN and WWF have been concerned with the restoration of these degraded areas (project "Conservation of the Environment in the Inland Delta of the Riverve Niger, 1985-88 »). Three sites, later established as Ramsar sites, were selected to conduct these trials: the forests of Bouna, Dentaka and Akkagoun. 151The Bouna site initially seemed the most promising. Few results were ultimately obtained due to the lack of a lasting agreement between the administration and “the stakeholders”, notably the fishing and livestock communities. 152At Dentaka, despite initial conditions that seemed less promising, the protection of the forest resulted in a spectacular regeneration of the Acacia Kirkii stands, which now shelter a dozen species of nesting waterbirds and some 80,000 pairs, making it probably the largest colony in West Africa. 153After a difficult start, the Akkagoun forest, on an island in Niger, was effectively protected and the forest, reduced to 7 hectares in 1984, occupied 47 in 1991 and 170 in 1999. 154In both cases, success was undoubtedly facilitated by the return of good floods and by the dynamics of Acacia Kikii. However, these successes also highlight – and the failure of Bouna confirms this judgment – ​​the extreme importance of the involvement of local populations through the fundamental role of local management committees. This point, which is crucial in our eyes, must be placed in the current, very favorable context of decentralization which should make it possible to extend this type of experience to the forests of Pora and Niasso, then to the 26 other sites considered. On the fauna 155There is a scarcity or, in some cases, a near disappearance of large reptiles (Nile crocodile, python, monitor lizard) and large herbivorous mammals (hippopotamuses, manatees). Observations of hippopotamuses, carried out between 1999 and 2001, seem to indicate the presence of around thirty individuals in the Débo complex (Youvarou circle). Twenty-five to thirty individuals have also been reported in Niger, in Diaka and in the Seri plain. 156Manatees are strictly protected and very discreet, which makes the collection of information about them very delicate. Difficult to observe, they are sometimes accidentally caught in the nets of fishermen who are supposed to release them but who most often keep a prudent silence on these incidents. However, it would seem that the manatee occupies quite a number of sites in the delta, with a few dozen individuals living in the Débo and on the large arms of the river, particularly around Mopti. Waterbirds 157The inner Niger delta, as we have highlighted, is of prime importance in West Africa for the nesting and feeding of numerous colonies of waterbirds, both Afrotropical birds and paleoarctic species. In addition to their own interest, birds are excellent bioindicators of the good or bad health of the ecosystem and, as such, their long-term observation provides information on current developments in the inner delta. 158The distribution of waterbirds varies throughout the year according to the seasons and, according to a multi-annual rhythm, according to the magnitude of the flood. Generally speaking, waterbirds concentrate in the delta from the start of the receding waters, which gradually uncover food stocks in November-December. They leave the delta with the rising waters, sharing this rhythm with many animals, including domestic animals. 159The level of the flood of the year strongly influences the distribution of birds in the delta itself. Very unfavourable years lead to a very high concentration of birds in the Débo complex, which becomes a refuge area. In more favourable years, the birds disperse in the delta with a very marked drop in their presence on the Débo. 160The observations gathered by the “Wetlands” project do not allow us to draw up a clear pictureand the developments underway in the delta. At most, they allow us to outline trends, some of which could prove worrying. 161B. In the early 1980s, Lamarche drew up a list of 143 species of waterbirds in Mali, 125 of which frequent the inner delta. It would seem that the “Wetlands” project only reports 103 of them. The same observations as those made on large reptiles and large herbivorous mammals can be made for large birds. The Goliath heron and the Jabiru are said to have disappeared from the delta, the white stork, a Palearctic species, and the crowned crane are becoming rare. It would even seem that currently the number of crowned cranes in captivity in Mali is greater than the number of animals living in the wild, of which there are only about fifty left in the delta. 162Observations on smaller birds are more ambivalent. Under the effect of drought and very poor hydrology, Glossy Ibis populations are said to have declined by 50% between the early 1980s and the early 2000s. However, other species have held their own, their numbers remaining stable, such as the Black-tailed Godwit, a Palearctic migrant in sharp decline in Europe. 163The international importance of the inland delta is clearly indicated by the application of the Ramsar Convention, with, in particular, criterion No. 6 setting at 1 the proportion of a species sheltered by a wetland for it to be recognised as being of international importance. In 2001, twenty-seven species frequenting the delta, in particular the Débo area, met Ramsar criterion No. 6. Thirteen of these species are Afrotropical and fourteen are of Paleoarctic origin. Of the former, two species are currently threatened and, of the latter, one species is threatened. In total, of the hundred or so species frequenting the delta (three-quarters of which do not have sufficient numbers to meet Ramsar criteria), around ten species currently appear to be threatened. Bamako and the Sudanese-African context of Mali 165Most of the literature on the water issue in Bamako and, in general, in developing countries (DCs) deals only with drinking water supply problems, more rarely with sanitation problems and, very exceptionally, with the treatment of pollution affecting water (TECSULT, 1994; Sow, 1997). In addition, the lack of research on the quality of wastewater in the African context – an essential preliminary to the definition of water purification processes – was noted by the BCEOM in 1984 and is still very much to be deplored with regard to the city of Bamako. Indeed, bibliographic research on the subject shows that little data is measured. Publications on the problem of water quality in Bamako (from consultancy firms, administrations or even researchers) often use the same data, which has the dual disadvantage of no longer being up to date and often being unreliable, as they are less and less well transcribed and understandable over time. It is in this context that the Equanis research programme of the IRD Centre in Bamako made it possible to carry out systematic weekly monitoring of the chemical quality of surface water throughout the Niger River valley and its tributaries, from 1992 to 1998, accompanied by specific measurement campaigns concerning chemical pollution.imic: trace elements, heavy metals, nitrate, ammonium (Picouët, 1999; Palangié, 1998; Paget, 1999; Derolez, 2001) and biological pollution between the cities of Bamako and Koulikoro (Palangié, 1998) and on the agricultural axis of Bani (Bonnefoy, 1998). 166The demographic evolution of Bamako has followed a sustained growth rate since the beginning of the 1960s (figure 16). Several factors of a socio-political and material nature have weighed on this evolution: the decision to establish Bamako as an administrative center of prime importance for the country (1908: colonial capital, 1960: capital of the new independent state); the break-up of the Mali federation in 1959 which caused the return of Malian populations settled in Senegal; the liberalization, thanks to the change of regime in 1968, of movement between the countryside and the capital; the phenomenon of rural exodus following the impoverishment of the rural world; the concentration of activities and most of the socio-sanitary, administrative and educational facilities. 167Bamako has experienced the highest growth rate in the country. The highest rate ever recorded was 22.7 between 1958 and 1960 (years of mass repatriation of Malians from abroad). This rate fell sharply to 3.9 between 1960 and 1966 (years marked by the political will for regional development). From 1974 to 1976 under the military regime, it rose to 7.3. In 1987, the date of the last census, the population of Bamako stood at 677,883 inhabitants. Growth continued at a sustained rate of 4.2% until 1993. Overall, unpolluted surface waters 168According to all the studies conducted on the quality of the waters of the Niger River (Iwaco, 1996; Equanis, 1997; Gihrex, 2000 and Ghenis, 2001), the Niger River, like most major African rivers, is currently very little affected by chemical contamination of its waters (Picouët et al., 2002). Indeed, the waters of the Niger River in its main bed are free of metal pollution, pollution by nitrates, nitrites, ammonium and phosphates and biological pollution. This result is logical given the low industrialization of the Niger river basin and the minor use of fertilizers and pesticides in agriculture. However, on this last aspect, weekly monitoring of the quality of well and borehole water as well as runoff water in the CMDT cotton-growing area of ​​Southern Mali showed significant point pollution by pesticides, particularly DDT, mainly linked to fertilizer storage problems or improper use (Bonnefoy, 1998). 169Furthermore, while the physicochemical quality of the water in the entire Niger River basin remains generally good, with the exception of certain points near industrial discharges on the Bamako-Koulikoro axis (Palangié, 1998), point bacteriological pollution at the level of human gatherings is widespread. Thus, the presence of high concentrations of coliforms and fecal streptococci is sufficient in itself to make this surface water undrinkable, according to WHO standards. However, this water is still commonly used for drinking, which causes significant health risks. Finally, in 1993, 1997 and 1998, following heavy rains, the waters of the river in Bamako were subject to DDT pollution that was serious enough for the population and users of the EDM network in particular to be warned in the press (see the article in the daily newspaper L’Essor of 29/06/1998). Although it lasted only a few days, this alert nevertheless demonstrated the possibility, as of today, of pollution of the Niger serious enough to disrupt the lives of the people of Bamako. Special case of the Bamako-Koulikoro axis 170Monitoringof surface water quality at 18 risk points in the Bamako-Koulikoro urban area (Palangié, 1998) shows that all water discharge points into the Niger River exceed WHO quality standards on at least three parameters (Table 16). The parameters on which urgent priority action is needed are BOD5, COD, suspended solids and heavy metals. However, all BOD5, COD and suspended solids contents are still lower than or equal to the average values ​​of wastewater in industrialized countries, with the exception of discharge water from the Dar-Salam power plant. It is emphasized that the latter are by far the most polluted and should necessarily undergo pre-treatment in the industrial plant itself to resolve pH and heavy metal problems and to bring their other characteristics closer to those of other wastewater. 171BOD5, COD and suspended solids are almost always much higher in rainy weather due to runoff water which carries away a lot of organic matter. Heavy metals, for their part, are found in greater concentration in dry weather because the effluents are not diluted by the runoff water. It can also be deduced that soil drying is not a significant source of pollution by heavy metals. With rain and the volumes of water to be purified, the great variability of the parameters that biological purification must reduce, namely BOD5 and COD, is a major difficulty for the proper ongoing operation of a treatment plant. An essential preliminary would therefore be the separation of the wastewater networks leading to the plants and the rainwater drainage network (Palangié, 1998). 172Our measurements also show that a significant proportion of the pollutant loads are linked to suspended solids larger than 0.7 µm. The decantation of Bamako's wastewater should therefore, on its own, eliminate a significant proportion of the pollutant loads. However, the sludge resulting from this decantation would contain a significant proportion of pollutants and should therefore be subject, particularly for agricultural amendment, to storage and use precautions. In addition, the ability of suspended solids to decant is directly linked to their particle size: the finer the particles, the lower their sedimentation rate, sometimes much too low to consider decantation within a reasonable time. A study on this subject is therefore necessary. In average urban wastewater, it is estimated that approximately 66% of the BOD5 is present in particulate form, or 34% in the dissolved phase (Dégremont, 1978). These levels certainly do not come from an anthropogenic activity in the city of Bamako since its concentration hardly changes between upstream and downstream of the city. This iron therefore probably has a geological origin. Occasionally polluted waters, an unstable balance with high risk 176Thus, all previous studies and our measurements agree to highlight the current unstable, and therefore fragile, balance of maintaining the quality of surface waters despite the high flow of flood waters from the Niger River. Major industrialization projects, agricultural development in the Niger Valley and the systematic and untreated discharge of effluents from riverside towns into the river all constitute major risks of significant and sometimes irreversible pollution. According to the Bamako Sanitation Master Plan (1993-2003, p. 117), the flow rate of the Niger is sufficient to ensure its self-purification. It is generally considered that wastewater can be discharged into a watercourse without prior treatment if the following conditions are met: no facility for which pollution could prove harmful must be located nearby downstream of the discharge point (for example a pumping station); the wastewater flow rate must not exceed 1/500 of the minimum flow rate of the watercourse. 177When the effluent flow rate is between 1/500 and 1/100 of the minimum flow rate of the watercourse, the wastewater must undergo primary treatment (screening, desanding, rapid settling in 4 hours, etc.). When the wastewater flow rate is greater than 1/100 of the minimum flow rate of the watercourse, secondary treatment is necessary (lagooning, biological purification, etc.). In the case of Bamako, the minimum flow rate of the Niger is 62 m3.s-1 for a 10-year recurrence period. The self-purifying capacity of the river therefore allows the discharge of 0.124 m3.s-1 of wastewater without prior treatment, which corresponds to an equivalent population of 143,000 inhabitants (based on a consumption of 75 litres of water per person per day, the high hypothesis of the forecasts for 2005). The population connected to the sewer network was, in 1998, 44,000 people (4 of the total population of Bamako) to which must be added the population equivalent to the discharges generated by the administrative sector (estimated at 53,350 people) and the equivalent population corresponding to industrial effluents (approximately 30,000 people). With a total equivalent population of 127,350 people, we remain below the threshold for breaking the self-purification of the Niger River, which therefore makes the installation of a treatment plant unnecessary. The equivalent population should not reach this threshold until after 2005, when it is estimated at 139,250 people; which is still a close deadline. 178In fact, this calculation is very incomplete: it only takes into account the population connected to the sewer network, which is, in fact, an extremely small minority, and it does not consider, as was established in the study of the rainwater drainage network in this report, the fact that the gutters that lead to the Niger also serve as open sewers for a very large part of the population of Bamako. The equivalent population announced is therefore necessarily very underestimated. In addition, the equivalent load for industries only corresponds to biological pollution (BOD, MES) and completely obscures the impact of toxic or non-biodegradable compounds. Finally, if the EDM pumping station is located well upstream from the city center, the use of the waters of the Niger River for laundry, bathing, washing dishes or even drinking by the population means that there are, in many places downstream, discharge points where pollution can be harmful. Widespread pollution of the surface water table 179Due to the large number of point sources of pollution in the Bamako district, the almost complete absence of mitigation measures, the very shallow depth of the surface water table, the significant permeability of the soil in certain places (particularly on the right bank; the soils on the left bank appear, for the most part, impermeable) and the abundance of unprotected wells and poorly designed individual sanitation structures (Zallé and Maïga, 2002) which open direct communications between the surface and the groundwater, the surface aquifer is totally polluted. Several studies (Alpha et al., 1991; Iwaco, 1996) have characterized the pollution affecting it: high concentration of nitrates, nitrites, phosphates and chlorine which may come from various sources (detergents, fertilizers, decomposing organic matter), possible presence of pesticides and very high bacteriological pollution (coliforms and fecal streptococci, total germs) from infiltration wells that are too deep or undersized, from non-watertight cesspools and from the contribution of fecal matter by runoff water flowing through wells that generally have no coping. 180The water from the surface water table is therefore, according to WHO potability standards, unfit for human consumption. The 1996 Iwaco study has since shown that nitrate and nitrite concentrations had increased significantly in some of the wells sampled in 1991. However, it tempers the results by noting that the 1991 samples were all taken in old high-density neighborhoods where the problem of water table pollution logically arises with maximum acuity. In market gardening areas, in particular, the quality of well water is much better with nitrate, nitrite and phosphate concentrations often below the drinking water standards. In addition, wells can be places of local concentration of pollutants due to their direct communication with surface pollution. In other words, well water is not necessarily representative of the quality of the entire surface water table. With this in mind, a study of the quality of drilling water carried out for the occasion is necessary. On the other hand, the wells in the industrial area sometimes show pollution levels similar to those in the graphs and are, in additions, largely contaminated by heavy metals and toxins (arsenic, chromium). 181The increase observed in recent years in the pollution of the water table, coupled with the explosion of the population and the urban expansion of Bamako, suggests that if no measures are taken, the problem will rapidly worsen, depriving the majority of the population of its main water resource (66 in 1998). Threat to the quality of water in the deep aquifer 182The fractured sandstone aquifer is connected to the surface water table via fissures and major accidents that remain open to a depth of more than 100 m. Expected to be a source of drinking water that can be exploited by drilling, the water in the fractured sandstone aquifer has already been the subject of a prospecting study (Giorgi, 1995). The observed quality of the waters of the fractured aquifer is perfect with the exception of low nitrate levels, although it is not possible to know whether they are the result of the infiltration of waters from the surface water table or of local pollution introduced during drilling. In any case, the good quality of the waters proves that the transfers existing between the two water tables are slow enough to guarantee the purification and/or filtration of waters coming from the surface. This slowness is partly explained by the high pressure in the fractured sandstone aquifer which, by opposing gravity, slows the descent of waters from the surface water table. 183However, this balance risks being upset by the exploitation of the deep water table by drilling: the opening of communications with the surface will not only allow direct access to pollution if measures to protect the structures are not taken (although the natural gushing of water a priori prohibits a transfer through the conduits from the surface to the water table), but, above all, will cause a loss of pressure which will accelerate transfers in the direction of the surface water table/fractured sandstone aquifer. In this respect, and even more so if the pollution of the surface water table worsens, serious pollution of the fractured sandstone aquifer is perfectly possible. 184The migration of pollutants to the deep aquifer is a risk that Bamako cannot take. This risk is all the more real since there is already much speculation concerning the possibility of supplying the city with drinking water using deep drilling. This enormous risk of possible pollution of the deep water table is an additional and major argument in favor of rapid intervention of measures against pollution of the surface water table and treatment of surface water in the Bamako-Koulikoro demographic axis. Finally, it should be noted that there is a major fault at the cliff of the Bankoni hill directly connecting the water of the deep water table with the runoff water. However, this area is today a storage area for car wrecks and treatment of used batteries which pose an enormous risk to the future quality of the water of the deep water table. Summary of the situation in Bamako and recommendations 185The situation in the district of Bamako can be summarized by saying that the city is in an environmental impasse. As things stand, and to exaggerate slightly, the growth of both the population, urban space and consumption will inevitably lead to a breakdown characterized by environmental degradation that will expose city dwellers to major health risks and will lead to the destruction of all water resources whose different compartments communicate with each other (with the exception of the reservoir on the upper plateau, which unfortunately does not lend itself well to drilling because of a thick lateritic crust). It should be noted that the side effects could also be the disappearance of fish resources (due to the pollution of thelution of Niger) and intra-urban agricultural resources (due to soil and irrigation water pollution). Some of these impacts have already been observed and the only question is how long it will take for this worst-case scenario to come to fruition. 186The hydrogeology of Bamako shows that the low permeability of the soils on the left bank only allows the surface water table to be polluted via wells and individual sanitation facilities. A first measure to preserve the surface water table in the short term would therefore be to impose the protection of wells against runoff water by building coping stones and to readapt the very many inadequate or poorly designed sanitation facilities, in particular: by increasing the capacity of overused pits; by ensuring the watertightness of any underground structure receiving domestic wastewater and sewage or by adapting the depth and position of infiltration structures so as to guarantee a sufficient distance between them, the water table and the wells; by enforcing urban planning laws. 187Other medium-term measures should help to prevent access to polluted water. We too often see children bathing in rainwater drainage channels that serve as open sewers or people bathing and doing their laundry at the sewer discharge points in Niger. With this in mind, the following measures appear necessary: ​​covering rainwater drainage channels with removable slabs (not only to isolate polluted water from the population but also to ensure that the lack of light prevents the growth of plants that obstruct them) and preventing the almost systematic use of channels as dumps for household waste, branches, etc. Water access to the channels would be ensured by sufficiently large side vents, like the gutter outlets in European cities, and the removable nature of the slabs would allow for cleaning, the frequency of which would then be spaced out; fencing, over a few dozen meters, the banks of the Niger upstream and downstream of the sewage discharge points into the Niger, which seem to be, for the moment, the preferred places for the population to use its waters because of their easy accessibility by following the clear banks of the watercourses. This measure may seem extreme, but it could only be temporary while waiting for the treatment of discharges into the river and sufficient awareness among the population. 188In the longer term, water treatment will become imperative because of the increase in the population and the resulting waste. Household waste, in particular, will have to be safely dumped or, better, recycled and destroyed by incineration in special units. In terms of water management, sufficient measures seem logical: installing biological treatment plants before the main sewage discharge points and rainwater drainage channels into the Niger. Even if it is unsuitable, the stormwater drainage network must be used for the circulation of wastewater now that it is there; in parallel and subsequently, separate the wastewater drainage networks from the stormwater drainage networks to ensure the consistency of the quality and volumes of wastewater to be treated; in parallel and subsequently, install small biological water treatment structures on the scale of a few blocks of houses to free ourselves from a centralized water drainage system that is completely unsuitable for the constraints of rapid and anarchic urban development. To do this, the macrophyte lagoon technique (Kane and Morel, 1998), successfully tested in Dakar and Niamey, seems well adapted to the climatic conditions by allowing sufficient purificationfisante for a small surface area per connected inhabitant. The advantages of such decentralized installations would be considerable: on-site reuse of purified water and discharge or infiltration of much healthier water into the external environment. 189Finally, the most urgent thing is to regulate industrial discharges by imposing treatment/control on factories, particularly for the Dar Salam power plant. Conclusion 190The inadequacy, poor design and lack of maintenance of sanitation infrastructure in Bamako are responsible for serious physicochemical pollution of the surface water table and widespread biological pollution of surface water responsible for serious public health problems. For the moment, the quality of the Niger's water remains acceptable thanks to its high flow rate and despite its role as receiver of all the city's wastewater. The deep aquifer also seems to be preserved as long as deep drilling is not carried out. But the very rapid growth of the population of the Bamako-Koulikoro urban area and the resulting waste production risks worsening the situation in the short or medium term to the point of contamination of all water resources, if no measures are taken to treat wastewater and discharged for the moment as is into the environment. Viable technical solutions for the treatment of polluted water and for the protection of water resources exist and are applicable in the Malian context, in particular biological purification. The most worrying elements in this context are the lack of political will and/or application of laws to, firstly, protect water resources and, secondly, develop the infrastructure necessary for proper management in the long term. 191The most urgent treatments concern the purification of effluents to reduce BOD5, COD and suspended solids, for which treatment by biological purification is entirely appropriate. Industrial discharges must be controlled effectively and the population must be educated. Finally, rather than considering exploiting the deep water table, it seems more appropriate to urgently improve surface water treatment infrastructure and continue to draw on this inexhaustible reservoir in quantity due to the presence of the Niger River. 192As for the rest of the Niger River valley, there is still no major risk of water pollution due to the low population pressure. But, of course, the conclusions reached for the Bamako-Koulikoro axis can be repeated for the cities of Mopti, Ségou, Diré and Timbuktu. As our monitoring of water quality in the Bani Valley and the inland delta shows, there are regular problems of point pollution always linked to misuse by the population. Thus, outside the large cities, the problem of water pollution is more a problem of health education for the population than a technical problem of access to the resource. Highlighting the problems 193On reading the previous chapter, two observations are clear: on the one hand, there are many human actions and activities that affect the circulation and availability of water, and on the other hand, there are also many human activities that are sensitive to changes in the circulation and availability of water. One could quickly deduce that all activities interact with all activities and that this forms a very complex and inextricable system of interaction – which would be a way of avoiding the question. To avoid this, we propose to organize the analysis of interactions according to a single logical framework based on two steps: listing the effects (in terms of environmental changes)ntals on the hydrosystem) of each human activity or action; study the impacts of each type of environmental modification on the utility functions and uses of the hydrosystem (in particular based on knowledge of their environmental quality needs). 194The notion of "environmental modification" therefore plays a pivotal role that helps to clarify, by tracking them precisely, the paths taken by the interactions. Furthermore, the notion of "utility functions and uses" replaces the notion of "activities" in output, because it is broader and does not prejudge too precisely what man does with the possibilities offered by the ecosystem. Thus, "providing quality and regularly renewed water tables" is a utility function of the hydrosystem that does not prejudge the existence or not of village populations drawing from the water tables, nor what they do with this water. 195These semantic clarifications having been made, all the information contained in the previous chapter can be re-situated in a single three-dimensional table (figure 17) which is read from left to right with a chicane at the top (blue arrow). Sources and impacts 235Environmental changes are considered with reference to the existing situation of the Niger River in its middle section or with reference to its “potential” evolution (particularly in the event of new developments) in the near future. Knowledge acquired on other comparable tropical rivers will also be used. 236The sources (or origins) of the changes are the human activities or actions that cause, by deliberate effect or by secondary effect and directly or indirectly, the changes described. Origins 238We are dealing here with changes that affect, on a large scale and in the longitudinal dimension, the hydraulic cycle by modifying the quantity or regime of water inputs. It should be noted that, from a fisheries point of view, the water cycle can be considered to be affected at a given point if the appearance of the annual cycle of the presence, level or quality of water at this point is modified.
