In both cases, this is not negligible since it would correspond to a loss of 12 of the annual deltaic production, i.e. 12 of 40,000 t at the beginning of the 1990s (for Laë) and 12 of 120,000 t currently19. 242With the hypothesis of creating the Fomi reservoir, the filling volume of which will be triple that of Sélingué, it is almost certain that the weakening of the flood wave crossing Mali will become very significant and detrimental to fish production. 243Modifications of type (1bis), even if they are linked by nature and origin to those of type 1, must give rise to a specific analysis, insofar as the concept of threshold then takes on a determining importance. We know, in fact, that the dependence of the lakes, both those on the left bank (Tanda, Kabara, Faguibine) and those on the right bank (Aougoundou, Niangaye), on the power of the flood is not as linear or as closely coupled in time as that of the flood plains adjacent to the river. Indeed, located below the river but at a good distance from it, the lakes are supplied by channels whose supply is governed by thresholds. When the water level recedes, the lakes do not flow back into the river and therefore keep the water received. In addition, they have the shape of a basin, which means that they can remain in water for up to two or three years after a single filling, losing depth through evaporation but retaining most of their surface area in water (the most determining parameter for fish production). This is why the condition of fish productivity of these lakes is expressed differently from that of flood plains since they would only need to benefit from a satisfactory flood (which would cross the threshold necessary for their supply) every two or three years to remain fully productive. As a corollary, they are little affected by the occurrence of a single isolated bad flood. The determination of the flood intensity threshold necessary for their filling can be done from the examination of the history. For example, with regard to Lake Aougoundou, we know that no significant contribution to the lake occurred between 1981 (6.28 m in Mopti) and 1994 (6.42 m in Mopti). The lake was therefore dry from the end of 1983 until November 1994 and abundant woody vegetation (Prosopis sp.) was thus able to colonize it. As the highest level reached in Mopti between these two dates was 5.71 m (in 1988), we can deduce that the level in Mopti necessary to fill Lake Aougoundou is somewhere between 5.71 m and 6.28 m. Water management that would ensure that this threshold is crossed every other year would place this lake in a permanent condition of almost full fish productivity. On the other hand, if the flood remains just below this threshold each year, the lake's production becomes zero (and not just low) since it will then dry up completely. In other words, for fishing in a lake of this type, a succession of fairly low floods (e.g.: 5.60 m in Mopti) is much less interesting than a regular alternation of floodsvery low (e.g.: 5.20 m in Mopti) and average floods (e.g.: 6 m in Mopti). Type 2 modifications: calendar shift (delay) of the flood 244These modifications have the same origins as the previous ones, namely the need to fill the large reservoirs at the time of the flood, apart from natural causes (delay in wintering). However, to the extent that the reservoirs existing today are relatively modest and quickly filled, the flood rise continues beyond the time of their filling in an almost natural way. The shift effect is therefore for the moment almost negligible, but it should also be remembered that this shift must remain small because it is important for the fish that the peak of the flood occurs before the cold season (before the end of November, and even a little before if possible). If new large dams were installed on the upstream Niger, it is possible that the calendar delay effect could reach two or three weeks and that this would cause inconvenient impacts on the downstream part of the delta and in the loop, by making the flood wave coincide with the peak cold season (December-January). However, this remains to be verified by calculation and hydraulic simulation. In certain areas (the Niger loop up to Ansongo), it has been hypothesized that the loss of plant cover could cause an earlier arrival of the flood wave linked to local winter rains. The impacts on fish life are not well known. Changes in the lower part (low water) of the annual hydraulic cycle 245Modifications of type (3), namely changes in the lower part (low water) of the annual hydraulic cycle which extends into the delta approximately between the end of February and mid-June, can be of several types: a re-increase in the flow level and the “base” level of the low water; a weakening of the flow level and the “base” level of the low water; sudden jumps in flow and water level, sometimes reaching 10 cm of rise in 24 hours. 246The first category of these modifications is an effect of the progressive release of water from the large reservoirs upstream (by turbines and for the regular production of electricity) throughout the duration of the low water. It is proven in the delta: the low waters in the delta are today more sustained than before the creation of Sélingué, of the order of 50 cm to 1 m of additional level. The impacts of this support are beneficial to the life of the fish which then go through a particularly difficult period: little water, little oxygen and high vulnerability to fishing gear. It is clear that by increasing the chances of fish survival at low water, this phenomenon, as R. Laë (1994) has already noted, considerably reduces the risks of "true overexploitation" (or "recruitment" overexploitation, i.e. involving an attack on the annual reconstitution capacity of populations due to excessive depletion of the number of breeders). 247The second category can be caused by withdrawals intended for irrigating off-season crops. These are withdrawals by threshold dams for gravity irrigation of large areas and also pumping for small irrigated areas. The impact is necessarily negative for fish resources, but, for the moment, it is completely masked by the positive impact of the phenomenon described just before. It seems, in fact, that the contributions of the quantities turbined at low water compensate for and exceed these withdrawals; which means that the low water levels of the 1990s generally remain higher than those of the years before the Sélingué dam was filled. However, as water withdrawals for irrigating off-season crops are increasing steadily, there is a fear that the balance will soon be reversed. 20 248The third category of these changescations is caused by sudden but limited releases (a few days to fifteen days) that occur at the level of large upstream dams. These releases are linked to technical incidents (case of May 1999) or to deliberate management decisions (for example: raising the level to a threshold of agricultural interest; emitting a "visible" flood wave to satisfy the authorities of a downstream country suffering from a water shortage). The impacts of these regime changes are temporarily negative for fishing exploitation by hindering the activity (loss of traps carried away by the current, loss of time to rebuild the trap dams on the arms of the river) and by causing a drop in catches for a few days (the fish disperse and become unpredictable during these regime changes). But the impact on fish survival is rather positive for the same reasons. The complete destructuring of the natural hydraulic cycle 249Modifications of type (4) can lead to a complete destructuring of the natural hydraulic cycle. This can occur, for example, with the implementation of short but fairly strong artificial floods (flash floods) which would be of a power comparable to or greater than the natural flood (which would, in return, be greatly reduced or even cancelled by the filling of the dams). However, modifications of such magnitude are not yet current in the Niger River in Mali. They could, however, become so in the future, particularly downstream of Tossaye, if all the upstream works "in the pipeline" are completed (Fomi and Tossaye, in addition to Sélingué already existing and without forgetting Markala which draws on the low water). The share of natural dynamics in the water cycle would then become low or zero. We know that short artificial floods are not suitable, in general and except for special arrangements, for fish reproduction (Welcomme, 1999). If the hydraulic regime of the river were to become completely artificial and controlled, much weight would have to be given to ensuring that the "fish resource" and "fishing" aspects that require significant flooding are taken into consideration in water management. However, there are examples where this has been achieved with some success (Diawling Delta). Environmental changes/disturbances affecting the connectivity and morphology of the hydrosystem, impacts on fishing. Origins Changes characterized by the introduction of discontinuity in the aquatic space 250There are two possible types of changes, both affecting fish mobility: 1/ Breaks in connectivity in the longitudinal direction 251These breaks, which are due to the construction of large dams or large weirs, hinder the long-distance upstream/downstream migrations of a number of species that need to make such movements to reproduce more effectively. These include characidae (Alestes, Bricynus, Hydrocyons) and Distichodus, species with pelagic and gregarious behavior. The abundance of these migratory species then decreases as happened recently on Lake Sélingué with the construction of a hydroagricultural weir upstream on the Sankarani, in Guinea. It is important to specify that, for a migratory fish, a hydroagricultural weir with a drop of 1.50 m is as inconvenient as a dam with a 10 m dike that the water crosses by a bubbling spillway and by turbines. Because, in both cases, the obstacle is total, at least in the downstream to upstream direction21. The only palliative to such obstacles is fish ladders, which we now know how to make effective by building them much less steeply and with intermediate resting pools (the old very steep ladders, such as those used in Markala, are practically ineffective: only salmon can be caughtwould climb them!). But these new effective devices are expensive and the large dams built recently are not equipped with them (e.g.: Sélingué). 2/ Connectivity disruptions caused by the development of the plains and by channelization 252Although less spectacular and less known than the previous problem, the phenomenon of the multiplication of infrastructures (small dikes, small sluice structures) that are being built today almost everywhere, in particular to delay the submersion of perimeters and traps (ORM zone type), probably has a very significant impact on the life of species and on fish production. Indeed, almost all species need access to the plains to reproduce, feed and grow. However, many species do not dare to cross the narrow and bubbling passages represented by sluices and spillways and, as a result, abandon the use of floodplains thus developed. Only a few species, such as Tilapia zillii, are able to exploit such plains for the growth of their juveniles. To prevent the damage they can cause to crops, rice farmers install obstacles (very fine nets) on the small channels inside the plain so as to prevent them from accessing the fields. With such infrastructure and practices, it is almost certain that rice farming in controlled submersion is becoming a harmful factor for fish productivity, especially if its influence on the delta extends. Because, while it is known that fish productivity is conditioned by the extension of the areas of flooded plains, it is still necessary for these plains to be able to be actually frequented and exploited by fish! 253 Possible channelization works (to facilitate navigation or to protect urbanized areas) could, in the long term, have the same negative effects, but they have remained very limited to date. 254Even if the development of the plains, as it is practiced today, has a generally negative impact on fish, there are certain specific forms of development that could, on the contrary, increase local fish production or, in any case, promote the capture of fish. These include, for example, cofferdam systems that allow, when the water recedes, to retain water a little longer (a few weeks more) in rice fields or in small ponds, thus keeping the fish in the fattening phase until it is decided to drain them and capture them, which is then easy (noting that the fish will then have been able to acquire a more interesting size than if they had been captured at the usual period of water withdrawal). Such light developments, which require little investment but very fine adaptation to the terrain and sustained attention on the part of the villagers, are unfortunately not those that are currently promoted and supported by the development offices. In addition, some studies should be conducted on the optimization of their operation and on their possible impact, because knowledge is lacking on the subject, at least in Africa (however, there is a lot of knowledge in Asia, with the development of the fish and rice combined production model). Changes to the hydrosystem in the direction of its expansion: creation of new watercourses or new bodies of water 255With the creation of large hydroelectric and hydroagricultural infrastructures (large dams, large irrigated areas), new bodies of water or new watercourses appear, the fisheries interest of which is far from zero. 256This is how Lake Sélingué produces some 3,000 t of fish per year (ODRS data, Sélingué Rural Development Office), or 80 to 100 kg/ha of water (at high water), which is in line with known “standards”. Notethat Lake Sélingué itself benefits, due to its management method, from a regular seasonal fluctuation in its level and surface area, which produces a flood pulse effect on the river plains, which undoubtedly promotes its fish productivity. 257The large supply and drainage channels of the Office du Niger (but also smaller areas such as Sotuba) are also populated with fish and are the subject of subsistence or professional fishing (for commercial purposes). Some species (Heterotis niloticus) have found refuge there, because they now find a better habitat there than in the delta. Changes to the hydrosystem in the direction of its reduction: filling, landfall. Origins and impacts 258It is known that all continental bodies of water tend to fill up due to sedimentation and (possibly) plant colonization. This phenomenon is normally compensated (at least in part) by the annual violence of the flush, at the time of the flood. However, several phenomena can disrupt this balance and play in favor of filling. These are: riverbank agriculture (for example flood recession crops) which promotes local erosion and mechanically causes earth to descend, day after day, into the adjacent body of water (e.g. the near disappearance of Lake Bâm in Burkina Faso). To combat this risk, artificial bodies of water such as Sélingué have been surrounded by a perimeter or servitude zone in which crops are (theoretically) prohibited; the regression of plant cover in the watershed which promotes gullying and erosion, carrying increasing quantities of earth towards the bottom of the watercourses with each storm. All the activities causing the regression of plant cover (burning, overgrazing, logging, intensive agriculture) contribute to this process; desertification which loads the wind with sand and undoubtedly promotes the “clogging” (wind this time) of the natural channels in the north of the delta and in the loop with, as a consequence, the increasingly permanent isolation of the remote lake basins which therefore remain dry. 259All these mechanisms are quite similar and work against fish in the short term (increase in turbidity) as well as in the long term (reduction in aquatic spaces). Environmental changes/disturbances affecting water quality: impacts on fishing and origins Changes in water quality in the direction of nutrient enrichment 260The Niger River is not naturally rich in nutrients. A large part of the nutrients present in the delta water and necessary for the development of chlorophyll assimilation and autotrophic trophic chains (based on phytoplankton or macrophytes, cf. R. Arfi, 2002) comes from on-site recycling of organic matter, particularly from plant detritus and livestock faeces (Orange et al., 2002). This is why any additional input from agriculture (if fertilizers are used) or from urban waste could theoretically improve water productivity. However, it must be noted that the fish productivity of the delta, even without these inputs, already complies with the best standards, since it can exceed 100 kg/ha in favorable areas (Batamani, according to data from the fisheries observatory and the thesis -in progress- of A. Kodio) and that it reaches 50 kg/ha on average in the region. This probably comes from the fact that a large part of the production is based on heterotrophic pathways (e.g.: consumption of organic waste by small scraping invertebrates which themselves become prey for fish). It is therefore not certain that additional enrichment is desirable. For the moment, this enrichment remains moderate and verys local (if we consider the river strictly speaking) because the use of agricultural fertilizers remains not widespread. 261In certain limited areas such as channels and drains of the perimeters, the enrichment effect by fertilizers and/or organic matter is, on the other hand, very sensitive with excesses leading to eutrophication and the development of harmful plants (water hyacinth). The same is true on the outskirts of very large cities (Bamako) where the river receives significant quantities of wastewater. The impact on fish and fishing is then very negative, but it remains a local impact. Changes in water quality due to the addition of toxic substances 262Intensive agriculture uses toxic substances to combat insects, nematodes or unwanted plants. This is why the channels of large perimeters are not only eutrophic but also very polluted (presence of toxic substances). As a result, it is not certain that fish from these environments can be considered a recommended consumer product, especially with regard to fish caught in the "lost" drains (falas flowing north of the Office du Niger) which are, due to evaporation, places of increased concentration of pesticides. 263The impact of corn and cotton cultivation (and related fertilizers or pesticides) which tends to develop in the upstream area of ​​the impluvium should be better studied. Indeed, massive fish mortalities have been observed locally (at Lake Sélingué) in the middle of winter, which may lead to questioning possible sudden inputs of drainage water from these crops. 264The agricultural product processing industries (e.g. processing of cane, peanuts), textile industries (use of dyes) and chemical industries (batteries, medicines) are all present in Mali. They also bring toxic substances to the river. 265The same applies to urban waste, used petroleum products (used oil) and used car parts (batteries, oil filters) which are not subject to a systematic recovery and reprocessing effort. Here too, the contribution to the river is not negligible, at least at a local level. 266However, broad-based studies show that the Niger River in Mali is still a generally clean river and remains favourable to fish life and fishing. Possibilities for regulating the volume of available water: existing or future river developments Problem statement 267The Niger River is a very long river (nearly 4,200 km long) with a very contrasting regime. Indeed, the flow of the river in Mopti can go from more than 3,000 m3.s-1 to less than 30 m3.s-1. This very strong irregularity in the annual and interannual rhythm of the river reflects a whole series of difficulties in its exploitation (navigation, fishing, irrigation, etc.). Beyond Mopti – if we exclude the Yamé which flows down from the Bandiagara plateau – and up to Niamey, the river receives very few active tributaries. In addition, the contributions of these tributaries (Gorouol, Dargol, Sirba) are too weak to significantly modify the river’s regime. In this part of its course, like the Nile, the middle Niger loses half of its water in its “crossing of the desert”. 268The “Malian” flood reaches Niamey in January or February (this is the rain that fell in the upper valley during the previous winter and which has travelled a long way, notably crossing the inner delta). Low water levels in Niamey normally occur at the end of May/beginning of June. These low water levels can be very low, or even result in a virtual cessation of flow. They were less than 20 m3.s-1 in 1943, 1944, 1945, 1947, 1948 and 1950. In 1975-76, the flow rates fell to 3 m3.s-1, causing a virtual cessation of flow. 269Activities such as fishing or crop irrigation depend, in thispart of the valley as elsewhere, of the river's water resources and the distribution of these resources in the annual cycle. Finally, let us recall that the water supply of the city of Niamey depends on the river for almost 80%. The Niger, a large river with very little development 270The river, in its upper and middle courses, is currently little developed. Indeed, the majority of the major developments currently in service are located in Nigeria and Cameroon, on the lower course of the river and on the Benue. However, several major projects are currently being studied. They could significantly modify the river's regime and have significant impacts on downstream users, starting with the inner Niger delta. 271Several types of hydraulic developments exist for the regulation and exploitation of the waters of the Niger River and its tributaries: dikes (irrigated areas, protection of built-up areas, regulation of rainwater, etc.); retention or diversion dams; water diversion channels; irrigation and drainage channels; navigation channels and water level raising structures (locks, weirs). Existing hydraulic structures 272The largest existing hydraulic structures (Table 22) are all located in the Malian part of the Upper Niger watershed. These are the Sélingué (Sankarani) and Markala (Niger) developments. The Sotuba (Niger) development does not constitute a major reservoir. It can be said that apart from the abstraction for irrigation, the Sotuba development does not modify the downstream regime of the river. On the other hand, Talo does not seem to have a measurable impact in terms of flood heights, which was predictable given the nature of the planned structure – a spillway – and its size, all in all, modest. 312In conclusion, attention was focused on the possible negative impacts of Talo on Djenné. The simulation shows that this will most likely not be the case, except for a delay of about a week in the flood schedule. On the other hand, the simulation reveals potentially significant flooded areas upstream of the dam. It seems highly desirable that more detailed topographical studies be carried out in order to determine precisely the importance of these flood zones and the levels reached by the water. These two flood zones could receive irrigated areas par gravity. It should also be noted that the areas modeled by Carima are of the order of 150 km2, or 15,000 ha, a surface area significantly smaller than the 24,000 ha of the project. It reaches well into Douna. Thus, the dam’s backwater curve will directly affect the boundary condition at Douna. Consequently, this boundary condition of the Bani must be pushed further upstream. 317We note that at Sofara (PK 238), the maximum level of the Bani is higher than the left bank. There is therefore an overflow. This is taken into account by the two-dimensional Kali box, placed at Sofara. 318Impacts of the dam on the Bani: 319The Tako hydrograph (with the box) is deformed by the dam as shown in Figure 31. Figure 31 Hydrograph at Tako Impact of the dam320The sudden differences in flow illustrate how quickly the box fills. Indeed, the box that was modeled seems to fill quickly and abruptly. However, there is no evidence that this is actually the case. It would be necessary to have detailed topographic data in order to model the box more precisely. On the other hand, it seemed important to model the Mopti hydrograph (figure 32) in order to assess the influence of the dam on floods in the inner delta. Figure 32 Hydrograph in Mopti Impact of the Djenné damFigure 33 Limnigram in Mopti Impact of the Djenné dam321The Bani hydrograph in Mopti shows the same deformations as that of Tako: namely a sudden variation in the regime linked to the speed of filling of the compartment then an equally marked support (month 11) during emptying. 322Given the importance of the flow of the Niger at Mopti compared to that of the Bani, the Mopti limnigram after the confluence with the Niger no longer shows the same deformations as shown in Figure 33. A slight shift in the limnigram can be detected during filling (months 7/8) and emptying (months 11/12) without any notable influence on the flood heights conditioning the flooded areas in the rest of the delta. Technical options for better shared water management meeting different needs Current management of the Niger River water resources 323Current management of the Niger River water resources in the Republic of Mali is the responsibility of a wide range of governmental, parastatal, and non-governmental technical institutions. Generally, all of these institutions have sectoral concerns. 324These institutions and actors can be classified into the following categories: Institutions responsible for the inventory and scientific knowledge of water resources, public services responsible for hydrology and hydrometeorology such as the National Directorate of Hydraulics and the National Directorate of Meteorology, research institutions such as the Institute of Rural Economy, the National Center for Scientific Research, the Research Institute for Development. Institutions responsible for the direct exploitation of water resources public services responsible for irrigation such as the National Directorate of Rural Development and Equipment, rural development offices; public services responsible for energy such as the National Directorate of Energy, Energy of Mali; public services responsible for navigation such as the Malian Navigation Company; public services responsible for the supply of drinking water such as the water service of Energy of Mali; associations of river transport professionals; associations of industry and trade professionals; associations of agriculture professionals; socio-economic development NGOs. Institutions responsible for the exploitation of aquatic products (fauna and flora) services responsible for fishing, livestock and water and forests such as Opération Pêche, the National Directorate for Nature Conservation, the National Directorate for Support to the Rural World; associations of fishing and livestock professionals. Institutions responsible for health and environmental issues: bodies responsible for water quality control: national health laboratory, DNH water quality laboratory; public services responsible for sanitation such as the National Directorate for Sanitation and Pollution and Nuisance Control and municipal road services. Other institutions involved in the water sector in MALI 325In addition to the ministerial departments of the State and the decentralized assistance and advisory structures (State technical services), other institutions are involved in the management of water resources. These include: Local authorities, with: The municipal council which is the project owner, responsible for water and sanitation policy at the local level; The district council which approves community projects with the support of technical services; The regional assembly which ensures the consistency of the projects developed with national programs. The populations, through village communities, water point management committees, user associations, etc. The structures carrying out the work (private sector): design offices, economic interest groups, construction companies, etc. Development partners (donors, NGOs, etc.). The interministerial coordination committee for the water and sanitation sector. 326Since the objectives sought and the uses made of water are not always reconcilable, an interministerial coordination committee for the water and sanitation sector was created by decree No. 95-447/PM-RM of 27 December 1995, whose responsibilities are: to monitor the implementation of the Government's policy on water and sanitation; to give an opinion on the legislative and regulatory texts relating to the water and sanitation sector; to give a technical opinion on international conventions, protocols and agreements relating to the sector; to draw up an annual report on the actions undertaken; suggest corrective measures and adjust strategies and objectives in the short, medium and long term; propose administrative, institutional and financial measures that can ensure greater efficiency and a better impact of the actions undertaken; ensure the coherence of the programmes and financing of the different components between them and their coherence with the national development plans. 327This committee has two working commissions bringing together the technical structures of the departments concerned: a "Water Management" commission an "Environment-Health" commission 328The "Water Management" commission was active in particular in monitoring the 2001 floods and is currently piloting the activities of the integrated flood management componentwater resources of the National Rural Infrastructure Program (PNIR) financed by the World Bank. Institutions created by or under the Water Code 329Mali has enacted the law establishing the Water Code (Law No. 02-006 of January 31, 2002). This code lays the foundations for new regulations for the water sector and legitimizes the structures responsible for water resource management. It recommends the establishment of a public water service development fund and creates a national council, regional and local councils, and basin committees responsible for issuing opinions and making proposals on water resource management and development projects. 330The Water Code, in its definition of the advisory bodies involved in the management of water resources (Title III), divided the national territory into large natural hydrographic units called basins, hydrographic sub-basins or aquifer systems. 331For the management of these hydrographic units, the Water Code created in its Article 67-Title II, with the administration responsible for water and the authorities of local authorities, the following institutions: a national water council (1); regional and local water councils (2); basin or sub-basin committees (3). 332The composition and operating procedures of the national water council and regional water councils will be set by decrees issued in Council of Ministers. 333The names and delimitation of basins, hydrographic sub-basins or aquifer systems will be set by regulation. 1/ The National Water Council 334The National Water Council is responsible for issuing an opinion: on draft water master plans and water development and management master plans, as well as on any amendments thereto; on water development and distribution projects of a national nature and on major regional developments; on all issues relating to water. 2/ Regional and local water councils 335The regional and local water councils are responsible for issuing an opinion on any issue relating to water submitted by the water administration. 336To this end, they may: formulate proposals relating to the management of water resources in the basin, the hydrographic sub-basin or the aquifer systems; formulate proposals for solutions to any conflicts over water use; propose the revision of the water development and management master plan and ensure its monitoring and evaluation at the regional and local level. 3/ Basin and sub-basin committees 337The basin or sub-basin committees are responsible for ensuring concerted management of resources at the basin and sub-basin level. To this end, they may: formulate proposals relating to the management of resources in the basin, hydrographic sub-basin or aquifer systems; propose the revision of the water development and management plan for the basins and hydrographic sub-basins or aquifer systems. 338It should be noted that the creation of the Upper Niger Basin was confirmed by interministerial decree No. 02-1878/MMEE/MATCL-SG of 4 September 2002. In application of the Water Code, interministerial decree No. 02-2578/MME-MAEP-ME-SG of 30 December 2002 sets out the responsibilities, composition and operating procedures of the “Water Management” commission of the Sélingué reservoir. This decree therefore reinstates the responsibilities of the technical committee for coordination and water management of Sélingué, which mainly operated during the drought years (1982 to 1990). 339The implementation of the Water Code requires the preparation of the implementing decrees necessary for its entry into force as well as the creation of the necessary institutions. Progress in terms of implementing texts has been made concernant the management modalities of the water fund, the composition, organization and operating modalities of the national water council, regional and local water councils and the conditions for obtaining authorizations and concessions. However, much remains to be done, particularly for the basin committees, the threshold for water withdrawals, pollution prevention measures, the conditions for developing and implementing the flood forecasting and warning plan and flood prevention. 4/ The Niger River Basin Agency, or ABFN 340Mali has created the Niger River Basin Agency or ABFN (Order No. 02-049/P-RM of March 29, 2002) whose mission is to safeguard the Niger River, its tributaries and their watersheds on the territory of the Republic of Mali and the integrated management of its resources. Decree No. 02289/P-RM of 30 May 2002 establishes the organization and operating procedures of the Niger River Basin Agency. Placed under the supervision of the Ministry of the Environment, the ABFN has, as its administrative and management bodies, a board of directors and a general management. 341The ABFN, at the first meeting of its board of directors held on 17 February 2003, adopted a work programme including the implementation of the institutional framework, the establishment of the observatory, the establishment of other technical functions, the preparation of the royalty policy, the study and establishment of regional branches, the study and establishment of the basin committee and external relations. The impacts of current and planned options 342The water resources management sector in Mali is therefore characterised by a sectoral policy resulting in a multiplicity of actors and the fragmentation of activities. As a result, there are a very large number of institutions in the sector (hence the dispersion of efforts) with mixed results both in the management of water resources and in the construction of works and developments. 343Despite the programmes put in place, the strategy has not always been oriented towards integrated management of water resources, so that we are witnessing, on the one hand, an aggravation of conflicts of interest between the different water users and, on the other hand, serious threats to the availability of water both in terms of groundwater and surface resources (not to mention the damage caused by human and natural pollution, due to lack of maintenance). 344The situation thus described highlights the institutional need to set up adequate structures for effective planning and concerted management of water resources. The absence of reforms in the sector will result in the worsening of conflicts, the continuation of sectoral management and a certain mortgage of a significant part of the national heritage for future generations. 345There is thus an uncoordinated use of the water resources of the river and its tributaries by various development actors; added to this is the lack of synergy between the different institutions responsible for the protection and management of resources at the country level. There is therefore insufficient coordination and cooperation in the management of river basin resources in Mali. 346There have also been overlaps of competences, a plethora of laws and regulations which, most of the time, lead to duplication of efforts and resources, and even conflicts. Many legislative and regulatory texts exist, but they are sometimes inconsistent or even contradictory in certain provisions and their implementation poses problems. Suggestions Review of legal texts 347It will therefore be appropriate to examine the legal texts with a view to: clarifying certain provisions pto bring the various legislative texts into line and to enable better synergy between stakeholders; determine the limits and skills of the ABFN in relation to the status of the technical services, in particular the National Directorate of Hydraulics and the National Directorate of Sanitation and Pollution and Nuisance Control, on the application of the Water Code concerning in particular basin committees, fees on water abstractors and polluters. With regard to flood problems Prevention and management of flood risks 348This function must first contribute to improving the current flood forecasting and warning system. In terms of risk prevention, the emphasis will be on maintaining the banks and beds of watercourses, on preparing risk exposure plans and on preserving soil capital and ecosystems (low water support). In addition, emergency relief will be efficiently organized in the event of a crisis to concretely demonstrate solidarity between river stakeholders. The river hydrological functioning models and geographic information systems will find a well-justified use here. With regard to low-water problems 349The stakeholder consultation frameworks that are the basin committees must operate in order to harmonize activity programs, promote the coordinated management of major hydraulic structures and facilitate mediation in conflicts between users. 350In addition to the aspects mentioned in the previous point, a strategy for mitigating the effects of drought must be put in place. Also, the definition of alternative scenarios for the use of water resources appears to be an imperative. This definition must be done in consultation with all users (prepared by the basin committees) under the facilitation of the ministries in charge of water, agriculture and the environment. The river hydrological functioning models and geographic information systems will also be able to reveal a certain efficiency in these decision-making processes. With regard to other problems Observatory of natural and socio-economic resources of the basin 351It will be necessary to invest in centralizing and disseminating the information necessary for sustainable management. This function will consist of supporting the ongoing efforts of specialized monitoring and research institutions and encouraging studies on natural resources in general and water resources in particular. Information and training of stakeholders 352A continuing training program aimed at improving the skills of water and environment professionals should be developed. Also, an information, education and communication program reaching all stakeholders should be implemented for users of water resources. Framework for preparing the financial strategy of the basin 353The State, through a national institution (the National Agency of the Niger River or the ministry in charge of water), should study the financial mechanisms for mobilizing internal resources dedicated to the development of knowledge and management of water resources based on the progressive application of the principles of collector/payer and polluter/payer. However, in the short and medium term, the State and development partners will have to provide the financial resources necessary for the establishment and operation of the Agency. 354The following other considerations must be taken into account for better management of the resources of the Niger River: the assessment of water resources must be based on an efficient collection and processing system using modern techniques for measuring, transmitting, storing, representing, modeling and disseminating information; flood prevention must involve the implementation ofsetting up early warning systems and treating watersheds with anti-erosion and reforestation measures; water planning and land use planning must be closely coordinated; the adequacy of water resources and needs must be sought at the scale of watersheds and large aquifer systems; the impact of hydraulic projects must be understood and then controlled with the establishment of regularly monitored impact indicators; the control of surface flows and the strengthening of water tables through infiltration must be carried out at the scale of basins; the qualitative protection of water resources must mainly be based on preventive and incentive measures; the prevention of waterborne diseases will be based on health education and the promotion of technologies. Instruments for implementing the options: description of the tools and data used 355Better management of water resources requires, among other measures, the following: contributing to improving the current hydrological monitoring system at the national level by modernizing its data collection, processing and analysis equipment; regulating withdrawals during floods and planning for minimum releases to support low water levels, in particular by associating them with authorizations or concessions for works; managing existing water reservoirs in a concerted manner; continuing water control using suitable hydraulic works that can operate both in periods of drought and in the event of floods. Regulatory system: sensors, controls for works 356Monitoring and evaluation (qualitative and quantitative) of the available hydraulic potential of the Niger River is carried out by the National Directorate of Hydraulics. 357For surface water, this monitoring is carried out by reading limnimetric scales (to measure the variation in water height), satellite data collection platforms (PCD) and field teams (gauging floods and recession). For groundwater, this monitoring is carried out by inventorying water points (wells and boreholes) with their characteristics, periodic measurements of water level in installed piezometers and limnigraphs (devices automatically measuring water height) installed on certain boreholes. 358Water quality monitoring consists of physicochemical, bacteriological and sedimentological analyses on samples taken from drinking water and surface water. Monitoring is regularly carried out on the Bamako and Kati water supply network. All other analyses are carried out punctually and on request. 359The monitoring results are processed in the following stages: processing and data entry on computer media in the form of files; data analysis using computer programs designed for this purpose; data editing in the form of documents made available to users and decision-makers (hydrological directories, flood notes, hydrological bulletins, well and borehole directories, piezometric measurement directory, piezometric fluctuation graphs, etc.). 360The hydrometric networks (68 surface water monitoring stations) and piezometric networks (60 groundwater monitoring sites) suffer from a lack of operating resources. The water quality monitoring network is embryonic (20 monitoring sites on the upper Niger and 11 on the inner delta). 361All stations have a battery of limnimetric scales as basic equipment. Twenty-four stations are equipped with remote transmission platforms (PCD including a pressure limnigraph for the Niger basin stations installed by the Hydroniger Project. Currently, due to their obsolescence, most of the platformsmy teletransmission stations are no longer functioning properly. 362The Upper Niger Hydroecological Management (Ghenis) project installed eight automatic Meteosat stations on the main river and its tributaries in June and July 2001, six of which were placed on the former Hydroniger project sites. These stations measure, in addition to the water level, dissolved solids (conductivity) or suspended solids (turbidity), dissolved oxygen and water temperature. 363The other scientific instruments are insufficient: flow measurement equipment, specialized laboratory equipment for pollution analysis (heavy metals and organic pollutants). The mathematical model of the Niger River developed under the auspices of the Niger Basin Agency is not available at the national level. 364Although its density is lower than international standards, the hydrometric network installed on the major rivers is sufficient to make a quantitative assessment of flows at the level of the major basins. 365On the other hand, small watersheds are not equipped as part of the national network. It is essential to develop regular monitoring of small rivers, lakes and lowlands that are most affected by hydro-agricultural developments by making more financial and logistical resources available to the DNH. 366The density of the hydrometric network (number of stations/10,000 km2) across all areas of the territory where flows occur is low compared to WMO/UNESCO standards for the non-sedimentary arid zone (level stations: 1.4 versus 2.4; river flow stations: 0.76 versus 2; solid flow stations: 0.01 versus 0.4), with water level data from all stations in the network being provided with more or less gaps depending on the stations, with flows relating to 50 of the stations in the network. 367The quality of the data changes over time depending on the resources made available to the hydrological brigades of the regional directorates. The more intense the monitoring (frequent repair of stations, regular payment of observers, frequent flow measurements), the better the quality of the data. 368These shortcomings in resource monitoring are recognized as one of the main obstacles to sound water management. 369The rational management of water resources and the planning of their exploitation absolutely requires constant improvement in knowledge of this resource, both quantitatively and qualitatively. 370The continuous monitoring of the evolution of water resources according to natural or induced inflows and outflows constitutes a fundamental obligation and a formal responsibility of the State. To this end, the monitoring networks must be improved by implementing the following measures: the adoption of the management system by geographical zones; optimizing the number, spatial distribution and maintenance cost of hydrological, hydrogeological, meteorological and water quality observation networks; decentralizing the monitoring and operation of water resource observation networks; strengthening the capacities of the services responsible for the inventory of water resources. 371To this end, the following actions will be gradually implemented: more efficient data processing, conducting studies for a good quantitative, qualitative and spatial knowledge of water resources in order to be able to mobilize and exploit them efficiently; developing a system for defining objectives and comparing the situation with these objectives using regular measurements and studies conducted on the resource; establishing decision-making tools, such as integrated models of natural resources and socio-economic activities, to:better define thedevelopment scenarios; better assess and reconcile needs, resources and management constraints; better plan the construction and management of hydraulic structures and developments or water quality management actions; perpetuate the use of the IT tool (GIS) for water resource planning (in synergy with land use planning); carry out the delimitation of water management units; and define the resources to be allocated to the different user sectors. Small operational forecasting models Estimation by hydrological balance 372The daily flow rate of the Sélingué reservoir was estimated by hydrological balance using the equation (Soumaguel, 1995): 373Qa = Qs Qst Qe Qi 374Qa = daily flow rate entering the dam in m3.s-1 via the watershed; 375Qs = daily flow leaving the dam in m3.s-1 taken as equal to the daily flow observed at the Sélingué downstream station; 376Qst = daily flow stored in the dam in m3.s-1 = ΔV/ΔT; 377ΔV = difference between the volumes of the day (d) and (d-1) in cubic meters (m3), the volume being determined by the height/volume curve from the average daily level upstream recorded; 378ΔT = one day expressed in seconds (s); 379Qe = daily evaporated flow (m3.s-1) estimated from a chart; 380Qi = daily flow taken from the reservoir for irrigation (data recorded at the perimeter level). 381At the daily time step, the calculation of natural contributions to Sélingué by this method is not sufficiently precise. It also very often leads to negative values ​​in low and medium waters which show the need for smoothing. The sources of error come mainly from the estimation of the surface area and volume stored in the reservoir from a single scale reading, the reading of which to the nearest cm is very tricky and even more hazardous in windy periods. 382On the other hand, at the monthly time step, the relative error on the term "variation in the volume of the reservoir" becomes much lower and the method, despite the shortcomings described above, gives consistent and very acceptable results. The "PROPAG" model 383Propag is software developed by Orstom (Lamagat et al., 1993). It is a model based on the analysis of the propagation times of flood waves between two sections of a watercourse which allows the reconstruction or extension of hydrometric data on large rivers. 384The reaches can be of any length and shape. However, for the modelling to be correct, the physical parameters governing the flow in this reach must have constant or quasi-constant values. 385When there are no relatively significant inputs other than precipitation, the analysis is carried out using samples of water heights at the upstream and downstream stations. On the other hand, if the inputs are significant, the analysis can only be carried out on the flow rates. This analysis is carried out by software that operates on the database and provides two output files: the propagation time file as a function of the H level or the Q flow rate at the upstream station; the steady-state correspondence file of the upstream variables (H or Q) and the downstream variables. 386These two files govern the transfer function from inputs to outputs, assuming that any intermediate inputs from the samples analysed are representative of the hydrological regime. 387When there is virtually no input into the reach and evaporation losses are only a function of the surface area and therefore of the water level, the transfer function, apart from observation measurements, provides an excellent transfer of the flood wave between the upstream and downstream stations, whatever the value of the input variable. 388This model was developed during studies undertaken by ORSTOM onr the Niger Delta in the late 1970s, then developed in association with Colorado State University and, later, with Stanford University in California. It has been used effectively on several large rivers (Niger, Senegal, Gambia, Nile, Mississippi). 389This model was also used to reconstruct missing daily height data at Sélingué from heights observed at Mandiana (Guinea) as part of the hydrology update for the rehabilitation of the Sélingué dam carried out in March 1996 by the GIE Orstom-EDF. 390For the Sankarani, the model was calibrated between heights at Sélingué and Mandiana using samples of average heights observed at the two stations during the period 1968-72. The extension of the average daily heights having been carried out in Sélingué, we have an extended period from 1954 to 1988. Multiple linear regression 391We know that the maximum natural flood in Koulikoro is a function of the flood peak of the Sankarani in Sélingué and that of the Niger in Banankoro but also of the propagation time to Koulikoro. 392To get a good idea of ​​this influence on floods, Soumaguel (1995) attempted a reconstruction of the flood hydrograph downstream that should have been observed if the Sélingué dam did not exist. The results of this work were then used to make a comparative analysis between the reconstructed natural values ​​and the observed flows. 393In Koulikoro, the regression of the natural flows was carried out with those of Sélingué and Banankoro with a delay of two days. That is to say that the flow on day (d) at Koulikoro QKj was linked to the flow of Banankoro on day (d-2) QBj−2 and to that of Sélingué on day (d-2) QS j−2 . This relationship is expressed by the following equation: 394Qkj = aQBj-2   bQSj-2   c 395in which a,b,c are parameters to be determined. To estimate them, we attempted a multiple regression between the three variable terms of the equation: these are QK j , QBj-2 and QS j-2 . The calibration is done over 9 years, from 1971 to 1979, from the average daily flows from July to December. The regression gave, with a correlation coefficient r = 0.9995, the following values ​​a = 0.948, b = 1.171 and c = 17.94. 396Finally, we found the following equation: 397QKj = 0.948 × QBj-2  1.171 × QSj-2   17.94 398The average of the algebraic values ​​of the deviations between the calculated flow and the observed flow is 0.40 and that of the absolute values ​​gives 2.26. 399The average (1971-79) flood hydrographs observed and calculated are compared in Figure 34: Figure 34 - Comparative hydrographs of the Niger at Koulikoro (average 1971-79)400The calibrated model was then tested on the years 1968, 1969, 1970 and 1980. 401The comparison between the calculated and observed numerical values ​​allows us to conclude that the model, thus calibrated and verified, gives good results in general. However, it will be noted that the maxima of very wet years are underestimated, for example those of the years 1970 and 1968.

text: TENDANCES ET PROSPECTIVE CONCERNANT LES FORCES MOTRICES ET AUTRES FACTEURS FORÇANTS Les évolutions de la société malienne et de ses besoins 1L’examen de la situation et des tendances – prolongées de façon prospective jusqu’en 2025 – de la population malienne et de ses besoins s’appuie essentiellement sur les informations fournies par l’« Étude nationale prospective Mali 2025 » (ENP, 2003). La population du Mali : situation, tendances en cours et prospective sur 2025 2La population du Mali était de 9,8 millions d’habitants au recensement de 1998. Cette population est inégalement répartie sur l’étendue du territoire national. En 1987, 65   de la population vivait sur 25   du territoire national, dans sa partie sud. En 1998, ce contraste s’était encore accentué puisque 30   seulement du territoire national renfermait alors 91   de la population résidente. La densité moyenne sur le territoire national est passée de 6,2 habitants au km2 en 1987 à 7,9 habitants au km2 en 1998, avec de fortes disparités selon les régions. En effet, si on relève dans la région de Tombouctou une densité inférieure à 1 habitant par km2, on note dans la région de Ségou 25,9 habitants au km2 en 1998. Enfin, le taux d’accroissement naturel qui était de 3,7   entre 1976 et 1987 est encore de plus de 3   par an entre 1987 et 1998. Ce rythme naturel de croissance de la population est considéré comme élevé car, en dehors de tout phénomène de migration, il aboutit à un doublement de la population tous les 24 ans. Toutefois, cette forte croissance naturelle est contrebalancée par une forte émigration de la population, ce qui fait du Mali un pays à croissance démographique effective plutôt modérée. En effet, la population résidente n’a augmenté que de 1,8   en moyenne entre 1976 et 1987 et de 2,3   entre 1987 et 1998. Ce taux de croissance annuel moyen sur cette dernière période a cependant été contrasté, atteignant 4,5   en milieu urbain mais seulement 1,2   en milieu rural. 3Á l’horizon 2025, la population future est estimée entre 16 et 20 millions d’habitants selon les scénarios. La population rurale ne représenterait plus que 51   du total (environ 9 millions) pour 73   aujourd’hui. Les plus fortes augmentations de population auront lieu à Bamako, où la population aura doublée, et dans les villes du nord. Mais, en valeur absolue, la région de Bamako et celle de Ségou-Mopti resteront les plus fortes concentrations du pays avec respectivement 2,9 millions et 2,4 millions d’habitants. Ce « triangle » Bamako-Ségou-Mopti représentera d’ailleurs les trois quarts de la population urbaine. Évolution des besoins alimentaires à l’horizon 2025 4La population malienne consomme principalement des céréales (204 kg/personne/an) auxquelles s’ajoutent, en quantité limitée, de la viande, du poisson et des légumes. Il faut noter que la population urbaine consomme un peu moins de céréales (180 kg/personne/an) mais davantage de viande, de poisson et de légumes que la population moyenne qui est encore en majorité rurale. Tableau 2 – Évolution de la consommation alimentaire au Mali sur la base des données de l’enquête budget consommation de la DNSI en 1988/89 (en tonnes) 5À l’horizon 2025, le Mali devra produire entre quatre et cinq millions de tonnes de céréales par an afin de satisfaire les besoins d’une population croissante. À l’exception des céréales pour lesquelles la consommation urbaine n’atteindra « que » 40   de la production nationale, les marchés urbains absorberont en 2025 la plus importante part (55 à 75  ) de la production en poisson, en viande et en fruits et légumes, contre moins de la moitié en 1995. La consommation alimentaire des villes en produits nationaux aura ainsi augmenté 3,5 fois plus vite que celle du milieu rural sur la période 1995-2025. 6Les productions de céréales, de poisson, de fruits et légumes et de viande devront donc doubler, voire tripler, d’ici 2025. Pour atteindre cet objectif, la croissance des surfaces cultivées ne suffira pas, l’augmentation des rendements devant devenir le facteur principal de la croissance de la production. Évolution des besoins en énergie du Mali à l’horizon 2025 7Les sources d’énergie traditionnelles (essentiellement le bois et le charbon de bois) représentent jusqu’à aujourd’hui la plus grande part (environ 90  ) de l’énergie consommée au Mali. Une autre part, assez importante, est représentée par les carburants utilisés par les véhicules ainsi que par le gaz domestique. 8La consommation d’énergie électrique – qui est celle qui concerne le plus directement la gestion du fleuve – représente jusqu’à ce jour une part relativement modeste, mais elle est en forte augmentation. Au Mali, on peut associer très étroitement l’évolution de la consommation électrique à celle de la production d’énergie électrique dans la mesure où le pays est quasiment en autarcie pour cette ressource qui n’était ni importée ni exportée jusqu’en 2002. Les choses ont un peu changé depuis, bien qu’il ne s’agisse pas d’une exportation au sens de la balance commerciale, avec l’approvisionnement du Sénégal et de la Mauritanie par le courant de Manantali. 9Selon l’Étude nationale de prospective (ENP, 2003), la production d’électricité a été multipliée par 4,8 entre 1980 et 2002, soit un taux de croissance annuelle moyen de 6,99   (fig. 3). Ce chiffre est à rapprocher du rythme de croissance de la population générale (1,8   par an) et surtout, du rythme de croissance de la population urbaine (4,5   par an), puisque, seules, les villes sont pour l’instant concernées par l’électrification en réseau. Mais il faut tenir compte aussi de l’extension du réseau qui était limité dans les années 1980 aux principales villes et qui s’élargit sans cesse, incluant un nombre croissant de villes moyennes et même de villes petites (26 villes électrifiées en 2002). Ce qui fait que le nombre d’abonnés croit plus vite que la population urbaine. Par exemple, il est passé de 66 000 à 102 000 entre 1995 et 2001, soit un rythme annuel d’augmentation de 7,25  . On retrouve bien là une valeur de croissance voisine de celle de la production électrique. 10Selon cette même étude, le taux de croissance de la population urbaine devrait se maintenir à 4,5   pour aboutir à une population urbaine prévisible de 9,15 millions d’habitants en 2025 (au lieu de 3,2 millions en 2002). Comme il est prévu que la totalité des villes de plus de 20 000 habitants ainsi qu’un certain nombre de petites villes de moins de 20 000 habitants (soit 93 villes au total) soient alors desservies par un réseau électrique, cela représenterait une population potentiellement connectée de 8,4 millions d’habitants (44   de la population totale du pays) à comparer au 1,75 million d’habitants vivant dans les 26 villes connectées en 2002 (soit 16,5   de la population totale). Il est donc logique de prévoir jusqu’en 2025 une poursuite de la hausse de la consommation d’électricité au même rythme que celui observé durant les deux dernières décennies, c’est-à-dire de l’ordre de 6,5 à 7   par an. Cela ferait passer la consommation effective d’électricité de 430 000 millions de KWh (soit 0,43 TWh) en 2003 à environ 2,00 TWh en 2025, soit une multiplication prévisible de la consommation par un facteur quatre à cinq.
