Evolution of electricity production in MaliSource: ENP, 2003Climate forcing factors in the Niger Basin A climate marked by several modes of variability 11According to Hulme (2001), it is not really possible to define average values ​​that could be described as “normal” in terms of rainfall in the northern Sudanian and Sahelian zone. The normality of this climate is in fact its great variability affecting several time scales. However, the overlapping of these scales of variability has long hampered understanding of the driving processes and consequently the ability to identify trends andto model changes. The term "trend" must be considered here with great caution: what may appear to be the trend on a given time scale may, in fact, be part of a cycle on a longer time scale. 12Following the approach of Ward (1998) who demonstrated the interest in distinguishing climate oscillations that occur at different periodicities (or frequencies), we attempt here to decompose the variability of the Sudano-Sahelian climate into several individualized components and to show which of these components can be linked to what is perceived as the "trend" by humans on a decadal scale. Variability of the internal structure of the rainy season 13Le Barbé and Lebel (1997) showed that the decreases in rainfall in the Sahel during recent decades are essentially associated with a decrease in precipitation during the central months of the rainy season (July-August), while the total duration of the rainy season does not change significantly. According to d’Amato and Lebel (1998), it would be, more precisely, a decrease in the frequency of cyclonic passages during these two central months. Thus, the study of changes in the structure of the rainy season can lead to an understanding of the intimate mechanisms of monsoon dynamics and consequently, to hypotheses on the factors that create the trends affecting the total amounts of rainfall in the medium and long term. Inter-annual variability of total rainfall amounts 14This variability characterizes the variations recorded from one year to the next or from a small group of years (2 or 3 years) to the one that follows it. This scale of variability exists, but it is relatively less important than in other regions of Africa. Oscillations with a quasi-five-year, quasi-three-year or quasi-two-year periodicity in fact represent only 15 to 20% of the total variability. This means that, as a general rule, the years that follow one another tend to resemble each other in terms of rainfall rather than to oppose each other. However, it seems that this statistical observation made by meteorologists examining the long series of the last century is no longer valid for the very last decade which is, on the contrary, characterized by strong interannual oscillations with dry years (1996, 1997, 2000, 2002, 2004) closely interspersed with rainy years (1994, 1995, 1998, 1999, 2001, 2003, 2005). Inter-decadal variability of total rainfall amounts 15A large proportion of the variability of the Sudano-Sahelian climate falls within this time scale which is also called low-frequency fluctuation. According to Moron (1997), there is a quasi-decadal pulse of periodicity over 12-13 years which would represent, by itself, 12 to 14 of the variability. The "typical" durations of dry or wet phases would therefore be rather 5 to 10 years. The double dry decade from 1973 to 1993 could be attached to this category of variability even if it constitutes a sort of anomaly by its very long duration. Multi-decadal variability of total rainfall quantities 16We can classify in this category the developments that are revealed on the scale of the century and of history. It seems that there exists - certainly since the end of the 19th century and probably since the 17th century (Hulme, 2001) - a tendency towards a progressive decrease in rainfall over this very long horizon. This trend would also affect the Sahara which is also known to have been much greener (and richer in fauna) in prehistoric times than today. However, given the very strong interdecadal variability, such a historical trend does not prevent very rainy episodes lasting several years from still occurring in the future, as was the case around the middle of the20th century. 17Compared to all the described variabilities, it seems that ground surface conditions play a role in amplifying climate oscillations; that is, they tend to reinforce current rainfall situations (positive feedback) with a certain inertia. This may be a factor in explaining the predominance of interdecadal variability over interannual variability. Changes perceived and discussed by humans 18A succession of wet and rainy episodes has been documented in colonial archives since the beginning of the 19th century. We know that a very dry episode occurred in the first half of the 19th century, probably of comparable intensity and duration to that of 1973-93. Another very marked dry episode occurred at the beginning of the 20th century. On the other hand, the years 1950 to 1960 were abnormally wet, which resulted in very powerful floods (Fig. 4). Figure 4. Electricity production is entrusted to a hydroelectric power station equipped with four Kaplan turbines of 11.9 MW each. An irrigation intake serves an irrigated area of ​​1,500 ha intended for populations displaced by the dam, but the direct withdrawals made by Sélingué for irrigation are very low. 26The retention area extends over two river valleys, each 65 km long. When the reservoir is at its maximum level (level 348.5 m reached each year at the end of September), its volume is 2.63 billion m3 and its surface area is 430 km2. 27The Sélingué dam is managed with a total filling in a few weeks (between the last days of July and September 20) by the annual natural flood, then with a destocking and turbine phase as the needs for electricity and downstream flow support increase, from January to June, to finally reach an almost total emptying at the beginning of July. The residual volume is then less than 10 of the full volume. Over the entire annual cycle and if we stick to qualitative terms, the effect of the dam on the downstream flow is therefore simple to describe: it is a "regulation" with flood clipping then support of the low-water flow. Sélingué is also the only structure with the capacity to support low-water flows, both for the water supply of the Office du Niger at the end of the dry season and for that of the city of Niamey, which is located nearly 1,500 km downstream. 28From the managers’ point of view, the use of the dam to support low-water flows downstream has been the subject of great attention, with, in particular, the following instructions: maintaining a minimum level of 60 cm at the Koulikoro scale and a guaranteed minimum flow of 40 m3/s downstream of Markala. 29The effect of filling the reservoir on the annual flood of the Sankarani (and therefore on that of the Niger, downstream) has, however, received little attention. However, it can be estimated that the peak flood reduction must be of the order of 400 m3/s, which are therefore removed from what the natural flood would be downstream in the absence of a dam. Indeed, having to fill approximately 2 billion m3 in eight weeks necessarily leads to the withdrawal of approximately 413 m3/s (on average) during this same period of time. It should be noted that this filling phase, therefore of withdrawal, affects the entire phase of the natural rise of the Sankarani's contributions, including the peak flood, since it continues until around September 20. Rain-fed or "traditional" rice cultivation (excluding AHA) 61This very old system does not require any hydraulic development. It is based on the use of local varieties of "floating rice" capable of overcoming a submersion of three meters. The rice field is located according to the flood height expected by the rice farmer who relies on his experience and can move his field each year. Ploughing takes place either in February-March after the harvest, or in May-June just before the return of the rains. Sowing is done broadcast, the rice rises with the rain then continues its development with the flood water which then floods the plains. Floating rice derived from Oryza glaberrima can withstand a 3 m layer of water provided that the rate of rise of the water does not exceed 5 cm per day. 62The harvest takes place in the water, between the end of October and December, depending on the varieties used. This does not prevent production results from remaining very random. This mobility of rice fields, which was of the order of ten kilometers in the 1950s (Gallais, 1967), worsened with the great irregularity of the floods of the 1980s. It is therefore acceptable, in the first analysis and taking into account statistical uncertainties, to attribute to this basin almost the entire figure of national production and its evolution, i.e. 55,000 to 140,000 t of fresh weight equivalent depending on the year (fig. 8). The bulk of the production of the Niger basin is itself quite concentrated: approximately 80% (40,000 to 120,000 t/year) comes from the delta regioninterior of Niger considered in its extended definition (from Ké-Macina to Diré, including lakes). The rest comes from the Sélingué reservoir lake (4,000 t/year), from the part of the river upstream of Macina, from the region of the Niger bend between Diré and Gao or from the southern tributaries (Baoulé). 89Thanks to this high production, Mali is practically self-sufficient in fish, at least in years of average or good floods (production greater than 100,000 t). Small quantities of frozen sea fish are, however, imported and consumed in the capital, while fresh and smoked fish from Mali are exported to Burkina Faso and Côte d’Ivoire. 90The number of fishermen is not easy to assess precisely, both for reasons of definition (where does the notion of “fishermen” begin and end?) and for reasons of statistical coverage. On the first point, several categories of fishermen can be defined by establishing a correspondence with the international terminology promoted by the FAO. First, there are people who fish but whose main profession is something else, for example agriculture. They can be considered occasional fishers and they can have a very varied ethnic origin. There are also fishermen who combine agriculture and fishing in a fairly balanced way. They generally belong to large multi-active households that split from December-January to May-July: some men stay in the village to harvest, rest and prepare the rice plots while the others leave on migration to devote themselves to fishing full time until the rainy season when they will have to return to the village to take care of the fields too. The latter can be considered part-time intensive fishermen. Finally, there are households and individuals who devote themselves full-time to fishing, often undertaking seasonal migratory circuits in order to always be present where fish is most available (full-time fishers). In Mali, the last two categories described generally claim Bozo or Somono identity (Fay, 1989; Bauman et al. 1994). Source: FAOSTAT (2004)Figure 8. The vast majority (over 95%) of production comes from the Niger basin.91At the end of the 1980s, major surveys estimated that for these last two categories of "real fishermen", the number of households was around 30,000 for the delta alone. This represented approximately 60,000 active men engaged in fishing (Morand et al., 1991). However, this figure is probably far outdated today, and fishermen from other regions of the Niger Basin in Mali should also be added. A number of fishermen (active men) of 80,000 therefore appears to be a plausible minimum figure for today. 92But we must also take into account the many people who work in fishing without being fishermen: net traders, fish traders, fish processors, small landing stage workers (carriers of crates, packers of batches to be shipped). 93Taking all these categories into account and accepting a minimalist ratio of 1 job on land for 1 job as a fisherman, strictly speaking, we can estimate that at least 160,000 people have a job directly linked to the sector. This allows us to estimate – by adopting the ratio accepted for rural West Africa (Hugon, 1998) of two non-professionally active people for one active person – at nearly 500,000 people (children and the elderly included) the population whose livelihoods are based significantly or exclusively on fishing. This estimate, even rough, allows us to estimateto state that the fishing sector is very important for the population of Mali even if it does not generate significant revenue for the state budget. The relative contribution of the fishing sector to national wealth was estimated at 4.2% of GDP in 1995 (Breuil et al., 1996). 94At all points along the river, fishing takes place in campaigns of eight to nine months. It begins intensively at the beginning of the receding waters, in November or December depending on the location, then continues as the receding waters and the low water levels progress until the next flood rises (end of June or beginning of August, depending on the location). Fishing is intensive and catches decrease as the campaign progresses. It is estimated that three-quarters of the fish biomass present in the river at the beginning of December is thus "harvested" during a fishing campaign (Kodio et al., 2002) before the next flood allows the biomass to be replenished between July and November. This replenished is "total" - at least if the flood is good - and no negative effect of the fish harvested during a campaign "n" on the volume results of the following campaign "n 1" is ever noted. 95Apart from the case of Lake Sélingué where production is remarkably stable, fish production performances in the Niger River valley and particularly in the delta vary greatly from one year to the next. They are closely correlated with the power of the annual flood and in particular with the magnitude and duration of the flood (fig. 9). This is explained by the fact that the growth of young fish hatched at the beginning of the flood (in July) then takes place in the flooded plains until November (Bénech and Dansoko, 1994; Niaré, 1994). These same fish will then be caught during the fishing campaign during the low water period and then during the low water period. 96The performance of fish production can also be assessed in relation to the areas that generate it. This is possible in the inner delta where the areas flooded by the flood (7,000 to 20,000 km2 depending on the year) can be linked to production (40,000 to 120,000 t depending on the year and the flood - Laë, 1992b) showing an average productivity of 60 kg/ha of flooding. This is within the generally accepted range for this type of environment, which is 40 to 100 kg/ha (Welcomme, 1989). However, if we consider specific areas of the delta that are favourable and intensively exploited, we observe, locally, high values ​​of 100 kg/ha, or even more. 97Moreover, the potential for developing village fish farming remains significant, but it concerns other areas (outside the regions of large-scale commercial fishing) and other populations, which are more agricultural (Niaré et al., 2000). While the herd is relatively stable in the large traditional livestock breeding regions in the north of the country (Mopti), it is tending to expand in the south: for example, in the Sikasso region, the herd increased from 336,000 head in 1970 to 741,000 head in 1995, an increase of 121. This is due to the exceptional productivity of its flooded pastures, which remain "green" for seven to eight months. The best of them, the bourgoutières, have an annual productivity of between 20,000 and 30,000 kg of dry matter (DM) per hectare, with a green fodder production period lasting from December to July. It should be remembered that the usual Sahelian pastures rarely exceed 2 t of DM productivity and that they generally remain green for less than four months in the year. The bourgoutières also exist in the river valley, upstream of the delta but especially downstream, in particular in the Niger bend where they play an important role in the organization of Gourma livestock farming. However, they only have a limited extension in these areas. 101The inland delta therefore remains the only natural region in Mali – and in West Africa – which allows a high pastoral load over a vast area since it concentrates approximately 20% of the national cattle herd on 1.5% of the territory. 102The inland delta is submerged by the flood from August onwards, and it is then deserted by the shepherds whose herds begin a long transhumance towards the pastures of the Sahel. The return takes place in November-December according to a schedule dictated by the speed of the receding water, the herds then traveling through the delta following a network of tracks and shelters whose use is strictly regulated by custom. 103Apart from watering, the shepherds are not, in the strict sense, users consuming the water resource but, just like fishermen, they depend very closely on the annual flood, the magnitude of which directly conditions the existence and productivity of the plant formations that constitute the fodder resource of their herds. 104Livestock farming can therefore be threatened by floods that are too low since the reconstitution of plant biomass depends, in part, on the flood. 105For a very low flood (5.10 m), the losses in fodder production are around 40%. It should be noted, however, that the loss in fodder production is significantly lower than the reduction in the flooded surface area which, for a flood height of 5.10 m, reaches around 80% of the flooded surface area at 6.60 m. The explanation is that the plant formations that are not affected by the flood have production that is not zero. They continue to produce thanks to the rain and the capillary rise of the water table. The variability of the floods therefore affects the fodder production of the inner delta with a response slope lower than that of the flooded areas. In terms of carrying capacity, it can be deduced that the delta, which can support 1.5 million animals in a very good year, can only feed 900,000 animals in a bad year (i.e. following a low flood). However, it seems that fodder production is very resilient: after one or two years of low flood and poor fodder production, the return of a good flood allows a rapid return to higher production (Hiernaux and Diarra, 1986). HEALTH AND EVOLUTIONARY TRENDS OF THE NIGER RIVER ECOSYSTEM Surface water quantities 117In this region of the world, surface waters are, more than anywhere else, drastically dependent on the climate due to extreme variability in rainfall deficits (see “Climate forcing factors in the Niger Basin” p. 29). The drought of the 1970s and 1980s is largely responsible, on the one hand, for the current strong seasonal variations (with very low low water levels) and, on the other hand, for the strong interannual variations. The question of whether there is a recent trend towards a deterioration in the rainfall-runoff relationship (i.e. there would be less runoff – therefore less flow in the river – than in the past for equivalent rainfall) is still under debate. 118Some surface waters, particularly in the north and northeast of the Inner Niger Delta, are lakes that are filled when the flood crosses certain thresholds. In these cases, the relationship between rainfall and surface water resources is less immediate. Indeed, located below the river but at a good distance from it, the lakes are supplied by channels whose supply is governed by thresholds (Orange et al., 2002). When the water recedes, the lakes keep the water received due to the thresholds and therefore do not flow into the river. In addition, because of their basin shape, they can remain filled for up to two or three years after a single filling, losing depth through evaporation but retaining most of their surface area in water. This is why these lakes only need to benefit from a satisfactory flood crossing the threshold necessary for their supply every two or three years to maintain their character as a lake and a water resource. Correspondingly, they are little affected by the occurrence of a single isolated bad flood. But, conversely, these lakes do not benefit from the improvement effect that can exist between a "very low" flood and a simply "low" flood because in both cases, the thresholds allowing their supply are not crossed (this was the case during the entire period 1981/93). The determination of the flood intensity threshold (height) necessary for their filling can be done from the examination of the filling history. Quantities of groundwater 119Groundwater exists in large quantities in Mali. It is characterized by an annual renewal flow of 55 billion m3 of which only 105 million m3 are exploited, or barely 0.2. 120The reserves are classified into two broad categories according to the mode of water deposit: generalized aquifers and fissured aquifers which are generally narrowly localized. 121Generalized aquifers are associated with poorly or unconsolidated detrital formations of essentially continental origin which have accumulated in sedimentary basins.entary to the Secondary and Tertiary. These aquifers are generally multi-layered with intergranular porosity and occupy a little more than half of the national territory. They contain old and generally non-renewable waters due to the low rainfall and their often too great depth which does not allow their periodic supply. The flow rates of the boreholes of these aquifers are greater than 10 m3/h for more than half of the cases and can sometimes exceed 50 m3/h. 122Fissured aquifers are associated with crystalline formations (the basement) or ancient sedimentary formations of the Precambrian and Primary. They are characterized by semi-continuous or discontinuous water tables depending on the density of the fracturing networks that affect them. A distinction is made between discontinuous aquifers, semi-continuous aquifers which benefit from a high contribution by rainfall thanks to their geographical location and finally, superficial aquifers. Water quality Surface water quality 123According to all the studies conducted on the quality of the waters of the Niger River (Iwaco, 1996; Equanis, 1997; Gihrex, 2000; Ghenis, 2001), the Niger River is, like most of the large African rivers, still relatively unaffected by chemical contamination (Picouet et al., 2002). Indeed, the waters of the river are generally and for the majority of its course in Mali free of metal pollution, pollution by nitrates and ammonium, pollution by phosphates and biological pollution due to the large volume of water involved in the flow of the river (dilution effect). This result is logical given the low industrialization of the Niger watershed, the minor use of fertilizers and pesticides in agriculture and especially, the anthropogenic desert (low population). 124However, on this last aspect, weekly monitoring of the quality of well and borehole water as well as runoff water in the cotton-growing area (CMDT of Southern Mali) has shown the existence of significant occasional pollution by pesticides, particularly DDT, mainly linked to problems of fertilizer storage or misuse (Bonnefoy, 1998). 125Furthermore, while the physicochemical quality of the waters of the Niger River remains generally good – with the exception of certain points near industrial discharges on the Bamako-Koulikoro axis (Palangié, 1998) – there are occasional phenomena of bacteriological pollution at most of the residential sites. In these places, the high concentration of coliforms and faecal streptococci makes the surface water undrinkable according to WHO standards. However, this water is still commonly used for drinking; which induces significant health risks. 126In addition, the Bamako-Koulikoro reach deserves special examination given the high concentration of habitats and activities, both industrial and agricultural, which are installed on its banks. Monitoring of 18 risk points (Palangié, 1998) on this reach has shown, in fact, that all the water discharge points into the river exceed WHO quality standards on at least three parameters. The parameters on which urgent action is needed as a priority are: BOD3, COD4, suspended solids (SS) and heavy metals. However, all BOD, COD and SS contents remain lower than or equal to the average values ​​of wastewater in industrialized countries, with the exception of the discharge water from the Dar-Salam power plant which is, by far, the most polluted. Our measurements also show that a significant proportion of the pollutant loads are linked to suspended matter (SS) larger than 0.7 µm. The decantation of Bamako's wastewater in suitable facilities (to be built) should therefore, on its own, make it possible to eliminate a significant proportion of the pollutants. 127In conclusion, all the studies areagrees to emphasize that the quality of the surface waters of the river is still generally good except at certain points or particular reaches, but that it is threatened: major industrialization projects, agricultural development in the Niger Valley and the systematic and untreated discharges of effluents from riverside settlements all constitute major risks of significant pollution in the future. Groundwater quality 128At the groundwater level, two quality problems can be described, both located in the Bamako district: that of the Bamako surface water table and that of the deep aquifers beneath this same water table (Palangié, 1998). 129Concerning the Bamako water table (or superficial aquifer), it can be said that it is totally polluted due to its very shallow depth, the large number of point sources of pollution in the Bamako district, the almost complete absence of mitigation measures, the significant permeability of the soil in certain places (particularly on the right bank) and the abundance of unprotected wells and poorly designed individual sanitation works (Zallé and Maiga, 2002) which open direct communications between the surface and the groundwater. Several studies (Alpha et al., 1991; Iwaco, 1996; Palangié, 1998) have characterized the pollution affecting it: high concentration of nitrates, nitrites, phosphates and chlorides that may come from various sources (detergents, fertilizers, decomposing organic matter), possible presence of pesticides and very high bacteriological pollution (coliforms and fecal streptococci, total germs) coming either from infiltration wells that are too deep or undersized, or from non-watertight cesspools, or from the contribution of fecal matter by runoff water that flows into wells that are generally without a rim. The water from this surface water table is therefore, according to WHO potability standards, unfit for human consumption. The increase in pollution of this water table observed in recent years, coupled with the explosion of the population and the urban expansion of Bamako, suggests that if no measures are taken, the problem will rapidly worsen, depriving the majority of the population of its main water resource (66 in 1998). 130Still in Bamako, there is a threat to the quality of the water in the deep aquifer ("fractured sandstone aquifer"), which is all the more worrying since this aquifer is expected to be a source of drinking water that can be exploited by drilling in the near future. However, this aquifer is connected to the surface water table via fissures and major accidents that remain open to a depth of more than 100 m. So far, the observed quality of the water in this fractured aquifer is very good, but this balance risks being broken by drilling of the deep water table: opening up communications with the surface will not only allow direct access to pollution (if measures to protect the structures are not taken) but above all, cause a loss of pressure which will accelerate transfers in the direction of the surface water table towards the deep aquifer. If, in addition, the pollution of the surface water table worsens, serious pollution of the fractured sandstone aquifer becomes perfectly possible. 131The other aquifers in the country, whether superficial or deep, are a priori little affected by pollution given the general quality of the surface water. Only very specific points, such as the water tables under large cities, may be exceptions here and there. Geomorphological stability: erosion/sedimentation/sanding Erosion 132Rainfall, relief, lithology of the basin and the resulting soil quality are the main explanatory factors for the erosion rates observed on theNiger. Studies of spatial variations in suspended matter flows carried out by the DNH (National Directorate of Hydraulics of Mali) with Orstom and then the IRD from the 1970s to the 1990s show that erosion is increasing on the Koulikoro-Ké-Macina reach due to changes in lithological conditions (Picouet et al., 2002). The low level of material exports in the upstream Niger basin is remarkable in comparison with other large basins in the world. It should also be noted that as the increasingly desert areas approach, the vulnerability of soils to wind erosion increases significantly and that material flows (represented by sand) increase in the river after it passes through the interior delta. This gradient tends to show that the human or agricultural activity factor, which is much more present in the south (upstream of the basin), has not, to date, generated significant erosion phenomena. Sedimentation 133Given the low concentrations of suspended solids (SS) transported by this river, sedimentation is generally very low in the Niger River Valley. However, studies have shown the existence of a certain sedimentation phenomenon in the Inner Niger Delta. Indeed, the balances of losses of suspended matter flows transported by the river between the delta's inlets (Ké-Macina and Douna) and its outlet (Diré) show that the Inner Niger Delta retains between 0.15 million tonnes (during "dry" years, i.e. with a small flood area) and 1.3 million tonnes of sediment (during years of heavy flooding) annually. In fact, sediment losses across the entire delta represent an increasing, almost linear, function of the incoming suspended matter flows. But in detail, it is necessary to underline a difference in behavior between the upstream delta and the downstream delta: if there is always an accumulation of sediments in the upstream delta, the balances on the downstream delta are relatively balanced. 134Indeed, in the upstream part, the delta is an immense classic flood plain where the numerous meanders feeding the innumerable ponds and the significant plant cover constitute perfect sediment traps. In this part of the delta, the quantity of material deposited is a direct function of the importance of the hydraulicity of the flood. However, it should be noted that the quantity of sediments involved is very low if we relate these tonnages to the surface area of ​​the delta. There is therefore no concern about filling the delta. On the other hand, these sediment contributions are major contributions to maintaining the fertility of the environment. 135In the downstream part of the delta, after passing the upstream plain and the central lakes, the waters are very lightly loaded and the quantities of sediment involved are therefore low. The recovery of flood remains in the minor beds and probable slope erosion at the start of the flood, then the remobilization of the flood recession and wind erosion after the flood at the start of the dry season are undoubtedly the major processes in the sedimentological functioning of the downstream delta. 136Finally, the Gihrex work (Integrated Management, Hydrology, Resources and Operating Systems project, IRD Environment and Environment Department) has shown that there is a particular threat to Lake Debo, the large central lake of the inner Niger delta. Indeed, thanks to decades of drought, the bourgou has developed very widely on its banks and has even been planted by farmers. This fodder retains the terrigenous sediments brought by the river and associates organic matter with it from year to year. However, despite the resumption of flows over the last ten years, we have noticed that a muddy plug has formed at the outlet of Lake Debo. This plug represents a significant danger for the ecology of the lake, its navigation and, in the long term, for life.of the Niger River (Orange et al., 2002). "Silting up" of the river 137The common term "silting up" can cover different phenomena: the increase in the sand stock, the mobility of sandbanks and the problems of loss of beaches or destabilization of certain banks which can locally result in narrowing of the riverbed. 138Concerning the first phenomenon, all scientific data show that there is no increase in the total sand stock in the riverbed, on the Malian part of the Niger River. However, the second phenomenon (the natural mobility of sandbanks) exists and causes inconvenience to river users. This phenomenon is very largely linked to the lack of dredging of navigation channels; which is systematically done in all rivers with sandy beds. 139As for the problems of loss of beaches and destabilization of certain banks, they are linked to the intensive exploitation of sand from the riverbed near urban areas. Furthermore, an impression of silting up of the river can arise when banks "appear" following a drop in water levels, particularly during very low water levels (e.g. June 1999). 140Finally, in the Niger bend, wind transport of sand causes the disappearance of cultivation areas or the local obstruction of channels and arms feeding ponds or basins. It also causes the blocking of meanders in the secondary arms of the river: the Koli-Koli has thus become impassable for navigation today. 141It is also necessary to highlight a phenomenon contrary to silting up and which is linked solely to human activity: "desanding" linked to the exploitation of sand by man for construction. This activity is very widely developed near large urban centers and particularly around Bamako and Koulikoro. In this reach, the sand banks have retreated by around a hundred kilometers in 10 years! This changes the ecology of the river by destroying spawning grounds due to the disappearance of aquatic vegetation. It also changes the shape of the flows and, in particular, guarantees less risk of flash floods. Sand mining is the major environmental problem of the life of the river. Soil fertility 142In Mali, in general, the decline in soil fertility is one of the major constraints to the increase in agricultural production. Generally speaking, it is more linked to demographic pressure and in particular to the reduction of fallow periods than to water or even wind erosion. Indeed, erosion phenomena, when they occur, are often associated with processes of local redistribution of soil fertility without broad consequences. 143In the particular case of the Inner Niger Delta, fertility is maintained by the "on-site" combination of natural ecosystem processes and processes generated by traditional production systems that exploit this fertility (in particular livestock farming). However, the sedimentary contributions of the river from the upstream basin (which are of a moderate but not negligible volume) play a complementary role. It should be recalled here that these contributions are all the higher when the flood is strong and the flooding is significant. 144In large irrigated areas, such as those of the Office du Niger, soil fertility is not only affected by an increase in alkalinity but also by a decrease in their organic and mineral fertility (potassium), the impact of which is beginning to be felt, particularly in the Macina area. Furthermore, the phenomenon of soil salinization exists in the areas, but it has been well studied and the risk factors are now known, which allows it to be better controlled. It should be noted, however, that several risk factors are worsening, which should encourage increased vigilance. These factors are: the extension ofcultivated areas and the reduction in available water volumes, thereby limiting leaching; the development of off-season crops, which results in permanent flooding of irrigation canals and contributes to the recharging and rise of the water table, a phenomenon that promotes the concentration of salts on the surface of the soil; the increase in summary developments (in terms of the quality of levelling and the drainage network). Resources and plant populations General situation 145In Mali, all observers agree that the forests are under threat, but there is great uncertainty about the real extent of the decline of these forest formations. It seems, in fact, that the area of ​​woody formations has experienced a fairly limited annual decline of 0.05 (87 km2 per year, or 1,000 km2 in total in 15 years) over the last fifteen years, which is essentially attributable to the increase in cultivated areas and the disappearance of several forests in the Mopti region. Thus, deforestation would be limited, contrary to the feelings of the villagers, and this can be explained by the fact that the process of natural reconstitution of forests is continuing. 146Generally speaking, there is no major effect of drought, in terms of the presence or disappearance of species, on the biodiversity of flora in Mali. But if there is no disappearance of species, there is a scarcity of some of them. Plant populations of the Inner Niger Delta 147The inventory carried out by CIPEA researchers highlights a list of 189 species in this area, with 137 herbaceous species for the delta and 52 woody species. Compared to the neighboring Gourma, which has 350 species, this is a relatively poor flora, like that of the majority of floodplains. This poverty of the delta's flora, however, contrasts with a high seasonal production of biomass, which is 15 to 20 times higher than that of neighboring Sahelian areas. The delta's forests 148According to the Woody Resources Inventory Project (Pirl), forest formations cover 4.5 million hectares for the entire Mopti region, while crops and young fallow land extend over 1.8 million hectares. These are mainly shrubby savannahs, rarely wooded, as well as various palm groves. Thickets dominated by various species are also observed. 149The inner delta and the Farimaké plains to the northwest include three families of forest formations of very unequal importance (situation at the beginning of the 1980s): flooded Acacia kirkii forests supporting a 4 m water depth. Occupying an area of ​​5,000 ha, they play a fundamental role in the reproduction of water birds; Acacia nilotica and seyal forests, flooded mainly by runoff but can be flooded secondarily by flooding: the height of the water depth does not exceed 0.6 m. They occupied 115,000 ha; the dry forests of the edges and mounds of the delta which occupied 425,000 ha. 150In addition to these forest formations, in the south of the area, there are park-type wooded formations composed in particular of Faidherbia albida, a tree that is also found on the sandy flats of the Andropogon gayanus savannahs as well as on the periphery of rice fields. 151Since this period, no general study has taken stock of the general evolution of the vegetation of the inner delta, or that of the forests in particular. Observers agree in recognizing the fact that the forests have been seriously threatened for about thirty years under the combined effects of drought, low flooding from the end of the 1970s and population growth which increases the anthropogenic pressure on resources. It can also be argued that this trend has been aggravated byby the destruction of common management rules that were observed by local communities of breeders, fishermen and farmers, this destruction being attributable, to a large extent, to land laws and the dysfunction of the administrations in charge of forests before 1991 (Marie, 1989; Moorehead, 1997). 152With regard to the forest formations of the Mopti region, the potential annual production of wood energy (quantity that can be exported annually without affecting the forest capital) was estimated at 1.8 million tonnes according to the Pirl. As for the stock of wood energy, it was estimated at 40 million m3 for the entire Mopti region, including 3.5 million m3 of dead wood. 153On the basis of the work of the Pirl (1988), the Domestic Energy Strategy (SED) project recalculated the annual productions as well as the areas occupied by the different forest formations of the delta (table 15). 154It appears that the stock of standing dead wood is relatively abundant, especially in the north of the delta. It would provide more than 70% of the firewood supply for the populations of the river valley. We distinguish: bourgoutières, pastures of grasses with floating stems. These develop on plains receiving 4 to 5 m of water per year, but they only survive deep submersion if the water level rises gradually. These are the most productive courses in the delta with average production of 20 t/ha. They occupy approximately 160,000 ha; the vetiver groves which occupy approximately 30 of the delta (640,000 ha). Their average production varies from 10 to 12 t/ha depending on their ecology; wild rice fields are also well represented: they cover 15.4 of the delta (approximately 340,000 ha). Their production is between 6 and 8 t/ha; the eragrostaies which occupy 190,000 ha. Their pastoral value varies between 5 and 8 t/ha; and the very slightly flooded formations (andropogonaie, panicaie, etc.) which occupy approximately 200,000 ha. Their average productivities are around 5 t/ha. 156There is little information, due to a lack of diachronic studies, on the evolution of the herbaceous plant formations of the inland delta in relation to the low floods of the 1980s and 1990s. However, it has been shown that the flooded formations of the inland delta are in ecological equilibrium with an average flood height of 6.60 m in Mopti. 157From this reference situation, a distinction must be made between a cyclical evolution linked to a temporary deterioration of the floods and which results in a reversible evolution (the plant formations regaining their previous equilibrium with the return of good floods) and an irreversible evolution of the environment which would result in the installation of a new flood/plant formation equilibrium adapted to floods of less than 6.60 m. 158Concerning the first hypothesis, i.e. a temporary weakness of the floods, a study (Hiernaux and Diarra, 1986) carried out after the very bad flood of 1984, the weakest of the century, highlights the following points: the deep formations (bourgoutières, deep vetiver groves, etc.) are little affected by the weakness of the flood, as are the highest formations (panicaies, andropogonaies, etc.) which depend more on rain than on the flood; the intermediate formations (orizaies, eragrostaies, high vetiver groves, etc.) are, on the contrary, very affected in their production and in their structure, the dominant species being decimated and replaced by a very irregular population dominated by annual species.Sahelian. 159It would therefore seem that the deep formations of the delta present, like the least flooded formations, a certain resilience to hydrological hazards. Their production, which remains non-zero when they are not affected by the flood, partially buffers the hydrological hazards, this being valid only in the event of a temporary crisis not leading to an irreversible modification of the ecosystem. 160As for the second hypothesis assuming a lasting change in hydrology resulting in a definitive loss of water height, one may wonder what the consequences would be. To do this, a simulation was carried out, the value retained for the average drop in the flood level being -1 m compared to the previous equilibrium (climax flood at 5.60 m instead of 6.60 m: such a hypothesis could correspond just as well to a climate change as to the creation of a new major development on the river upstream). 161This simulation shows the following: the dry formations of the delta, located on the edges and on the exposed mounds, would practically triple their surface area to reach more than 900,000 ha; the deep flooded formations, located in water layers between 150 cm and 400 cm, would undergo a significant reduction. In particular, the formations located between 150 cm and 280 cm would occupy an area approximately ten times smaller than at present. 162Furthermore, the deepest formations, those located in a water layer between 280 cm and 400 cm, could disappear in favor of shallower formations. In addition to the loss of fodder production (these formations provide 20,000 kg and 15,000 kg of dry matter per hectare respectively, which is significantly more than the delta average of around 6,000 kg), this would also result in a significant reduction in biodiversity with the disappearance of Acacia kirkii forests, a breeding ground for many species of Palearctic migratory birds. 163The consequences for fodder production would be significant since fodder production would only be 6 to 7 million tonnes per year instead of the 15 million tonnes corresponding to a flood of 6.60 m. The reduction in production and carrying capacity would be in the order of 55 to 60. Instead of being able to accommodate 1.5 million head each year, the delta could only feed 600,000 to 700,000. The loss would not only be quantitative but also qualitative, linked to the very significant reduction of the "bourgoutières", the best pastures in the delta. Under these conditions, it is reasonable to assume that the organization of livestock farming, as it still exists today, would not withstand this change. The case of water hyacinth 164Water hyacinth, which appeared in Mali in 1990 around Bamako, is potentially present along the entire course of the Niger River upstream of the inner delta. In reality, it is only present in large numbers in certain very specific areas, in irrigation canals and in certain branches of the river near towns, i.e. where the water is "polluted" or at least very rich in nutrients. There, it constitutes a nuisance that can be very significant locally, particularly in relation to the operation of the water intakes of the structures. There are, however, methods of control by biological or mechanical means, the latter being the one currently used at the Office du Niger. Fish resources and populations 165From a biogeographical point of view, the ichthyofauna of the Niger River belongs to the Nilo-Sudanian ichthyological province (Lévêque and Paugy, 1999). This province, although very vast and formed of three large basins (Nile, Chad, Niger) and various other small basins (Senegal, Volta and others), has kept a remarkably homogeneous faunal composition due to the contacts that have remained or still remain mabetween these basins. The large size of this biogeographical province explains its richness in fish species and, in particular, the richness of the Niger River. The number of species populating the region of the upper Niger and the inner Niger delta is in fact 130 to 140 according to Daget (Daget, 1954). 166However, half of them are little known or at least very rarely caught by fishing gear, particularly because of their small size. In fact, these species only enter into the composition of catches as an accessory and accidental measure and not as targeted species. It is clear that, concerning such species which are not really part of the fishery resource, it would be futile to try to characterize any situation and even more so to try to identify evolutionary trends. Only missions by researchers specializing in systematics, working by poisoning small portions of the river or its branches, are able to provide information on the presence of these species and this can obviously only be done very punctually. 167Consequently, the information presented concerns the species that are (or were) encountered in fishing catches, that is to say a number limited to around sixty species. It is therefore not possible to answer absolutely and without any bias the question "is there a loss of biodiversity?". On the other hand, it is possible to say whether, among the species mentioned as fished thirty or sixty years ago, some have become rarer in the catches, or even no longer appear at all. 168The examination of the available series on fish in the Niger River at the delta and Mali level shows, in fact, that the fishery resource today presents a slightly different aspect in its specific structure from that which it had in the 1950s and even at the end of the 1960s (Quensière et al., 1994; Wetlands, 1999). Very few species have disappeared (and probably only locally), but a certain number of these have become considerably rarer while the share relative to other species has increased. More specifically, we see that the one or two cases of disappearance or near-disappearance of species in the delta region (Epsetus odoë and perhaps Arius gigas) occurred long ago, between the beginning of the 20th century and the 1960s. However, four other species or groups of species (Gymnarchus niloticus, Parachana obscura, Heterotis niloticus and three species of the genus Polypterus) have declined sharply since the 1960s, apparently linked to the scarcity of certain types of environments (the marsh belts of tall wild grasses around permanent bodies of water). On the other hand, other species, notably belonging to the genera Clarias and Chrysichthys, have seen their catches increase. In terms of volume, fish from the Cichlidae family (tilapias in the broad sense) now dominate catches alongside the Clarias and Labeo genera. The "captain" Lates niloticus is present but in limited abundance. 169Furthermore, the demographic structure of the populations has also changed. All exploited populations have acquired a "rejuvenated" structure, characterized by a dominance of young individuals (three quarters of the fish captured are "0 " individuals, i.e. in their first year of life) and of fairly small size (Laë, 1995), while large individuals (over 3 years old, over 50 cm) have become very rare in most areas of the river and particularly in the inner delta. However, where exploitation pressure has remained lower (as in the rivers of the upper basin), large fish are still found. 170While changes in specific composition seem mainly linked to the loss of certain types of natural environments, it is thought that changes in the structure ofdemographic are a direct consequence of fishing pressure. 171However, it is noted that, for the moment, these different structural changes do not affect the resource in any way from the point of view of its productivity, that is to say its ability to produce annually harvestable biomass: fish production (in tonnes per year) had, admittedly, fallen considerably during the period of great drought (1973-93) but it has risen again since the return of average or good floods and it always remains proportional, each year, to the power of the flood and the extent of the flood (see fig. 8 and 9, "Fishing" p. 52 et seq.). There are also statistical relationships that make it possible to predict the production of a fishing campaign in the delta from the flooded surface area or from the flow of the river at an upstream station. Laë (1992b) thus establishes a relationship between catches and a flood index calculated on the two previous floods (respectively n and n-1): 172Annual catches from Julyn to Junen 1 = 173780.95 (Flood index)n  770.71 (Flood index)n-1   32,304 174As for the “resource declines” regularly announced, they are only temporary phenomena linked to the occurrence of a particularly bad flood and generally denied the following year. Or they are due to artefacts linked to the assessment method such as, for example, the excessive focus on catches made per unit of effort (ratio-type index which obviously falls when fishing effort increases, which is the case). 175However, there are a number of "damages" linked to the recent developments described: on an ethical level, we can regret the loss or rarefaction of certain species that often represented original bio-ecological types; we can definitely diagnose an economic loss linked, on the one hand, to the excess of resources devoted to fishing effort to catch an annual quantity of fish (which is closely dependent on the extent of the flood/inundation and which is therefore not extensible) and, on the other hand, to the decline in the average sizes of fish caught, and therefore in their specific value per kg. 176Finally, it must be remembered that the continuation of the "good productive functioning" of the fish resource is closely conditioned by the maintenance of the river-plain ecosystem in good health and, in particular, by the maintenance of a large annual flooding of the plains. Wildlife resources and populations 177The examination of this component is particularly interesting for the Inner Niger Delta, which is a large area with original and rich natural aquatic and marsh environments. Because for the rest of the river valley in Mali, there is less to say. The fauna (apart from fish) is not significantly different from the surrounding Sudano-Sahelian fauna. However, this fauna is relatively poor because it has been damaged by increasing anthropization (agriculture, land clearing, hunting) and by the last major drought. 178The Inner Niger Delta contains a wide variety of aquatic habitats (marshes, lakes, pools, plains and floodplain forests) which host, all year round or seasonally, colonies of fish, reptiles, mammals and aquatic birds which find favorable conditions here for their reproduction and feeding. While the Inner Niger Delta shares this role with several other wetlands in Sudano-Sahelian Africa, including the Senegal Delta (Djoudj), the Hadejia-Nguru plain in Nigeria, all the floodplains dependent on Lake Chad, the Logone and the Chari, and the Sudd marshes in Sudan, it is the largest of these wetlands in West Africa. Only the Okavango marshes in Botswana for southern Africa and the Sudd marshes in Sudan can be compared to it. 179However, the biodiversity of the delta isfar from being intact. Indeed, for the past thirty years, the degradation of the hydrological regime combined with the increase in anthropogenic pressure has led to increased pressure on the natural environment with consequences for large wildlife. 180In particular, we have observed a disappearance of large carnivores that frequented certain upper parts of the delta as well as its margins (case of the panther and the lion, the latter being perhaps still present in small numbers in the neighboring region of Gourma) and also a significant scarcity of large reptiles (Nile crocodiles, pythons, monitor lizards) and large herbivorous mammals (manatees and hippopotamuses, the latter being however less affected). 181However, for waterbirds, the inner Niger Delta remains of prime importance in West Africa, both for nesting and migratory rest or wintering. These are either Afrotropical birds or paleoarctic species. However, the distribution of these waterbirds varies throughout the year, according to the seasons and from one year to the next, depending on the magnitude of the flood. 182It is not possible to draw a clear picture of the changes underway in the delta from the observations made by different projects. However, it is possible to outline trends, some of which could be worrying. While 125 species of waterbirds frequented the delta in the early 1980s, the "Wetlands" project reported only 103 at the end of the 1990s. Large birds (goliath heron, jabiru, white stork, crowned crane) seem particularly affected by the decline in their presence or numbers. For small species, the trends are more contrasted: glossy ibis populations, for example, are said to have declined by 50% over the last twenty years. On the other hand, other species have held up well, with their numbers remaining stable. 183It seems that the maintenance of large colonies of waterbirds is linked to the integrity of the flooded Acacia kirkii forests, which were seriously threatened by the decline in hydrology and by clearing during the 1980s/90s. The return of better floods after 1994 and effective protection measures (Dentaka and Akkagoun forests) may have reversed this trend. Conclusion on the state of health of the Niger River and its ecosystems 187It has been a long time since the Niger River and its valley have been home to "virgin" ecosystems or even ecosystems preserved from anthropization and its effects. Many factors (climatic, anthropic) have intervened over the last sixcentury and have impoverished the wealth (biodiversity) of the ecosystems associated with the river. As a result, neither the Niger River as a whole nor the delta in particular can today be considered large wilderness areas. Furthermore, localized pollution phenomena have appeared here and there and may constitute threats for the future. 188However, despite these developments, the basic ecological mechanisms of the productivity of the river and its ecosystems, expressed in terms of the capacity to generate quality biomass without inputs, are intact and are still remarkable for their quantitative performance – compared to that of other natural environments in Africa and in the world. And these mechanisms are activated without difficulty as soon as water arrives in sufficient quantity. INSTITUTIONAL FRAMEWORK AND EXISTING MANAGEMENT INSTRUMENTS 189The societies that populate the Niger River valley have long established community or customary rules to manage the use of space and its resources. In particular, a pastoral code defining pastoral territories (leydii) managed by Fulani clans was formalized in the 19th century by the Fulani Empire of Macina. Fishery resources have also long been subject to rules of use applied under the control of "water masters". These traditional systems of management rules have been studied and described by many authors following 190A.H. Bâ and J. Daget (1955) and Gallais (1967). The political, economic and environmental changes of the second half of the 20th century have considerably affected and destabilized the proper functioning of these systems, which nevertheless remain very anchored in minds and behaviors. 191This chapter deals with "modern" institutions and codes resulting first from the efforts made at the beginning of Independence to replace these traditional systems, then from recent decentralization reforms which are now attempting to reconcile modern management rules and local traditional powers. 192The institutional reforms that Mali has been undergoing since 1991 are currently being complemented by a new approach to water resource management that can only be understood within an international framework given the transboundary nature of the Niger Basin. The international framework IWRM or “shared vision” 193A set of international initiatives on water management and governance that emerged at the Paris Conference in 1998 and was reaffirmed at the “Earth Summit” (Johannesburg -2002) guides water policies at the national and regional levels. 194This new water policy, IWRM (Integrated Water Resources Management) is defined as a process that promotes the coordinated development and management of water, land and related resources, with a view to equitably maximizing the resulting economic and social well-being, without compromising the sustainability of vital ecosystems. 195WIRG, which is defined as a “shared vision”, establishes the principle that good water governance can only be integrated management at the watershed level. In agreement with the Member States, international bodies and donors have focused on large transboundary river basins. These large basins include the Mekong in Asia, the Lake Chad and Lake Victoria basins in Africa, the Orange and Volta river basins and the Niger River basin. In this context, the application of WIRG – which has become the official policy of the Republic of Mali – is leading to profound legal and institutional reforms. They should make it possible to move water management from a sectoral and technical management approach to an integrated management approach operating by basin and sub-basin. 196Implementing WIRG in Malibuilds on the very significant changes that have occurred in recent years in water legislation, in the scope of the structures responsible for water governance, and in their relationships with each other and with civil society actors. An international institution: the Niger Basin Authority (NBA) 197The main international institution is the Niger Basin Authority (NBA). Composed of nine riparian states (Cameroon, Côte d'Ivoire, Benin, Guinea, Burkina Faso, Mali, Niger, Nigeria, Chad), it was established by the convention of 21 November 1980 signed in Faranah (Republic of Guinea). From its headquarters in Niamey, its aim is to promote cooperation between member countries and ensure the integrated development of the Niger Basin in the areas of energy, hydraulics, agriculture, livestock, fisheries and fish farming, forestry and logging, transport and communications, and industry. 198The objectives of the NBA are as follows: to harmonize and coordinate national policies for the development of water resources in the Niger Basin; to promote and participate in development planning through the preparation and implementation of an integrated basin development plan; to promote and participate in the design and operation of works and projects of common interest; to ensure the control and regulation of all forms of navigation on the river, its tributaries and sub-tributaries; to participate in the formulation of requests for assistance and the mobilization of financing for studies and works necessary for the development of the basin's resources. 199The NBA keeps itself permanently informed of the development plans of the States. The States, for their part, must keep the NBA's executive body (executive secretariat) informed of all projects and works that they propose to undertake in the basin, in particular developments likely to modify the water supply. They refrain from carrying out on the portion of the river (or its tributaries and sub-tributaries) under their territorial jurisdiction, any works likely to pollute the water or negatively modify the biological characteristics of the fauna and flora. The legal and institutional framework in Mali The codes The State and Land Code 200In the field of water, the State and Land Code differentiates: the natural public domain which includes in particular navigable or floatable watercourses and their banks (25 m passage zone), non-navigable and non-floatable springs and watercourses, lakes and ponds, etc.; the artificial real estate public domain including river ports, navigation canals, irrigation or drainage canals, aqueducts, dependencies of these works when they are carried out for a public utility purpose. The Water Code by Law No. 2-006 of January 31, 2002 201Law No. 2-006 of January 31, 2002 sets the rules for the use, conservation, protection and management of water resources. It applies to all waters dependent on the hydraulic domain, that is to say the hydraulic public domain of the State and the hydraulic public domain of local authorities, regulated by the State and Land Code. The overall, sustainable and equitable management of water resources as well as their protection is ensured by the State, which can transfer part of the hydraulic resources to decentralized communities. A master plan for water development and management, established for twenty years by the Ministry of Water, sets the objectives for the use, development and quantitative and qualitative protection of water resources and aquatic ecosystems. This code lays the foundations for new regulations in the water sector and legitimizes the structures responsible for water resource management.these in water. It advocates the establishment of a public water service development fund and creates a national council, regional and local councils, and basin committees responsible for issuing opinions and making proposals on the management of water resources and on development projects. Each at its own level, council or committee, has an advisory role on the management of resources, development projects, possible conflicts over water use, etc. The Pastoral Charter codified by Law No. 004 of 27 February 2001 202The Pastoral Charter defines the fundamental principles governing the exercise of pastoral activities and organizes the management of pastoral space. It defines the essential rights of pastoralists in terms of animal mobility and access to pastoral resources as well as their obligations (mainly, in fact, to preserve the environment and the property of others). Pastoral areas consisting of grassy and aerial pastures, community bourgoutières, salt lands, watering points and stopover lodges are the domains of the State and local authorities. Access is open in accordance with the regulations setting the time limits and procedures for the passage of animals and in accordance with local customs and usage rights. The management of pastoral resources is the responsibility of local authorities on their territory, which therefore manage pastoral tracks and can regulate access to resources and charge shepherds for their use. The Local Authorities Code (1995) and related texts 203The Local Authorities Code recognizes local authorities as legal entities, financial autonomy and the authority to regulate, through their deliberations, their respective affairs in terms of environmental protection and state and land management. Local authorities may, in particular, create and manage collective facilities in the area of ​​rural or urban hydraulics and organize rural activities and agro-sylvopastoral production. If the domain of a community is composed of a public domain and a private domain, the State may, for reasons of general interest, transfer the management of part of its natural or artificial public domain to this decentralized community, which is then responsible for ensuring its conservation. Law No. 96-050 on the principles of constitution and management of the domain of local authorities 204The natural public domain of local authorities includes all dependencies of the public domain of the State located on their territory and for which the State has transferred the conservation and management: watercourses, ponds, lakes and lakes, protection perimeters, natural sites declared public domain by law. 205The artificial public domain includes developments and works carried out for reasons of regional, district or municipal interest. 206Local authorities are responsible for the management, development, conservation and safeguarding of the ecological balance of their area. They draw up a land use plan which, reviewed and corrected periodically taking into account the national plan, will specify the agricultural, pastoral, fish farming, wildlife, mining and housing areas. 207The pastoral area includes: grazing areas, fallow land over 10 years old, pastoral routes and water points. The competent bodies of the communities regulate the organisation of pastoral activities in collaboration with professional organisations and technical services and set the rates of fees collected for authorisations to access pastures after consulting the Regional Chamber of Agriculture. 208The fish farming area includes the hydraulic and fish farming developments that the communities carry out on their territorye and public waters granted to them by the State. Here again, professional organizations are consulted and a fee is collected for fishing permits. Political, administrative and associative institutions 209The Ministry of Mines and Water is the main institution for river management in Mali. It exercises statutory and principled supervision over the entire water sector for which it has institutional responsibility, mainly through the National Directorate of Hydraulics (DNH). The DNH is responsible for inventorying and assessing hydraulic resources at the national level. It assesses all projects that affect water and ensures direct project management (for example, the Upper Niger Hydroecological Management project, Ghenis). 210The Regional and Sub-Regional Directorates of Hydraulics and Water (DRHE) are decentralized services under the coordination and control of the DNH. They have a support and advisory role for local authorities by combining the functions of management, project management and control. They are very active and are regularly consulted. Approach by operational functions: some examples 218The consultation function – prior to policies or management decisions – is provided for by the Constitution of Mali, which envisages three main frameworks to ensure it: the National Assembly, which, with its Rural Development and Environment Committee, has the initiative for environmental laws jointly with the High Council of Local Authorities; the High Council of Local Authorities, whose mission is to study and give an opinion on all local and regional development policies. The Government is required to refer these questions to it for advice; the Economic, Social and Cultural Council, which has jurisdiction over all aspects of economic, social and cultural development, including the protection and defence of the environment and the promotion of the quality of life. 219In terms of water management and in a more immediately practical way, consultation will be able to be ensured by the new committees or basin or water management commissions that have been defined, or even already set up, at different levels of the organization chart of State institutions (see "The legal and institutional framework in Mali" p. 84). 220A good example is given by the national water management commission which, since its establishment, aims to better coordinate the management of Sélingué and Markala, which are the responsibility of very distant institutions. In particular, it allows the Markala dam (and therefore the Office du Niger) to better benefit from the regulation provided by Sélingué. It has also set a minimum threshold of 40 m3/s to be respected downstream of Markala (at low water) in the interest of users located downstream. 221The planning function is entrusted to the various ministries and the national directorates attached to them. It results in the definition of sectoral policies presented in the form of master plans.rs. All sectoral policies are theoretically coherent and now refer to the Strategic Framework for Combating Poverty (CSLP), which is the reference policy line at the national level and which therefore applies to all sectoral policies. An example of a sectoral policy is the Rural Development Sector Master Plan (SDDR), which constitutes the reference framework for rural development interventions for the period 2000/10. The strategic orientations of the SDDR are the result of a diagnostic analysis of the evolution of the sector and are the result of a consensus between all the actors (State, local authorities, producers, civil society, development partners). These strategic orientations constitute the foundations of the areas of intervention and the development programs of the sector. Among the priority areas of intervention, the development of irrigation occupies an important place. This resulted in the definition of a National Irrigation Development Strategy (SNDI) outline that prioritizes the development of fully controlled facilities and highlights six objectives: making the design of irrigation structures more rational and reducing their cost; encouraging the participation of non-governmental entities and facilitating their access to financing; improving the management of irrigated areas; increasing production and productivity on irrigated areas; reforming the institutional and legal framework for the sub-sector; and minimizing negative environmental impacts and social conflicts created by irrigation. 222Generally speaking, the options taken in the SNDI aim to increase the areas under irrigation and improve the productivity of production systems. Information and monitoring functions 223The inventory, monitoring, information and knowledge-building functions, particularly through the regular collection of data and the publication of statistical reports, are carried out separately at the level of each of the State institutions responsible for a particular sector or component of the environment. All of these services can potentially provide information that would cover the monitoring of all components of the rural sector and the environment quite well, particularly around the Niger River.
