Ces analyses ont été réalisées auprès du seul laboratoire autorisé à Antananarivo, l’Institut Pasteur. Deux séries de résultats d’analyse, commandées par l’entreprise de distribution de l’eau malgache la JIRAMA, apportent certains compléments. Même si, là encore, l’exploitation des données est limitée du fait de leurs natures. La première série effectuée au point de production et d’alimentation de l’eau potable n’identifie que les paramètres physiques de l’eau au niveau du lac (ressource brute), puis au niveau des sorties MI et MII (soit après traitement de l’usine). La seconde série aux bornes-fontaines ne présente qu’une vision incomplète puisque la pratique du tirage au sort ne permet pas une analyse sur le long terme (entre une dizaine et une trentaine de bornes-fontaines à chaque fois différente).                                          17Nous avons effectué une analyse du système d’approvisionnement en eau potable en ses 5 étapes selon le modèle précédemment défini. Notre diagnostic établit dans le contexte des quartiers précaires et denses de la capitale que la ressource en eau est à la fois menacée et menaçante tant en quantité qu’en qualité.                                          18D’un point de vue quantitatif, nos résultats obtenus dans ces quartiers contrastent avec les données recueillies à l’échelle de la CUA par ARTELIA. Seuls 8   des ménages affirment être raccordés au réseau de distribution, loin des 33   annoncés par la Banque mondiale et des 53   par le SDAU (Banque mondiale, 2011 ; ARTELIA, 2014). La borne-fontaine apparaît dans les descriptions faites par les enquêtés comme un lieu public majeur dans la vie quotidienne des Antananariviens. Ainsi, les temps d’attente aux bornes-fontaines peuvent être relativement longs, comme le symbolise la longue chaîne de bidons (supérieur à 30 minutes en moyenne et jusqu’à deux heures dans certains fokontany) (figure 4). Dès lors, les pratiques du transport et du stockage dominent (92   des enquêtés). Le transport s’effectue essentiellement dans des jerricans ou des seaux d’eau. Comme dans la plupart des pays africains (Jaglin, 2005 ; Ginisty, 2014), la tâche de la collecte incombe le plus souvent à la femme et aux enfants, entrainant une organisation quotidienne et familiale spécifique (Ognard, 2018). Pour pallier le déficit de service public (Jaglin, 2005 ; Blanchon, 2006 ; Burt et Ray, 2014), des alternatives s’organisent autour de la revente d’eau. Les porteurs revendeurs d’eau (« mpatsaka » rano) jouent un rôle important dans l’approvisionnement en eau, en particulier dans les quartiers difficiles d’accès. Ce service proposé aux alentours des bornes-fontaines s’adapte à une clientèle hétérogène composée de familles à revenu moyen ou faible. Ce service est en moyenne plus cher qu’à la borne-fontaine, le bidon de 20 litres étant acheté à 1 Ar./l et revendu entre 50 Ar. (à Antetezana Afavoany). L’autre forme de revente d’eau est celle des particuliers. Si cette forme de revente peut être intégrée dans des stratégies familiales de solidarité, elle relève le plus souvent de stratégies marchandes comme à Mandrangobato où le prix pratiqué est sensiblement le même que celui appliqué aux bornes-fontaines (1 à 2 Ar. le litre). Dans l’ensemble, ces diverses stratégies attestent d’une part de la diversité des situations de mal branchement et de fait de l’adaptation urbaine avec un « artisanat de services informels » (Jaglin et Zérah, 2010). Le niveau de consommation d’eau est un autre indicateur des inégalités sociales par rapport à l’accès à l’eau. Le manuel des procédures du ministère malgache de l’énergie et des mines donne comme norme 30 litres/personne/jour quand la moyenne de l’OMS s’étend entre 20 et 50 litres/personne/jour. De nouveau, les résultats de nos enquêtes contrastent avec ceux d’ARTELIA où la consommation moyenne observée est de 32 litres/personne/jour. Selon nos enquêtes, 13   des ménages vivraient avec moins de 40 litres par jour par ménage, 38   avec 40 à 80 litres par jour par ménage, 15   avec 80 à 120 litres par ménage et 25   avec plus de 120 litres par ménage. Ces situations de mal branchement participent à des différenciations dans l’organisation quotidienne des familles contribuant ainsi à forger des modes de vie différenciés au sein de la capitale (Ognard, 2018). Cette contamination a été notée en 7 sites sur les 15 prélevés avec une concentration d’escherichia coli variant de 8 à 13 coliformes/litres selon les lieux et une concentration de 25 à plus de 100 pour les entérocoques intestinaux. Ces 7 prélèvements non conformes montrent donc une contamination bactériologique significative de la qualité de l’eau consommée. La contamination à la fois par les germes escherichia coli et les entérocoques intestinaux définit des situations de péril fécal auxquelles sont soumises les populations.                     20Cependant, les paramètres physiques restent eux conformes à la réglementation. Ces données sont en partie conformes aux résultats des séries d’analyses de la JIRAMA. Au lieu de production, sur les 4 années (2009 à 2014) répertoriées seuls 3 évènements de pollution physique ont été identifiés. Ils ont eu lieu les 27/01/2009, 30/12/2009 et 05/03/2012. Le paramètre mis en cause est la turbidité qui supérieure à 5 NTU qui rend l’eau légèrement trouble. Le principal risque associé est alors l’augmentation de la capacité de transport de micro-organismes nuisant à la désinfection. À l’échelle des bornes-fontaines, pour les années 2013 et 2014, ce système de désinfection est incriminé. La turbidité est élevée sur 39 échantillons sur les 508 effectués sur les deux années. À noter que ce paramètre n’est pas pris en compte par la JIRAMA comme facteur de conformité de l’eau puisque ces échantillons ont été déclarés conformes à la norme, alors même que le seuil de 5 NTU, défini par la loi malgache et les recommandations de l’OMS, est ici dépassé. Cette dissension entre lieu de distribution et lieu de captage interroge le rôle joué par le transport et les canalisations.                     21Par ailleurs, les différents modes d’approvisionnement, c’est-à-dire la nature de la source, entrent également en ligne de compte pour l’appréciation du risque et du niveau de contamination de l’eau distribuée. La seule source analysée à Manjakaray semble contaminée par les entérocoques mettant en cause l’approvisionnement à une source non améliorée.                     22Deux prélèvements sur quatre effectués auprès des ménages présentent des contaminations d’origine bactériologiques. Là encore, la source du prélèvement est intéressante. Les deux prélèvements sains ont été effectués auprès de gargotes alors que ceux contaminés ont été effectués auprès des ménages. Le temps de stockage et le récipient peuvent être mis en cause. Les gargotes procèdent d’après nos enquêtes à un renouvellement régulier de leur approvisionnement en eau, ce qui n’est pas forcément le cas pour les ménages. D’autre part, l’absence d’altération de la qualité physique de l’eau permet d’émettre l’hypothèse que les manipulations et les conditions d’hygiènes sont ici en cause. Certains ont marqué une conscientisation de l’impact de leur manipulation sur la qualité de l’eau en affirmant l’utilisation d’un désinfectant, le Sur’Eau (14   des enquêtés). Tsiny à Anatihazo déclare ainsi « l’eau est potable car j’utilise du Sur’Eau pour être sûr ». À l’inverse, à Anatihazo toujours, Jacqueline dénigre la qualité de l’eau en affirmant que l’eau n’est pas potable et qu’elle « doit rajouter du Sur’Eau ». Toutefois, de nombreux retours nous ont été faits sur la difficulté d’obtention de la solution de traitement en accord avec les observations des références bibliographiques (Dunston et al., 2001).                     23Compte tenu de la faible empreinte spatiale de nos analyses, cette expérience n’est pas représentative de l’ensemble de l’agglomération mais permet de dégager certaines tendances quant à la qualité de l’eau et aux pratiques des populations.                     24Les perturbations qui détériorent l’accès en quantité et en qualité se concentrent autour des problématiques de transport : à l’échelle de la CUA, au niveau des canalisations mais également à l’échelle individuelle à travers les pratiques de transport et de stockage.                                          25Parallèlement, l’absence d’un système d’assainissement opérant amène une importante partie de la population à évacuer les eaux ménagères de manière inadéquate, favorisant un risque sanitaire (figure 5). 80   des personnes interrogées rejettent ainsi leurs eaux usées (cuisine, vaisselle, lessive) à l’air libre. Le raccordement au tout-à-l’égoût ne concerne qu’une minorité (7  ). Cette donnée peut être complétée par l’équipement sanitaire : la fosse perdue (technique locale rudimentaire avec un simple trou) se présente comme le mode le plus répandu. Les latrines se trouvent le plus souvent à l’extérieur et sont partagées par plusieurs familles (72   des réponses). On remarque que certaines pratiques comme les défécations « à l’air libre » peuvent augmenter le risque sanitaire. Le « péril fécal » reste une donnée sensible dans ces quartiers. Cette analyse peut être corroborée par les défaillances du système de récolte des ordures de la JIRAMA déjà mentionné dans l’ouvrage Antananarivo et ses ordures (Raharinjanahary, 2011) avec un manque de bacs, de personnels et de camions poubelles (478 bacs à ordures pour 1 million d’habitants). Les pratiques de la décharge sauvage comme l’attestent nombre de canaux obstrués de la ville ou encore les pratiques d’incinération et de mise au trou dans la cour (23  ) des déchets, ne font qu’accentuer le problème. En effet, l’Ikopa est le seul collecteur de tous les déchets liquides restitués à l’aval de la ville d’Antananarivo. Il reçoit sans aucun traitement les effluents urbains provenant de la station de pompage des 67 ha au niveau d’Antopenaka, les matières de vidanges transportées par camion au site d’Ambohitrimanjaka et les eaux polluées du canal Andriantany au niveau du village d’Andriantany (ARTELIA, 2014). La qualité environnementale et sanitaire de l’eau de ces effluents paraît compromise. Elle a été évaluée à l’échelle de la Commune Urbaine d’Antananarivo (CUA), grâce aux deux campagnes de prélèvements des eaux sur l’Ikopa effectuées en 2008 et 2013 (ARTELIA, 2014). Au cours de ces études, les usages de l’Ikopa (lessive, briques, sable, barrage) ainsi que les rejets d’effluents dans le cours d’eau (rejets municipaux et rejets industriels) ont été inventoriés, et une campagne de prélèvements d’échantillons et d’analyses d’eaux réalisée. Au travers de ces études sur les principales caractéristiques de la rivière Ikopa, la ressource apparaît de relative bonne qualité au niveau de la prise d’eau de Mandroseza, même si elle reçoit des effluents pollués en amont notamment industriels et domestiques (au niveau de la centrale thermique d’Ambohimanambola).                                            Figure 5 – Photographie de canal à ciel ouvert servant de réceptacle à ordures à Mandroganbato I                        Source : Ognard, 2018.                                          26L’analyse diachronique montre une dégradation de la qualité de la rivière Ikopa des 5 années entre 2008-2013. Elle est qualifiée de médiocre pour la plupart des sites de prélèvements avec des critères de pH inférieur à 5,5 et supérieur à 9,5, une conductivité comprise entre 500 et 3 000 μS/cm, une température comprise entre 30 et 35 °C. L’indicateur le plus parlant de cette dégradation de la qualité de l’Ikopa est la concentration en oxygène dissous du cours d’eau avec des niveaux compris entre 2 et 3 mg/l. De plus, l’évolution de la consommation globale en eau affecte directement la quantité totale de production d’eaux usées. Avec une production d’eaux usées estimée à 80   des eaux consommées, la quantité totale d’eaux usées produite au niveau de la zone d’étude est de 1 m3/s en 2013. Si les objectifs d’amélioration de l’accès à l’eau potable sont respectés, cette production double en 2015 (2 m3/s) et atteindra 3,2 m3/s en 2025. Comme la zone d’étude est drainée par le réseau hydrographique de la rivière Ikopa, la confrontation de ces flux avec les débits d’étiage de cette rivière, qui peuvent descendre à moins de 5 m3/s au niveau d’Ambohitrimanjaka, peuvent de plus en plus fragiliser la ressource et les quartiers en situation de la plaine inondable. En soulignant l’imbrication des réseaux d’assainissement à ceux de l’approvisionnement en eau, il ne s’agit pas seulement de questionner la mauvaise gestion des eaux usées (ARTELIA, 2014) mais d’identifier l’interdépendance de ces réseaux qui joue un rôle important dans la dégradation de l’environnement urbain. On parle de « vulnérabilité transversale » (Hardy, 2009). Elle est transcrite dans le profil épidémiologique de la capitale malgache. Selon les études épidémiologiques, l’incidence est le meilleur moyen d’appréhender l’évolution des maladies d’une population donnée (Vaughan et Morrow, 1991 ; OMS, 1994). Or, l’évaluation de cet indice n’est pas possible dans cette étude de cas étant donné la variabilité et le manque de fiabilité des données statistiques démographiques. L’étude s’appuie donc sur la prévalence, qui est le principal indicateur de la morbidité, s’appuyant sur le nombre total de maladies observées dans une population donnée à un moment précis. L’étude statistique ici présentée a été réalisée à partir des données de morbidité diagnostiquée par les Centres de Santé de Base (CSB) publics de la Commune urbaine d’Antananarivo (15 au total) dont la cohérence nous semble plus plausible que les données de mortalité fournies par le ministère. Dans un premier temps, à défaut de pouvoir évaluer l’incidence des maladies hydriques, une approche diachronique a été effectuée à partir des graphiques semi-logarithmiques pour établir l’évolution du phénomène morbide (figure 6). Les graphiques mettent en évidence des taux de croissance des maladies respiratoires et autres maladies qui semblent se comporter comme le taux de croissance total. Ainsi, l’existence de droites traduit des taux de croissance constants. De plus, les trois segments de droite sont proches et parallèles. Ceux-ci correspondent à des taux de croissance identiques. Les deux pathologies (maladies respiratoires et autres maladies) influencent donc fortement l’évolution de la distribution pathologique d’Antananarivo. Un deuxième groupe de pathologies se détache : les maladies diarrhéiques, des affections digestives et cutanées. Leurs taux de croissance présentent des profils sensiblement similaires avec des segments de droite qui connaissent de faibles variations de 10   à -10  . Ce deuxième groupe souligne donc la fragilité de la capitale malgache vis-à-vis des risques sanitaires hydriques notamment. Ces résultats amènent à dire, en se basant seulement sur la morbidité diagnostiquée, que l’état sanitaire, en identifiant le poids des maladies respiratoires et des maladies diarrhéiques, corrobore parfaitement une situation d’insalubrité et de précarité de nombreux quartiers de la ville d’Antananarivo. Réalisation : Ognard, 2018.                                                               28Cette double vulnérabilité linéaire et transversale de la ressource en eau de la capitale malgache atteste donc d’une fragmentation de l’espace urbain d’Antananarivo. Si Al Dabaghy (2014) a déjà noté le potentiel de « ressource politique transactionnelle de l’eau » à Diégo Suarez, cette double vulnérabilité de la ressource en eau dans la capitale malgache est en réalité le reflet de tensions entre au moins deux acteurs ; les élites et la population, en particulier les catégories les plus démunies. Elle pose la question de la gouvernance de la ressource en eau dans ce territoire.                                          29En effet, l’Ikopa est à la fois l’unique source d’eau potable de l’ensemble de l’agglomération d’Antananarivo, la principale source d’irrigation pour la plaine du Betsimitatatra et aussi le seul collecteur de toutes les nuisances restituées à l’aval de la ville d’Antananarivo. La préservation de la ressource en eau de l’Ikopa se retrouve compromise face à son statut ambivalent de source et d’effluent. En effet, si elle constitue la principale source d’alimentation de la capitale malgache, l’absence de traitement des eaux usées dans le petit cycle de l’eau est source de dangers, notamment sanitaires, pour l’ensemble de la CUA mais en particulier pour les quartiers précaires comme Isotry central. Ces risques sont particulièrement prégnants en saison pluvieuse et cyclonique où les bas-fonds intra-muros principalement situés à l’ouest de la capitale connaissent un débordement des canaux d’égouts à l’air libre. La ressource en eau devient un instrument de territorialisation de la capitale malgache où les services informels deviennent essentiels. En effet, l’absence de reconnaissance et d’encadrement de ces derniers est un autre exemple de cette volonté de cloisonnement de ces territoires et un attachement institutionnel à un modèle universel inadapté. Car cette inadaptation est le résultat d’un processus historique long de constitution des réseaux où les politiques successives ont oscillé entre efficacité et équité. Antananarivo n’a jamais véritablement connu l’âge d’or des réseaux de service public intégré et intégrateur au cours de laquelle aurait dû être réalisée leur universalisation. Dès 1945, une rupture est marquée avec l’équilibre écologique par l’occupation du lit majeur de l’Ikopa avec la création des quartiers d’Ampefiloha et d’Ambodin’isotry (ouest du lac Anosy) avec des fonctions désormais bien réparties entre ville « haute », devenue lieu de résidence des populations aisées, et « ville basse » devenant lieu du commerce, des loisirs et de l’habitat des populations les plus pauvres (Asinome, 2006). Cette marginalisation conduit à la fabrique de fractures sociales et urbaines qui sont entretenues dans le temps comme ici avec l’accès aux services publics. De même, au niveau sanitaire, la dichotomie du paysage urbain résultant des analyses statistiques correspond à celle opérée dans la mentalité malgache entre cet Est sur les hauteurs depuis longtemps mis en valeur par les Malgaches et cet Ouest caractérisé par cette situation de plaine inondable (derrière la digue) (Fournet-Guérin, 2006). On peut donc dire ici que le « territoire de santé » semble fortement imprégné des représentations et donc du « territoire vécu » (Fleuret, 2015). Pourtant, si le profil sanitaire dégagé pour l’Est confirme son statut privilégié au sein de la commune urbaine, le profil moyen dégagé pour l’Ouest nuance et atténue la stigmatisation de cette partie du territoire. Seul Isotry central s’impose par cette cartographie comme un « bas quartier » au sens où l’entend l’imaginaire malgache (autant socialement que géographiquement). Cependant, le CSB Isotry central joue un rôle particulier dans la carte sanitaire. Il coordonne et centralise l’ensemble des CSB de la commune urbaine. Ce quartier présente à la fois une meilleure offre de soin et également une position d’accessibilité. Ceci pourrait donc expliquer son poids prépondérant.                                          30À l’échelle des individus, l’altération de la qualité de l’eau produite par les manipulations dans la sphère domestique engendre des risques sanitaires pour des utilisateurs qui sont à la fois victimes et acteurs. Ils sont victimes d’un système déficient avec un accès faible en quantité. Mais ces populations marginalisées ont réussi à mettre en place des stratégies avec l’instauration d’autres choix pour pallier les services publics. Les actions privées apparaissent comme prépondérantes et peuvent être intégrées comme des « coping strategies ». Ces stratégies rendent ainsi la ville « habitable » pour les citadins les plus pauvres (Jaglin, 2005). Se déplacer pour aller chercher l’eau, la puiser, la transporter dans des récipients en plastique posés sur la tête ou portés à bout de bras sont des actes qui se répètent plusieurs fois par jour. C’est alors à la notion de résilience et notamment à la capacité de réponses de l’individu que l’on s’intéresse. Cette dimension est intéressante car en se plaçant à l’échelle des individus, on présuppose qu’ils ont une certaine latitude dans leurs choix et intègrent les aléas dans leurs arbitrages. Les stratégies adoptées par les agents dépendent de la perception qu’ils ont des risques auxquels ils font face et des ressources qu’ils sont en mesure de mobiliser. La prise de décisions s’accompagne d’un arbitrage dans les ressources entre le court et le moyen terme selon le risque perçu et subi. Ces décisions sont prises dans un contexte d’incertitudes selon les informations dont ils disposent. Ici, les menaces naturelles ne sont pas seulement perçues et vécues d’après la représentation de leurs effets, elles entrent en concurrence avec d’autres contraintes d’ordre économique et social qui s’en trouvent relativisées. Toutes ces stratégies attestent que les risques urbains ou sociaux (pauvreté, mal logement) apparaissent plus prégnants que les risques naturels (inondations) et sanitaires (risques de maladies hydriques et d’hygiène). Les enjeux autour des valeurs, des types d’individus, des types familiaux se trouvent dès lors posés dans l’appréciation de la perception des risques et donc d’une multitude d’inégalités face aux risques. À Antananarivo, en particulier dans les quartiers enquêtés en situation de plaine, les populations ont la conscience du risque, mais une sorte de résignation est entérinée faute de moyens. Ainsi, un couple à Isotry expliquait qu’il déposait ses déchets au pas de leur porte ou à proximité dans le quartier car il « n’a pas d’autre choix ». Il est conscient que cette pratique entrave potentiellement sa santé, notamment au moment de la montée des eaux lors des inondations. On assiste à une acceptation du risque et au développement de pratiques originales qui participent de la fabrication urbaine, de « bricolages urbains ».                                          31L’analyse du système d’eau potable en ces 5 étapes a permis d’identifier une double vulnérabilité de l’approvisionnement de la ressource en eau, à la fois « linéaire » et « transversale » dans la capitale malgache. Le système d’eau potable salubre interroge directement le rôle du transport, non seulement au niveau des canalisations mais surtout à travers les pratiques de revente et les manipulations domestiques puisque l’approvisionnement des populations se fait essentiellement aux bornes-fontaines. Si ces « coping strategies » permettent l’intégration des populations les plus pauvres dans la ville légale, ils mettent en évidence la fragmentation socio-spatiale de la capitale malgache. Parallèlement, l’attachement institutionnel à un modèle universel inadapté avec la persistance d’un statut ambivalent de l’Ikopa à la fois source et effluent, participe à la fabrique du risque et à un laisser-faire par les autorités du cloisonnement des territoires les plus fragiles de la capitale. Ce bien vital qu’est la ressource en eau est ainsi instrumentalisé et territorialisé.
text_en: 1 The administrative territory of the capital, which includes the majority of the population of the agg (...) 1In the Urban Commune of Antananarivo1 (CUA) (Figure 1), only 33% of the population has an individual water connection (World Bank, 2011). In a context of demographic growth in a capital that has become a two-millionaire city, serious deficiencies in terms of distribution and regulation create increased imbalances between supply and demand, particularly for the poorest populations such as those in the plain to the west of the CUA (Figure 1). This unequal distribution of infrastructure and water quantity is linked to the development of waterborne diseases such as the resurgence of cholera (Duston and Mac Afee, 2001). More commonly, diarrheal diseases, which are among the two leading causes of consultation at the public basic health centers (CSB) in the capital, particularly among children, constitute a real public health problem (Ministry of Health, 2007-2012). In reality, the danger to water resources is not limited to water deemed "drinkable" at its point of distribution. Because as in most countries in the South (Sy and Moussa, 2014), the landscape of standpipes dominates in Antananarivo. In fact, the vulnerability of the resource also includes issues of transport and storage, and in particular that of water handling in the domestic sphere which can contaminate water and damage health (Dos Santos, 2005; Lavie and Hassan El-Tayib, 2014; Amrose et al., 2015). Access to water resources can be analyzed here as an indicator of urban vulnerability in Antananarivo since it is one of the essential components and a good of the urban environment (D’Ercole and Metzger, 2008; Reghezza and Ruffat, 2015). This vital good that is domesticated water acquires an ambivalent status of threatened and threatening resource. It is a complex issue linking health and the urban environment. The study of the territorial vulnerability of the Malagasy capital with regard to water resources is illustrated here through fragile spaces, namely neighborhoods with high densities and precarious forms of housing and in which are found the people who count the least in social representations and where research needs are found (figure 1). By placing these fragile ecosystems at the heart of the analysis through the prism of the concepts of risk and vulnerability, our hypothesis is that safe water from source to consumption should be considered as a chain system (Burt and Ray, 2014; Amrose et al., 2015). Thus, we seek to determine all the interventions that could deteriorate access to drinking water in quantity and quality in these districts of the capital. This amounts to approaching the question of the security of water supply in quantity and quality. Production: Ognard, 2018 2The analysis begins by drawing up a picture of the theme of water shortage in cities in the South and its reality in the Malagasy capital. We then argue that a holistic approach is needed to address the multiple domains that influence health status in an urban environment context where the deficiency of urban services such as access to water is evident. 3Safe drinking water is essential for a healthy and dignified life and has been recognized as a right by the UN (UN, 2010). Yet in the Global South, many do not have access to running water.te, and of those who do have access, many receive water of questionable quality. There are many biological and chemical contaminants in drinking water and we limit the scope of this article to physical and microbial contamination. Microbial contamination is by far the greatest hazard to drinking water in the Global South. At least 1.8 billion people lack access to reliable drinking water (Onda et al., 2012). Nearly 1,000 child deaths per day result from diarrheal diseases caused by unsafe water, poor sanitation, and poor hygiene (WHO, 2014; Taglioni, 2019). Safe water systems from source to consumption have been conceptualized as a series of steps including treatment technologies, distribution models, and pre-consumer transport and storage practices as they jointly determine the safety of water prior to consumption (Amrose et al., 2015). However, in the literature, quantity and quality security of supply are often treated separately. There are articles focusing on networks through questions of quantity access while household approaches focus on water quality and health impacts. 4WHO considers access to piped water in the dwelling, plot or yard as the most improved form of access. Globally, 56% of the population had access to piped water in 2012 (WHO, 2014). In addition to access to piped water, public standpipes, wells and protected water sources are also classified as improved. Globally, 33% of the population had access to it in 2012 (WHO, 2014). The abundant literature on the efficiency of public water distribution services in the Global South is mainly focused on the volumes delivered. Because if the assessment of the security of water supply first considers its availability (Falkenmark, 1989; Bravard and Honnegger, 2006; Jemmali, 2013), the water crisis in cities in the Global South is no less a problem of shortage than an “infrastructure shortage” (Lavie and Hassan El-Tayib, 2014; Lavie et al., 2015). Indeed, most city dwellers are not served by running water supply systems, but the reality is far from uniform (Bromley, 1978). It presents itself as a hybrid model of superimposed supply strategies (Bakker, 2003). Far from a simplistic dual vision between artisanal and industrial supply modes, Bakker argues that this "archipelago" of formal and informal services coexists because the formal system is spatially unequal (Bakker, 2003). Indeed, where the level of infrastructure is deficient, informal supply modes dominate. However, these urban services were originally theorized as means of ensuring social and territorial equity because such systems are commonly considered prerequisites for modern urban life. Jaglin thus identified the failure of this universalist model of service expansion with the questioning of public monopolies as well as recent experiences of public-private partnership (Jaglin, 2005). Several authors agree that the nature of the problem is above all political (Jaglin, 2005; Blanchon, 2010; Aubriot and Riaux, 2013; Burt and Ray, 2014; Ginisty, 2014; Lavie et al., 2015). These regulatory and governance failures reflect the “depoliticization of power relations in societies” (Jaglin and Zérah, 2010). “The propensity to achieve the universalist model is primarily a matter of the ability to build national interest and inclusion in fragmented societies,” which is difficult to implement in fragile contexts in countries of the South. Urban informality has been conceptualizedlized as “an urban lifestyle” and “a set of survival strategies by the poor” (De Soto, 2000) and a “form of resistance to urban elites” (Bayat, 2000). The analysis under the prism of the concept of risk seems appropriate here. Vulnerability is not only a propensity to suffer damage but also includes a capacity to cause it, to modify it (Reghezza-Zitt and Ruffat, 2015). Depending on the estimate of the danger and the priorities of action, certain risks will become materialized and from there, politicized; unlike certain others which will remain forgotten, sometimes intentionally. Each human group, by defining a social order, itself a producer of hierarchy, reveals the choice of risks to be feared, of issues which appear as “what one is prepared to lose” (Metzgler and D’Ercole, 2009). 5Also, any household without access to running water must transport and store its drinking water. If the water is safe at the point of access, safe storage can provide some protection against contamination at home. This brings us to the question of practices. Despite a large bibliography on the management, practices and access to water in African cities (Dos Santos, 2005; Jaglin, 2005; Blanchon, 2010; Burt and Ray, 2014; Ginisty, 2014), it is rare to have a reference on the physical, chemical and biological qualities of this consumed water (Amrose et al., 2015). They often take the form of hydro-chemical monitoring. The rare exceptions of joint consideration of hydro-chemical monitoring, social and management practices concern the work of Nguimalet et al. (2005) conducting a systemic study combining hydro-qualitative diagnosis and analysis of drinking water management in the city of Bangui in the Central African Republic and the work of Emilie Lavie and Noha Hassan El-Tayib, focusing on storage practices that are responsible for a significant decline in the physical and biological quality of water in the city of Khartoum and an impact on water-borne diseases (Lavie and Hassan El-Tayib, 2014). 6To integrate these two dimensions of quantity and quality, we borrow here from the conceptual model “from source to sip” (Amrose et al., 2015). All safe drinking water systems have five stages that start at the water source and end at the point of consumption: the source, transport and storage at the source, a public or private access point, transport and storage (and sometimes treatment) beyond the access point, and consumption. Treatment before access must be implemented by public services. In the countries of the South, water is transported first through pipes and then from collective water points using buckets, barrels, carts and trucks. After collection, treatment can be carried out by the household. By following the path of water from the catchment to the household, all the steps determine the efficiency of the system. The organization of networks is not only reduced to that of a technical system but interferes in the social and spatial organization of the city. They are both vulnerable to risks and propagators of disturbances, because of their interdependencies (Hardy, 2009; Reghezza-Zitt, Rufat, 2015). Vulnerability refers to the idea that within any territory there are localizable elements that are likely to generate or spread their vulnerability throughout their territory, causing effects that can disrupt, compromise or even interrupt its functioning (Metzger and D’Ercole, 2011). In this logic, territorial vulnerability analysis aims primarily to identify, characterize and prioritize the spaces from which vulnerability is created and spread within the territory. IThere are two types of vulnerability of these supplies (Hardy, 2009). First, it is linear. Indeed, water and sanitation networks depend on operation as a system from upstream to downstream. A disruption in one of the links can cause a crisis in the entire system. At the same time, the vulnerability of supplies is transversal because most of these infrastructures interact. The loss of supply or sanitation can cause other problems in the functioning of the urban system. Technical and critical networks are strategic elements of urban resilience. Indeed, by assessing the capacity of networks to operate in degraded mode, we can identify possible malfunctions and the spread of harmful effects. Samuel Rufat defines shanty towns as the territories closest to the definition of the resilient city because they are capable of "operating in a degraded state" or because they facilitate "rapid reconstruction" (Ruffat, 2015). For him, it is in these territories that disasters are most often found. Far from enthusiastic speeches, this "poor resilience is passed over in silence but constitutes the ordinary of urban disasters. It is as if invisible because it is the daily life of the inhabitants of the ordinary city side and of DIY in the face of adversity more than of the spectacular side of crises and disasters" (Rufat, 2015). Thus, informal neighborhoods or shanty towns far from the viability networks are intrinsically the structure that can function the most in a degraded state. In Anglo-Saxon literature, we find this idea through the Bayat model which, going beyond the disagreements between the "passive coying" and the "active resistance" paradigm, affirms that informal services are those of the "silent encroachment of the ordinary" by which poor populations without noise and without fury bypass the ordinary channels of urban services (Bayat, 2000; De Soto, 2000). 7In the Malagasy capital, residents access the resource in two ways: the pipeline supply network that supplies both individuals and the city's mainly public standpipes and the rare wells observed (Figure 2). However, the capital is supplied with water from a single production site, located in Mandroseza, to the southeast of the city, on the northwest edge of the lake also called Mandroseza (Figure 3). This lake, originally natural, is fed by the Ikopa River which bypasses the city to the south. The construction of the Tana-Côte Est railway line in 1909 had put in place the dike on the right bank of the Ikopa. This dike forms the water retention on the marshy site. And the water filling of the area forms Lake Mandroseza, which has a surface area of ​​approximately 47 ha with an average depth of 2.5 m and provides a storage volume of 1.2 million m3 (Chardon, 1996). It is therefore on this site that the Mandroseza I and Mandroseza II facilities are concentrated. Built as the population's needs grew, the first production facilities dating from the beginning of the century and the most recent one, commissioned in 1993, attest to the dilapidated state of the infrastructure (Chardon, 1996). In total, the Mandroseza site could therefore produce at its maximum capacity, nearly 150,000 m3 of treated water per day. Given the obsolescence of the drinking water production, delivery and distribution system, the system distributes 140,500 m3 per day and only supplies 33 of the population of the CUA and 14 of the periphery with individual connections (ARTELIA, 2014). To function, a system needs the previous links, each element of the system depends on the one located upstream. Also, in terms of security of supply, the capital appearsas vulnerable in consideration of the city’s sole supply site. As such, a simulation of a pollution risk was potentially considered by the CUA (CUA, 2014) according to two distinct scenarios: that of the derailment of a train transporting chemicals or fuel, or deliberate poisoning in Mandroseza. In the event of contamination of Lake Mandroseza, the water stored in the city’s 37 water reservoirs, with its 150,000 m3, will only be able to provide one day of supply. However unlikely the occurrence of such events may be, this simulation nevertheless marks an awareness of the “linear vulnerability” of this supply, i.e. of an upstream-downstream operation. Contrairement à la plupart des risques sanitaires, les risques hydriques développent une originalité compte tenu de leur autre dimension, la dimension environnementale. Objets complexes à l’interface santé/environnement, ils iquestion the methodology and present a multidimensional vocation. We argue that a multidimensional approach highlighting the interdependencies between the political, the social, the technical and the microbiological contamination of drinking water, can help us understand both the unequal distribution of the quantity and the quality of water (Aubriot and Riaux, 2013; Sy and Moussa, 2014; Amrose et al., 2015). This is all the more true since we are in a territory that experiences iterative and multifaceted crises and where access to data is difficult (Fremigacci, 2014; Razafindrakoto et al., 2014; Roubaud, 2017). Methodologically, this involves combining quantitative and qualitative approaches with methods for quantifying material water flows and assessing microbiological contamination (Rusca et al., 2017). Geography, as a discipline that synthesizes related sciences, finds a fertile field of application here at the environment-health interface, particularly in the case of waterborne infectious risks. This approach is intended to be holistic in order to address the multiple areas that influence health status. 10Antananarivo is located in the central highlands of Madagascar at an altitude of 1,300 m. The city is nestled among 12 hills and is located on the natural floodplain of the Ikopa River, which runs along the city to the south and west. The metropolitan area covers 220 km2 with an estimated population of 1.5 million inhabitants. The administrative unit on which this research focuses is that of the fokontany, a basic administrative unit in Madagascar, significantly modeled on the village model (Fournet-Guérin, 2006); Antananarivo has 192. In a comparative approach, two fokontany per district were selected, the CUA having 6, or 12 fokontany (figure 1). 11It quickly became apparent in the context of this research that the Antananarivo territory can be described as "rough" in view of the many difficulties encountered. First of all, faced with the climate of multifaceted and iterative crisis that characterizes Madagascar and Antananarivo, access to the field had to be constantly negotiated, that is to say always constrained by several administrative obstacles and in fact the results are not always as fruitful as expected. Indeed, the vertical structure of power, specific to this type of territory, means that it is always essential to have the approval of the higher-level manager to carry out surveys and interviews. Since its independence, Madagascar has shown an economic trajectory in continuous recession. Ultimately, these crises follow one another to form a single structural crisis of the postcolonial state (Fremigacci, 2014). This "enigma" of the cyclicality of crises and the "paradox" of their interweaving between growth and politics show a growing gap between elites and local populations (Razafindrakoto et al., 2014; Roubaud, 2017). In fact, research in Madagascar and Antananarivo is hampered by the quality of the data given the available statistics biased by the age of the census. This dates back to 1993 and the data obtained at that time no longer correspond to reality. The census data disseminated by the National Institute of Statistics (INSTAT) since 2003 are mostly extrapolated with a growth rate of 2.5%. Faced with this lack of reliability of statistical data (Razafindrakoto et al., 2014; Roubaud, 2017), it seemed essential to us to develop our own surveys under various dimensions to approach local reality as closely as possible, thus highlighting the importance and centrality of field work. Moreover, this local reality quickly came up against our Western reference framework and its benchmarks. For examplethe, in the same habitat can coexist several heads of households and therefore several households (more than 44 of the households are composed of 5 individuals and more than 2/3 composed of more than 2 children, each household owns or rents in the house one to two rooms: the kitchen and sanitary facilities are at best communal and at worst non-existent). 12This research is the result of a doctorate carried out between 2011 and 2018, with five missions distributed according to the following table (table 2). The last 4 missions aimed to carry out different surveys to cover the various questions of this interface subject, hence the composite nature of the data collected. They are both quantitative and qualitative. According to our first 50 respondents, the vast majority live below the poverty line, i.e. on less than one euro per day. For the others (n = 250), this question concerning the standard of living was deliberately omitted as it constituted a real obstacle for the respondents to continue the survey and thus called into question the survey itself. References to origins were not addressed. However, it should be noted that only 34 of the respondents said they had lived in Antananarivo for less than ten years. 14Then, 22 interviews were conducted with focus groups of water professionals. These key informants are an important link in the water distribution chain in African countries because they are closest to the daily lives of residents (managers, BF managers, street vendors). Of these 22, 10 were conducted with participants in an AFHy (Women's Hygiene Promotion Association) belonging to the EAST NGO network. This association offers daily hygiene awareness actions, model actions for cleaning and beautifying neighborhoods (cleaning alleys, collecting and disposing of garbage, beautifying by planting flowers, role of empowerment and integration of women in neighborhood life). 1515 semi-directive interviews focused on health structures and health personnel were conducted (head doctors of the 12 public CSBs, 3 doctors from the CHU, 1 from the BMH, 3 neighborhood doctors, 1 midwife from a public CSB). This network of respondents was used to collect quantitative data that are used for statistical analyses (ACP and CAH). 16Finally, 15 samples taken for potability analysis complete this picture: 10 at standpipes, 1 in a spring, 4 from users including 2 in eateries and 2 in households complete this picture. These analyses were carried out at the only authorized laboratory in Antananarivo, the Pasteur Institute. Two series of analysis results, commissioned by the Malagasy water distribution company JIRAMA, provide some additional information. Even if, here again, the exploitation of the data is limited due to their nature. The first series carried out at the point of production and supply of drinking water only identifies the physical parameters of the water at the lake level (raw resource), then at the MI and MII outlets (i.e. after treatment by the plant). The second series at the standpipes only presents an incomplete view since the practice of drawing lots does not allow for a long-term analysis (between ten and thirty standpipes each time different). 17We carried out an analysis of the drinking water supply system in its 5 stages according to the previously defined model. Our diagnosis establishes in the context of the precarious and dense neighborhoods of the capital that the water resource is both threatened and threatening in terms of both quantity and quality. 18From a quantitative point of view, our results obtained in these neighborhoods contrast with the data collected at the CUA scale by ARTELIA. Only 8 households claim to be connected to the distribution network, far from the 33 announced by the World Bank and the 53 by the SDAU (World Bank, 2011; ARTELIA, 2014). The standpipe appears in the descriptions given by the respondents as a major public place in the daily life of the people of Antananarivo. Thus, waiting times at the standpipes can be relatively long, as symbolized by the long chain of cans (over 30 minutes on average and up to twohours in some fokontany) (Figure 4). As a result, transport and storage practices dominate (92 of those surveyed). Transport is mainly carried out in jerrycans or buckets of water. As in most African countries (Jaglin, 2005; Ginisty, 2014), the task of collection most often falls to women and children, leading to a specific daily and family organization (Ognard, 2018). To compensate for the public service deficit (Jaglin, 2005; Blanchon, 2006; Burt and Ray, 2014), alternatives are organized around the resale of water. Water carriers (‘mpatsaka’ rano) play an important role in water supply, particularly in neighborhoods that are difficult to access. This service offered around standpipes is adapted to a heterogeneous clientele composed of families with middle or low incomes. This service is on average more expensive than at the standpipe, the 20-liter can being purchased at 1 Ar./l and resold for between 50 Ar. (in Antetezana Afavoany). The other form of water resale is that of individuals. If this form of resale can be integrated into family solidarity strategies, it most often falls under market strategies as in Mandrangobato where the price charged is roughly the same as that applied at standpipes (1 to 2 Ar. per liter). Overall, these various strategies attest on the one hand to the diversity of situations of poor connection and in fact to urban adaptation with an “informal service industry” (Jaglin and Zérah, 2010). The level of water consumption is another indicator of social inequalities in relation to access to water. The procedures manual of the Malagasy Ministry of Energy and Mines gives the standard as 30 liters/person/day when the WHO average ranges between 20 and 50 liters/person/day. Again, the results of our surveys contrast with those of ARTELIA where the average consumption observed is 32 liters/person/day. According to our surveys, 13 households live with less than 40 liters per day per household, 38 with 40 to 80 liters per day per household, 15 with 80 to 120 liters per household and 25 with more than 120 liters per household. These situations of poor connection contribute to differentiations in the daily organization of families, thus contributing to forging differentiated lifestyles within the capital (Ognard, 2018). Figure 4 – Congestion at the Mandroganbato I standpipe Source: Ognard, 2018. 19From a qualitative point of view, microbiological analyses of the water distributed show contamination of fecal origin with the presence of coliforms at a proportion that exceeds the maximum acceptable concentration of less than one coliform per 100 ml for human consumption without health risk. This contamination was noted at 7 sites out of the 15 taken with a concentration of Escherichia coli varying from 8 to 13 coliforms/liter depending on the location and a concentration of 25 to more than 100 for intestinal enterococci. These 7 non-compliant samples therefore show significant bacteriological contamination of the quality of the water consumed. Contamination by both Escherichia coli germs and intestinal enterococci defines situations of fecal danger to which populations are subjected. 20However, the physical parameters remain compliant with the regulations. These data are partly consistent with the results of the JIRAMA analysis series. At the production site, over the 4 years (2009 to 2014) listed, only 3 physical pollution events were identified. They took place on 01/27/2009, 12/30/2009 and 03/05/2012. The parameter in question is turbidity, which is greater than 5 NTU and makes the water slightly cloudy. The main associated risk isthen the increase in the transport capacity of microorganisms that harm disinfection. At the standpipe level, for the years 2013 and 2014, this disinfection system is incriminated. Turbidity is high in 39 samples out of the 508 taken over the two years. Note that this parameter is not taken into account by JIRAMA as a factor of water conformity since these samples were declared compliant with the standard, even though the threshold of 5 NTU, defined by Malagasy law and WHO recommendations, is exceeded here. This dissension between the distribution point and the collection point questions the role played by transport and pipelines. 21In addition, the different supply methods, i.e. the nature of the source, are also taken into account in assessing the risk and the level of contamination of the distributed water. The only source analyzed in Manjakaray appears to be contaminated by enterococci, implicating the supply from an unimproved source. 22Two out of four samples taken from households show contamination of bacteriological origin. Here again, the source of the sample is interesting. The two healthy samples were taken from taverns, while the contaminated ones were taken from households. The storage time and the container may be implicated. According to our surveys, taverns regularly renew their water supply, which is not necessarily the case for households. Furthermore, the absence of alteration of the physical quality of the water suggests that handling and hygiene conditions are the cause here. Some have shown an awareness of the impact of their handling on water quality by stating that they use a disinfectant, Sur’Eau (14 of those surveyed). Tsiny in Anatihazo thus declares "the water is drinkable because I use Sur'Eau to be sure". Conversely, still in Anatihazo, Jacqueline denigrates the quality of the water by stating that the water is not drinkable and that she "must add Sur'Eau". However, we received a lot of feedback on the difficulty of obtaining the treatment solution in accordance with the observations in the bibliographic references (Dunston et al., 2001). 23Given the small spatial footprint of our analyses, this experience is not representative of the entire agglomeration but allows us to identify certain trends in terms of water quality and population practices. 24The disruptions that deteriorate access in quantity and quality are concentrated around transport issues: at the CUA scale, at the level of the pipes but also at the individual scale through transport and storage practices. 25At the same time, the lack of a functioning sanitation system leads a large part of the population to evacuate household wastewater inadequately, promoting a health risk (figure 5). 80% of respondents thus discharge their wastewater (cooking, dishes, laundry) into the open air. Connection to the sewer system only concerns a minority (7%). This data can be supplemented by the sanitary equipment: the lost pit (rudimentary local technique with a simple hole) is the most widespread method. Latrines are most often located outside and are shared by several families (72% of responses). It should be noted that certain practices such as defecation "in the open air" can increase the health risk. The "faecal hazard" remains a sensitive issue in these neighborhoods. This analysis can be corroborated by the failures of the JIRAMA waste collection system already mentioned in the work Antananarivo and itsgarbage (Raharinjanahary, 2011) with a lack of bins, personnel and garbage trucks (478 garbage bins per 1 million inhabitants). The practices of illegal dumping as evidenced by the number of blocked canals in the city or the practices of incineration and dumping in the yard (23) of waste, only accentuate the problem. Indeed, Ikopa is the only collector of all liquid waste returned downstream of the city of Antananarivo. It receives without any treatment the urban effluents coming from the pumping station of the 67 ha at the level of Antopenaka, the waste materials transported by truck to the site of Ambohitrimanjaka and the polluted waters of the Andriantany canal at the level of the village of Andriantany (ARTELIA, 2014). The environmental and health quality of the water from these effluents appears to be compromised. It was assessed at the scale of the Urban Municipality of Antananarivo (CUA), thanks to the two water sampling campaigns on the Ikopa carried out in 2008 and 2013 (ARTELIA, 2014). During these studies, the uses of the Ikopa (washing powder, bricks, sand, dam) as well as the discharges of effluents into the watercourse (municipal discharges and industrial discharges) were inventoried, and a campaign of sampling and water analyses was carried out. Through these studies on the main characteristics of the Ikopa River, the resource appears to be of relatively good quality at the level of the Mandroseza water intake, even if it receives polluted effluents upstream, particularly industrial and domestic (at the Ambohimanambola thermal power plant). Figure 5 – Photograph of an open-air canal used as a garbage receptacle in Mandroganbato I Source: Ognard, 2018. 26The diachronic analysis shows a deterioration in the quality of the Ikopa River over the 5 years between 2008 and 2013. It is described as poor for most sampling sites with pH criteria below 5.5 and above 9.5, conductivity between 500 and 3,000 μS/cm, and temperature between 30 and 35°C. The most telling indicator of this deterioration in the quality of the Ikopa is the dissolved oxygen concentration in the watercourse with levels between 2 and 3 mg/l. In addition, changes in overall water consumption directly affect the total quantity of wastewater production. With wastewater production estimated at 80% of the water consumed, the total quantity of wastewater produced in the study area is 1 m3/s in 2013. If the objectives of improving access to drinking water are met, this production will double in 2015 (2 m3/s) and will reach 3.2 m3/s in 2025. As the study area is drained by the Ikopa River hydrographic network, the confrontation of these flows with the low water flows of this river, which can drop to less than 5 m3/s at Ambohitrimanjaka, can increasingly weaken the resource and the neighborhoods in the flood plain. By highlighting the interweaving of sanitation networks with those of water supply, it is not only a question of questioning the poor management of wastewater (ARTELIA, 2014) but of identifying the interdependence of these networks which plays an important role in the degradation of the urban environment. We speak of "transverse vulnerability" (Hardy, 2009). It is transcribed in the epidemiological profile of the Malagasy capital. According to epidemiological studies, incidence is the best way to understand the evolution of diseases in a given population (Vaughan and Morrow, 1991; WHO, 1994). However, the evaluation of this index is not possible in this case study given the variability and unreliability of demographic statistical data. The study is therefore based on prevalence, which is the main indicator of the morbidity, based on the total number of diseases observed in a given population at a specific time. The statistical study presented here was carried out using morbidity data diagnosed by the public Basic Health Centers (CSB) of the Urban Municipality of Antananarivo (15 in total), the coherence of which seems more plausible to us than the mortality data provided by the Ministry. Firstly, since it was not possible to assess the incidence of waterborne diseases, a diachronic approach was carried out using semi-logarithmic graphs to establish the evolution of the morbid phenomenon (Figure 6). The graphs highlight growth rates for respiratory diseases and other diseases that seem to behave like the total growth rate. Thus, the existence of straight lines indicates constant growth rates. In addition, the three straight line segments are close and parallel. These correspond to identical growth rates. The two pathologies (respiratory diseases and other diseases) therefore strongly influence the evolution of the pathological distribution of Antananarivo. A second group of pathologies stands out: diarrheal diseases, digestive and skin diseases. Their growth rates present substantially similar profiles with straight line segments that experience small variations from 10 to -10 . This second group therefore highlights the fragility of the Malagasy capital with regard to water-related health risks in particular. These results lead to the statement, based only on diagnosed morbidity, that the health status, by identifying the weight of respiratory diseases and diarrheal diseases, perfectly corroborates a situation of insalubrity and precariousness in many districts of the city of Antananarivo. Figure 6 – Pathological evolution from 2010 to 2013 of 3 public CSBs Source: Isotry central CSB, 2010-2013. Production: Ognard, 2018. 27Jointly, a principal component analysis (PCA) and an ascending hierarchical classification (HAC) were carried out based on the morbidity results of the 12 public CSBs in the capital (figures 7 and 8). These results transcribe a geographical partition of the urban space of Antananarivo (figure 9). The Urban Commune of Antananarivo appears split in two, between an East with relatively favoured health conditions in a developing country city context (the dominant “other diseases” variable) and a West characterised by an average profile (where no disease appears to be predominant). At the intersection of these two groups, Isotry central, a district identified as precarious, crystallises the pathologies characteristic of developing countries: hygienic diseases with the predominance of diarrhoeal, respiratory and digestive diseases. Figure 7 – Factorial axes 1 and 2 of the principal component analysis Source: CSB central d’Isotry, 2010-2013. Production: Ognard, 2018. Figure 8 – Dendrogram of the hierarchical ascending classification Source: Ognard, 2018. Figure 9 – The geographical and health partition of the urban commune of Antananarivo according to the hierarchical ascending classification Source: CSB central d’Isotry, 2010-2013. Production: Ognard, 2018. 28This double linear and transversal vulnerability of the water resource of the Malagasy capital therefore attests to a fragmentation of the urban space of Antananarivo. If Al Dabaghy (2014) has already noted the potential of “transactional political resource of water”In Diego Suarez, this double vulnerability of water resources in the Malagasy capital is in reality a reflection of tensions between at least two actors: the elites and the population, particularly the poorest categories. It raises the question of the governance of water resources in this territory. 29Indeed, the Ikopa is both the only source of drinking water for the entire Antananarivo urban area, the main source of irrigation for the Betsimitatatra plain and also the only collector of all the nuisances returned downstream of the city of Antananarivo. The preservation of the Ikopa's water resources is compromised by its ambivalent status as a source and an effluent. Indeed, if it constitutes the main source of supply for the Malagasy capital, the absence of wastewater treatment in the small water cycle is a source of dangers, particularly health-related, for the entire CUA but in particular for precarious neighborhoods such as Isotry Central. These risks are particularly significant during the rainy and cyclonic seasons when the intra-muros lowlands mainly located to the west of the capital experience an overflow of open-air sewer channels. Water resources become an instrument of territorialization of the Malagasy capital where informal services become essential. Indeed, the lack of recognition and supervision of the latter is another example of this desire to compartmentalize these territories and an institutional attachment to an unsuitable universal model. Because this unsuitability is the result of a long historical process of network creation where successive policies have oscillated between efficiency and equity. Antananarivo has never truly experienced the golden age of integrated and integrating public service networks during which their universalization should have been achieved. As early as 1945, a break with the ecological balance was marked by the occupation of the major bed of the Ikopa with the creation of the districts of Ampefiloha and Ambodin'isotry (west of Lake Anosy) with functions now well distributed between the "upper" city, which became a place of residence for the wealthy, and the "lower city" which became a place of commerce, leisure and housing for the poorest populations (Asinome, 2006). This marginalization leads to the creation of social and urban fractures that are maintained over time as here with access to public services. Similarly, in terms of health, the dichotomy of the urban landscape resulting from statistical analyses corresponds to that operated in the Malagasy mentality between this East on the heights long highlighted by the Malagasy and this West characterized by this flood plain situation (behind the dike) (Fournet-Guérin, 2006). We can therefore say here that the "health territory" seems strongly imbued with representations and therefore with the "lived territory" (Fleuret, 2015). However, if the health profile identified for the East confirms its privileged status within the urban commune, the average profile identified for the West nuances and attenuates the stigmatization of this part of the territory. Only Isotry central stands out through this mapping as a "low district" in the sense understood by the Malagasy imagination (both socially and geographically). However, the Isotry central CSB plays a particular role in the health map. It coordinates and centralizes all the CSBs in the urban commune. This district offers both a better healthcare offer and also an accessible position. This could therefore explain its preponderant weight. 30At the individual level, the alteration of the quality of water produced by manipulations in the domestic sphere generates health risks for users who are both victims and actors. They arevictims of a deficient system with low access in quantity. But these marginalized populations have managed to put strategies in place with the establishment of other choices to compensate for public services. Private actions appear to be predominant and can be integrated as "coping strategies". These strategies thus make the city "habitable" for the poorest city dwellers (Jaglin, 2005). Traveling to fetch water, drawing it, carrying it in plastic containers placed on the head or carried at arm's length are acts that are repeated several times a day. It is then the notion of resilience and in particular the individual's capacity for response that we are interested in. This dimension is interesting because by placing ourselves at the level of individuals, we assume that they have a certain latitude in their choices and integrate hazards into their decisions. The strategies adopted by agents depend on their perception of the risks they face and the resources they are able to mobilize. Decision-making is accompanied by a trade-off in resources between the short and medium term according to the risk perceived and experienced. These decisions are made in a context of uncertainty according to the information available to them. Here, natural threats are not only perceived and experienced based on the representation of their effects, they compete with other economic and social constraints which are relativized. All these strategies attest that urban or social risks (poverty, poor housing) appear more significant than natural risks (floods) and health risks (risks of waterborne diseases and hygiene). The issues surrounding values, types of individuals, family types are therefore raised in the assessment of the perception of risks and therefore of a multitude of inequalities in the face of risks. In Antananarivo, particularly in the districts surveyed in the plains, people are aware of the risk, but a sort of resignation is confirmed due to lack of means. Thus, a couple in Isotry explained that they dumped their waste on their doorstep or nearby in the district because they "have no other choice". They are aware that this practice potentially harms their health, particularly when the water level rises during floods. We are witnessing an acceptance of the risk and the development of original practices that contribute to urban manufacturing, "urban DIY". 31The analysis of the drinking water system in these 5 stages made it possible to identify a double vulnerability of the supply of water resources, both "linear" and "transversal" in the Malagasy capital. The safe drinking water system directly questions the role of transport, not only at the level of pipes but especially through resale practices and domestic manipulations since the supply of populations is mainly done at standpipes. If these "coping strategies" allow the integration of the poorest populations in the legal city, they highlight the socio-spatial fragmentation of the Malagasy capital. At the same time, the institutional attachment to an unsuitable universal model with the persistence of an ambivalent status of the Ikopa as both source and effluent, participates in the creation of risk and a laissez-faire by the authorities of the compartmentalization of the most fragile territories of the capital. This vital good that is the water resource is thus instrumentalized and territorialized.

title: Montreal major polluter of St. Lawrence as E. coli plumes ...
snippet: Oct 11, 2021 — High concentrations of E. coli bacteria colonies are entering the St. Lawrence River in the Montreal area and following the current as far as ...
trans_snippet: Oct 11, 2021 — High concentrations of E. coli bacteria colonies are entering the St. Lawrence River in the Montreal area and following the current as far as ...
text: High concentrations of E. coli bacteria colonies are entering the St. Lawrence River in the Montreal area and following the current as far as Lake Saint-Pierre and Trois-Rivières, a recent study found. "In Montreal, in some places, there's up to a million E. coli colonies per 100 milliliters of water. The current standard for swimming is 200 colonies per 100 milliliters," said François Guillemette. He's an associate professor of environmental sciences at the Université du Québec à Trois-Rivières who specializes in the ecology of the St. Lawrence. The study was conducted aboard the school's Lampsilis research vessel, and it found that Montreal is a major river polluter. That's because the city does only a preliminary treatment of sewage, removing the solids but not disinfecting the water before releasing it back into the river.  Flowing plumes of E. coli can lead to beach closures, as swimming in high concentrations of the bacteria can lead to serious illness.  But it's not just the E. coli that's of concern. The bacteria is usually an indicator that other microbial pathogens are present, Guillemette said. These microbes, which include bacteria and viruses, can cause different infections and diseases, he explained. "Swimming east is generally not recommended if you are downstream from the city of Montreal wastewater treatment plant outlet, as the concentrations are very high," said Guillemette. Swimming still safe in most areas However, that's not to say swimming isn't safe. "For the most part along the St. Lawrence, the water quality is really beautiful for bathing," said Sarah Dorner, a water quality expert and professor at Polytechnique Montréal. "But we definitely need to keep improving." Dorner has been involved in testing the water quality at the new beach in Montreal's borough of Verdun, and the city was careful to close it when the bacteria was present in the area, she said. Bacteria can be more readily found when the water levels rise, and near discharge points, she explained, but it moves with the current and will clear out with time. Like Guillemette, she says the concern is more about what else can be found around E. coli plumes. The Verdun Beach occasionally closes temporarily because bacteria is found in the water, but the pollution clears out quickly, says Sarah Dorner of Polytechnique Montréal. (Ryan Remiorz/The Canadian Press) "It does indicate the presence of fecal material, but most often there are other pathogens that we are more concerned about," Dorner said. Dorner says Montreal's administration is, like other municipalities along the river, pushing for more access to the St. Lawrence — taking advantage of the waterway's natural beauty. At the same time, those cities and towns are aware of the risks associated with swimming in contaminated water and that is why there is increasing effort to protect the river.  Montreal works to improve wastewater treatment The Jean-R.-Marcotte wastewater treatment plant located on the eastern tip of the island of Montreal treats all sanitary wastewater, including collected rainwater, said Audrey Gauthier, a spokesperson for the city.   On average, the station processes the equivalent of the Montreal Olympic Stadium's indoor volume each day, she said.   The station began operations in 1984, greatly improving water quality in the area, after decades of rapid population growth and poor wastewater management. The station uses an advanced process to reduce the presence of phosphorus and suspended particles in water, Gauthier said, noting it meets current environmental standards. Back in 2016, Montreal dumped nearly five billion litres of untreated water into the St. Lawrence River and Quebec City dumped millions more that same year. (Ivanoh Demers/Radio-Canada) "However, the city wishes to go even further to improve the quality of the water in the St. Lawrence River," she said. Montreal has been working to build an ozone disinfection unit for treated wastewater that will reduce the risks to human health while protecting wildlife and the environment, she said.  "This new plant will make it possible in particular to eliminate more than 99.99 per cent of fecal coliforms as well as a very large proportion of pathogenic bacteria, viruses and other pollutants, thus allowing the practise of aquatic sports more than a kilometre downstream of the river," Gauthier said.  Former mayor Gérald Tremblay first announced the city would disinfect its wastewater using ozone gas in 2008, but there have been some delays in the years since. The new facility, estimated to cost around $500 million, still won't be ready for another couple years. Until then, Dorner says people can swim in the river as long as it's not too close to the wastewater treatment plant. "I wouldn't want people to think the St. Lawrence is really polluted and they shouldn't go swimming," she said. However, she said, "it's important to have good monitoring and let people know where the water is good for swimming."

text: by admin | Mar 16, 2019 | Headlines The Department of Environment and Natural Resources in Region 7 shares the ultimate plan to deputize people in the communities to help enforce environmental laws especially on the Clean Water and the Ecological Solid Waste Management along the premise of better water quality and sustainable rivers in Bohol.  In the ongoing struggle to effect the necessary upgrade in the water quality of the Abatan River as the Provincial Environment and Natural Resources Office entry into the Rivers for Life 2019 award, DENR Regional Executive Director Gilbert Gonzales leaked the plan that would advance community and stakeholder empowerment in the environment advocacy.  Rivers for Life or Recognizing Individuals and Institutions towards Vibrant and Enhanced Rivers (RIVERS) for Life (RFL) Awards, is a regional and national competition among ten rivers in Central Visayas which the regional committee has picked owing to their being under the same category.  Ten Central Visayas rivers: Batuanon River in Mandaue, Bulacao River in Bulacao and Luyang River in Luyang Carmen, in Cebu, Abatan River in Cortes, Wahig River in Inabanga and Manaba River in Garcia Hernandez in Bohol, Banica River in Valencia, Panam-angan River in Bais and Sicopong River in Santa Catalina in Negros Oriental as well as Señora River in Siqiijor have shown their waters contain coliform contamination but these are below 100 most probable number.  The goal is for the stakeholders in the region to help work to upgrade the water quality of these rivers in six months to make them safe for swimming, explains Bohol PENRO Charlie Fabre.  And as Bohol prepares for the second round of river clean ups this Friday, March 22, 2019, over 600 volunteers then collected some 2.5 tons of garbage from the stretch of the Abatan River to its estuaries in Cortes.  About 10 private organizations have also signed a memorandum of agreement with the DENR formalizing the adoption of several portions of the river where the collected garbage could have come from.  But for the volunteers to come and clean up the river in regular intervals is not sustainable, so that the DENR sees deputizing communities to enforce environmental laws as a better alternative.  Out to realize what DENR Secretary Roy Cimatu committed during the River Summit that the country would clean up all its rivers, the DENR uses the water quality as a parameter in testing the environment.   “All barangays along these rivers will be trained and deputized to enforce all environmental laws, or those which are applicable to the river,” DENR -7 RED Gonzales told the media in a press conference at the MetroCenter Hotel.   The move, according to Gonzales is because sustaining the clean-up can be a lot easier if communities help in managing solid waste, regulate the control of effluent discharge, put up the necessary and appropriate treatment of household sewage and the preferential option for fertilers that are less destructive. text: Save the American River Association Save the American River Association (SARA) is a grass roots non-profit organization founded in 1961 to spearhead the establishment of the American River Parkway — the "crown jewel" of the Sacramento County Park System — and adoption of the American River Parkway Plan 2008. Our mission is to protect and enhance the wildlife habitat, fishery, and recreational resources of the American River Parkway. Our volunteer, non-profit group of members and Board of Directors work to ensure that the American River Parkway will survive and prosper for the benefit of future generations. Current Land Related Issues  Current Water Related Issues  The water committee continues to meet with the Water Forum regarding outstanding technical issues on the latest proposed flow management standard. At the same time, SARA is still fighting efforts by water districts in the Sierra Nevada foothills to divert American River water and sell it to purveyors outside of the region. Enough water in the river is no help if the water is polluted. We have ongoing battles with the Central Valley Regional Water Quality Control Board over the issuing of sewer discharge permits that violate state and federal law. SARA continues to work with allied organizations to institute reforms in the way California's water is managed. The ongoing drought has focused attention on the unregulated use of ground water and reservoirs and the historical practice of allocating water that does not exist. We are engaged in raising serious objections to the proposed Delta tunnels as a water management strategy for California's future. LEARN MORE.
